events.title: Some Nvidia directors push to bring Huang back despite board opposition
events.summary: Despite Nvidia’s proclamation Tuesday that it didn’t plan to bring ousted CEO Jensen Huang back to the chipmaker, a faction of board members is pushing for his return, according to people familiar with the matter. Huang has met with a number of tech executives and spoken with at least one board member about the possibility of his return, the people said. The conversation with the director took place before the company’s earnings report and before Huang issued a public statement Tuesday that he’d be willing to return to the company if the board decides his return is in the “best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America,” Huang said. Hours later, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker wasn’t considering bringing Huang back and that the board had voted unanimously to accept his resignation. Spokespeople for Huang and Nvidia declined to comment. Despite the pushback from a minority of directors, other board members are starting to narrow the search for Huang’s replacement, some of the people familiar with the deliberations said. ARM CEO Rene Haas and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have both been considered, the people said. Haas has spoken to at least some Nvidia directors about taking the job, one of the people said, but he’s said he’s concerned about the optics of taking the job over calls to bring Huang back to the helm. Spokespeople for ARM and Marvell didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s also unclear whether Marvell’s Murphy would be able to take over as Nvidia’s CEO given the company is navigating a mega-merger with rival Lumentum.

events.title: LeBron James sues startup over viral AI ad allegedly exploiting his likeness
events.summary: The startup PlayVision allegedly used James’ AI-generated likeness and voice in an advertisement. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. James is seeking damages and an injunction against the PlayVision. NBA superstar LeBron James sued artificial intelligence-powered sports betting startup Bron and its two founders, accusing them of using his name, likeness and AI-generated voice without permission to promote their app. In a lawsuit filed Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, James accused PlayVision, which operates the Bron app, and co-founders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby of deliberately exploiting his "Bron" nickname to mislead consumers into believing he endorsed or was affiliated with the app. The complaint alleges that the startup released an AI-generated advertisement earlier this month depicting James in a basketball locker room, wearing a jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23, along with his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video showed the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app. James alleged that the defendants deliberately sought to provoke controversy to generate publicity for their app, with the advertisement attracting about one million views on X within a day. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." The NBA star's lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts and said it was working to change the app's name, according to the complaint. However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. Bron, operated by PlayVision, is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision is headquartered in California and participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch. — CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this story.

events.title: Intel cuts more jobs as CEO Lip-Bu Tan's efficiency push continues
events.summary: Intel just did another round of layoffs. Vernon Yuen/Nexpher Images via Getty Images Intel has laid off workers again, adding to a series of cuts this year. The job cuts add to a lengthy restructuring at the US chipmaker. Ongoing Intel restructuring has been focused on cutting management layers and refocusing projects. After a series of layoffs over the last two years, Intel has let workers go again in another round of cuts. The cuts are the latest sign that CEO Lip-Bu Tan's effort to make the chipmaker leaner is continuing into the final months of the year. This week, employees shared on social media about being affected by layoffs in Intel's global IT workforce. "As part of our broader strategy to become a more focused and efficient company, we continually assess our workforce to ensure priorities and resources are appropriately aligned," an Intel spokesperson said in a statement to Business Insider. Intel did not disclose how many employees were affected or identify the teams involved. The job cuts add to a lengthy restructuring at the US chipmaker, which has reduced its workforce and trimmed projects as it tries to revive its business after years of manufacturing setbacks and market share losses in AI chips. Intel has done several small rounds of layoffs this year. Tan, who became Intel's CEO last year, has said his restructuring plan was designed to lower expenses, reduce management layers, and shift resources away from lower-priority initiatives. Intel employed 81,100 people at the end of September, down from 85,100 at the end of 2025, according to company filings. Its headcount has fallen sharply since 2024, when Intel announced plans to cut more than 15,000 jobs, or about 15% of its workforce, under then-CEO Pat Gelsinger . events.title: Liberals' vote hits 25-year low as One Nation continues Tasmanian surge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmanian EMRS poll shows Labor, Liberals, One Nation in three-way battle, with health, cost of living biggest issues Despite a decline in the Liberals' fortunes, Jeremy Rockliff still came out on top as preferred premier. ( ABC News ) Labor, Liberals and One Nation are separated by just two points in the latest poll by EMRS. The Liberal vote is the lowest since 2001, while One Nation has climbed every quarter this year. A pollster says focusing on the cost of living and healthcare could help a party edge ahead. Labor, the Liberals and One Nation are locked in a three-way battle to be Tasmania's preferred party, with a pollster describing the situation as a "red hot mess". The latest polling by EMRS shows Labor has edged slightly ahead of the pack after being chosen by 25 per cent of responders, just ahead of the Liberals at 24 per cent and One Nation at 23 per cent. The polling firm's managing director, Brad Stansfield, said the results were all within the survey's margin of error of about 3 per cent, which suggested "any one of them could be in front next quarter". EMRS voting intentions, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) EMRS preferred premier, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) Cost of living and health dominated the results for major issues, which Mr Stansfield said could be driving the growth in support for both One Nation and Labor. While his party faltered, the state's premier, Jeremy Rockliff, saw his net favourability grow and he is still the preferred premier for 41 per cent of responders. However, support for Labor leader Josh Willie did rise to 33 per cent, which is his best result since taking the reins in August last year. It was Josh Willie's best result since taking over as leader. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) The poll results are produced through a survey of 1,000 people across Tasmania, with undecided voters excluded from results. Tasmanian brand Coal River Farm enters voluntary administration Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Multiple shots fired at Tasmanian home with person inside US tech billionaire flags interest in Hurricanes, Hobart stadium Liberals slide as One Nation surges Support for the Liberal government dropped two percentage points since August, with the November figure marking the party's lowest result in an EMRS poll since May 2001. Bridget Archer, the state's health minister, was asked about the findings at a press conference on Wednesday morning and said she would "leave the commentary to others". It's the first time Labor has been ahead of the Liberals since May last year, shortly before it called a no-confidence motion against the premier, resulting in a snap state election. Mr Stansfield said while the tight results showed Tasmanian politics was "a red hot mess right now", the Labor party would still be encouraged by the result, as it was "better to be ahead than behind". Cost of living was the most important issue for those polled. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) The popularity of One Nation has grown in every quarter since the party was first included in EMRS state polling in February this year, rising from 14 per cent to 23 per cent in nine months. Mr Stansfield, a former Liberal party adviser, said recent history, including the South Australian election and the Farrer by-election, showed poll numbers for One Nation had "tended to translate into votes". One Nation Tasmania marked the result with a post on social media, where it said it was "breathing down the necks" of the major state parties. Support for the Greens dropped slightly to 14 per cent, while independents were backed by 13 per cent of responders. Health came in at a close second. ( Pixabay : Engin_Akyurt ) Health, cost of living dominate issues vote When asked what the most important issue influencing their vote would be in a state election, 24 per cent of responders said the cost of living and 22 per cent said healthcare. There was a significant drop-off to the next most popular issue, which was government spending and the budget at 10 per cent. Some of the major topics which have dominated headlines in recent years were mentioned much less by responders, with just 6 per cent naming the Macquarie Point Stadium and 3 per cent saying data centres. The Macquarie Point stadium was not front of mind for respondents. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) Mr Stansfield said these results were "starker than normal" and showed issues dominating discussions in parliament may be "not of top line concern for voters".

events.title: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt
events.summary: Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: it revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday , up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies. The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year ; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year. But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor. Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic, OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications. It’s also become a big financier of the data center build out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio. The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earning call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm. Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate that she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies. “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital. events.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
events.summary: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have just as much to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as they do with slop software. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed. That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say. AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible. What they're saying : Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios. "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says. "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology." "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right." By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios. However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five. The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame. "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI." Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked. That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover. The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected. When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns. Go deeper: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool

events.title: Waymo is suspending highway operations — again
events.summary: Waymo previously suspended highway operations to address issues with navigating construction zones. Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images The California Department of Motor Vehicles suspended Waymo's freeway operations on November 11. The agency cited three incidents in which Waymo's robotaxis drove into construction zone closures. In May, Waymo self-suspended its freeway operations to address issues navigating construction zones. An issue keeps nagging at Waymo's robotaxi operations : The company's self-driving cars struggle to navigate highway construction zones. Now, California's vehicle regulatory agency has stepped in. In a statement to Business Insider on Tuesday, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said it was restricting Waymo from operating and testing on highways, citing three incidents in which Waymo's robotaxis "entered an active construction closure." The restriction took effect on November 11. The restriction will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the DMV that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the problems that prompted it. "The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026," a DMV spokesperson said. A Waymo spokesperson said that the recent incidents did not involve injuries or collisions and that, while the DMV order only limits freeway operations in California, the company will temporarily pause highway operations nationwide. "We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," the spokesperson said. As the DMV points out, the restrictions come several months after Waymo tried to address this exact issue. In May, Waymo said it self-suspended highway operations to improve how its autonomous cars behaved around construction zones. On July 29, Waymo announced that it was "gradually resuming" freeway routes. The company told TechCrunch at the time that it had implemented "software updates designed to improve the performance around freeway construction zones." The updates appeared insufficient to prevent the latest incidents. The DMV spokesperson cited two cases in which Waymo entered an active construction closure: one on November 5 when it entered a construction zone on US Route 101 near Burlingame, and another on November 6 involving California Highway Patrol vehicles. Waymo now has to provide evidence that it can detect construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations before it can resume freeway operations. events.title: Europe’s AI sector not ‘doom and gloom,’ but still lags
events.summary: Europe’s tech scene is still fighting the same battles that have held it back in the global AI race, leaders and CEOs from the continent said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the US, and to an extent China, are “radically in a different league” when it comes to scale and capital. Employing a soccer (or football) metaphor, he said those are the only two countries that are in AI’s Premier League, while the UK sits atop the Championship, the tier below. He’s “not happy enough” with that. Marco-Alexander Breit, director-general at Germany’s digital ministry, argued that Europe still needs more “innovation-friendly regulation” if it wants to compete. He said he agreed with most of the EU’s AI Act, but argued it “actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world.” Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak echoed some of the criticism, saying that “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, the continent is starting to figure out its niche: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch pointed to a rising need for cheaper, open-source, and sovereign AI — models that companies can run on their own premises, without relying on US models or exposing their data. Germany is leaning on its industrial base, with Breit pointing to the troves of data that manufacturers like Siemens and Bosch sit on. Narayan said the UK is looking to make inroads in inference chips and AI for drug discovery. “It’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” Breit said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? US president expected to meet with Chinese leader for third time this year; possible trilateral summit with Putin. United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year. list 1 of 3 What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair? list 2 of 3 US envoys and Putin agree to continue Russia-Ukraine peace talks list 3 of 3 China says US ‘fabricating’ Nvidia spy claims to justify tech ‘blockade’ The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs. Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large. The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next. “Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said. As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”. Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December. “The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement. As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology. In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks. Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry. Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”. “As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.” The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed. Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing. Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China. “Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne. Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart. Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”. The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi. China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.

events.title: Prosecutors allege man ‘destroyed’ US military plane at Irish airport
events.summary: Daithi O’Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight. An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”. An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians . “An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote. O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property. O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel. According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft. He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit. O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks. “As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement. “The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.” Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

events.title: Man charged over ‘brutal attack’ on Somali-American in Minnesota
events.summary: Rideshare driver Mohamed Yusuf is in a critical condition after he was allegedly assaulted by a passenger. A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”. Mohamed Yusuf suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma. list 1 of 3 ICE, Ilhan Omar and Somalis: Unpacking Trump’s obsession with Minnesota list 2 of 3 US border chief says Trump agrees to end deportation surge in Minnesota list 3 of 3 Somali intelligence helps US arrest alleged leader of Minnesota fraud “It was an incredibly brutal attack,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Tuesday. She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday. Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation. Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said. The court filing said Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1am on Saturday. His brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like the name Mohamed. “He was apparently pulled out of the car and was standing there when Patel drove over him and might have circled back and driven over him again,” Moriarty said. Patel’s parents called police for a wellness check after he arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior”, according to the court filing. When the officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show. Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was”, the filing says. Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging. Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, that it has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform. Rights advocates have raised concerns about rhetoric against Somali Americans by US President Donald Trump and his allies, and condemned his immigration crackdown in Minnesota . US rights advocates have also noted rising Islamophobia over the past two-plus decades following the September 11, 2001, attacks, and more recently due to anti-immigration policies, rising white supremacy movements and the fallout from Israel’s war on Gaza.

events.title: OpenAI bugging case defendant Alfozan set for trial in January
events.summary: A San Francisco federal judge set a Jan. 20 trial for Saudi national and former OpenAI engineering lead Abdulrahman Alfozan. Alfozan is accused of installing a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company. Alfozan's attorney wants to use an AI tool created by an OpenAI competitor to review evidence. Prosecutors are concerned about exposing proprietary OpenAI data if that is allowed. A federal judge on Tuesday set Jan. 20 for the start of the trial for Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan , who is accused of planting a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company as an engineering lead. If the trial starts on that date in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, it would be after an unusually short lag since Alfozan's arrest in October. Federal criminal cases, as a rule, do not go to trial so quickly. But Alfozan's attorney, David Rizk, sought the speedy trial after complaining at a court hearing that prosecutors have been slow in turning over evidence in the case. Rizk also said prosecutors have not given him any evidence that Alfozan engaged in espionage, after they argued successfully last month that he should be detained without bail , and after saying his alleged bugging "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." Among other things, prosecutors had noted that Alfozan is a venture partner at Saudi venture firm Raed Ventures alongside a member of the Saudi royal family, Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud . Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty in the case, is charged with one count of intercepting oral communications. He faces a maximum of five years in prison if he is convicted. Prosecutors have said Alfozan was arrested after staff at OpenAI found a recording device wrapped in toilet paper and installed in the back of a television in the conference room at its San Francisco headquarters in September. A surveillance camera captured Alfozan looking at the gadget in the room. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick Parker told Judge Vince Chhabria on Tuesday that government investigators have been locked out of Alfozan's phone, but they have also collected one other phone, a tablet, and two laptops. Prosecutors also obtained 160 hours of recordings from meetings in a conference room. The recording device itself is encrypted, but if data was backed up to another device, investigators would have been able to obtain it, Parker said. Chhabria told prosecutors that they must turn over all reports the FBI has created to Alfozan's attorney by Nov. 24, and that they must also move quickly to give the defense other evidence for use at trial. "We need to make sure that you get whatever discovery you're entitled to promptly," Chhabria told Rizk. OpenAI, which fired Alfozan after his arrest, has said it lacked proof of him taking source code or customer data. Chhabria also told Parker he wants to see, within seven days, any evidence that might exist showing Alfozan carrying out economic espionage, stealing trade secrets or acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Parker said he was not aware of any such evidence at this time. "At this point, I'm not suggesting the defendant stole anything," Parker said. The prosecutor told the judge that his team had a "serious concern" about Rizk's plans to review evidence turned over to the defense with an AI tool that competes with OpenAI. Parker noted that among the seized evidence is a laptop that might have proprietary OpenAI data. Chhabria replied, "I'm a lot less concerned about that than you are." The judge ordered Parker to submit a motion by Friday explaining why the defense's use of a competing AI to analyze evidence might be a problem. Rizk told CNBC he intends to use Anthropic's Claude. Anthropic, which aims to go public on Nasdaq this week, was founded by OpenAI employees. — CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report. events.title: Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
events.summary: The U.S. and Chinese presidents are expected to meet for a third time this year. Their summit comes alongside an APEC meeting in Shenzhen. That provides opportunities for meetings with leaders of Russia, Japan and other countries. SHENZHEN, China — Leaders of the U.S., China, Russia and other major Asia-Pacific economies face a series of critical issues from wars to tech security as they gather for an annual summit this week. Since the last APEC leaders' meeting, China's tensions with Japan have escalated . Barely stabilized U.S.-China relations face new tests in the wake of Washington's scrutiny of Nvidia 's China chip sales. And the Iran war , now in its ninth month, is still pressuring global energy prices, while the Russia-Ukraine war has dragged on. But expectations are low for any breakthroughs. Meanwhile for Beijing, host to this year's series of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings, the multilateral gathering is yet another venue to build its global influence. Chinese President Xi Jinping met Tuesday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the President of Vietnam To Lam . Vietnam is hosting next year's APEC meetings. Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen early Wednesday morning, where he was greeted by Chinese Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi, according to Chinese state media. U.S. President Donald Trump is in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit before heading to Shenzhen. Trump and Xi are expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting Wednesday and Thursday. Their summit around the gathering last year in South Korea ushered in a one-year trade truce of lower tariffs and some rare earths flows, which was extended by two months, to January 2027. In this week's summit, Trump does not plan to raise the issue of Nvidia and allegations that its former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, U.S. officials said. They said the talks would focus on implementing the trade agreement. The U.S. and China in September said they would lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from the other country, without specifying an effective date. China said this month that it would only increase purchases of U.S. agricultural products if those tariffs were lowered. However, Washington is already moving to tighten restrictions on loopholes that had given Chinese companies access to American artificial intelligence technology. So far, China's response has been to threaten countermeasures. "If there is room for genuine U.S.-China cooperation this week, it's on managing risk rather than sharing advantage," said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. That could include cooperation on an artificial intelligence security hotline. "Across Asia, governments under mounting pressure to pick a side will be watching Shenzhen for signs of how much room they still have to maneuver," Bhattacharya said. "Most have little appetite for a region split into two technology camps." On Thursday, Xi is set to meet with Trump and Putin, according to Beijing's official confirmation of the event, billed as the " China-Russia-U.S. Summit ." It's the first-ever gathering of the three leaders, albeit with low expectations that there will be sufficient time for thorough dialogue. But the event creates the opportunity for a globally influential photo-op similar to the one that Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had on the sidelines of a China-hosted Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in September 2025. Also closely watched will be any interaction with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Last November, her comments drew Beijing's ire after indicating Tokyo would support Taiwan if the island were seriously threatened by Beijing's military. Takaichi is expected to join the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in her first trip to China since becoming prime minister. She had met Xi on the sidelines of the APEC event last year in South Korea. Attendees from other APEC economies are hoping for more signs of cooperation. Anindya Bakrie, CEO of Indonesian conglomerate Bakrie & Brothers, told CNBC that when Trump and Xi meet, the narrative is hopefully one of peace and stability. Tech issues are likely to be in heavy focus. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is set to join Trump on the Shenzhen trip. Other American executives, such as Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, joined a two-day APEC CEO Summit that kicked off Tuesday. The APEC host city, Shenzhen, has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and is home to Huawei and BYD. The summit organizers are also using the event to showcase local robotics startups. A slew of tech company earnings is coming out at the same time as the APEC meeting, keeping the corporate side in the spotlight as well. Nvidia released quarterly results Wednesday morning Beijing time, following a tumultuous two weeks of scrutiny that forced the chipmaker's founder Jensen Huang to resign.

events.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang. In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit , interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this." The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China. "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period. Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader. "The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment." Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry. "It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us." She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects". "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this." The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China. The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US. Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped. He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection. "With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person." Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia. The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media. Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said. events.title: Nvidia’s tutorial on genuine good governance, needed by tech bros and governistas alike
events.summary: Charles de Gaulle said, “The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.” That rings especially true despite the pathetic cries of the ‘Bring Jensen Back’ bros. Nvidia’s strong earnings release today proves once and for all that Nvidia does not need Jensen Huang to return to flourish as a strong American national champion. Interim CEO Colette Kress deftly raised forecasts moving forward, pointing to the underlying strength of the business, which is far greater than any one individual, while winning plaudits for running the earnings call with command, presence, and impressive candor. And indeed, new board chair Harvey Jones definitely closed the door on Jensen Huang’s return as CEO amidst news that the SEC is now probing Huang and Nvidia. All this makes the unresolved governance questions and lessons from the Nvidia debacle even more important. In the aftermath of Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia this week, a tiny band of tech bros, perhaps intoxicated by their own sudden wealth and prominence, have cast good governance principles to the wind by unrealistically advocating for the return of Jensen Huang , decrying the “woke” politically correct management policies which they believe led to Huang’s exit. At the same time, a chorus of finger-pointing good governance advocates has joined the fray, throwing every pet theory of organizational structure and regulatory restraints on risk-seeking entrepreneurs. Both camps ignore the real collapse of board oversight, which is the tragically poor judgement of the CEO matched with the faulty character and faulty process of board oversight and not its clunky bureaucratic mechanics. The tech bro cheerleaders rooted for a messianic return of Huang, despite the ongoing investigations into his wide array of apparently corrupt actions and character collapses, such as his blatant violations of Nvidia’s code of conduct and unresolved national security concerns. The arrogant, naïve fantasies in the chants of these tech bros is encapsulated by Telegram founder Pavel Durov’s X post declaring, “ Jensen made a rookie mistake. He had a board ”, apparently forgetting that any executive who is entrusted with other people’s money owes a fiduciary duty to their shareholders first, above their own self-enrichment. They are happy to snag the money but then to dodge accountability. Then, on the other end of the critics’ spectrum, good governance advocates, self-declared governistas, have rushed to offer a smattering of bad solutions for Nvidia’s governance woes. These proposed solutions are as ludicrous as they are trite, and as irrelevant as they are ineffectual. For example, Charlie Elson at the University of Delaware somehow baselessly managed to blame a favorite bogeyman of many governistas, dual-class shares , for Nvidia’s woes — even though Nvidia has a single-class stock structure and not dual-class shares at all, a rather inconvenient fact which nevertheless did not detract from Elson launching into his tiring tirades. Elson bewilderingly argued in Directors & Boards that “in the end, this may spark, and I hope it does, a real reconsideration of the whole notion of dual-class stock in publicly traded companies”, as if that would be a panacea for all of Nvidia’s board woes, an argument which The New York Times also haplessly repeated. Similarly, governance professor Richard LeBlanc of York University proposed an independent chair as the panacea to all Nvidia’s governance woes, even though Nvidia already had an independent lead director who was the former CEO of Cooley Law Firm, Stephen Neal . All of these proposed governista solutions are irrelevant cliches offering insufficient and misguided recipes. Between clumsy New York Times op-eds , delusional Silicon Valley social media campaigns, and even an ideologically charged, anti-management Delaware Chancery Court judge, it appears that both anti-oversight tech bros and scolding governistas need to relearn some basic lessons about corporate board diligence. Here’s what these self-anointed governance experts miss and what the real lessons for boards from the Nvidia crisis are: Don’t build your business on other people’s money and then later resent accountability to them Don’t fall for mindless metrics which miss the actual process of governance — much like the way the “Goodhart’s Law” of economics warns over confusing the metric with the underlying phenomena Don’t confuse capital structure, whether dual-class shares or single class shares, as indicators of board caliber, board culture, and genuine independence Don’t fall victim to vague admonitions over “good faith” as genuine definitions of proper board diligence. Don’t rely on your accountants and attorneys to protect you – as the buck stops with you. The checklist fallacy that ISS , Glass Lewis, and many good governance advocates have fallen into All of the misguided proposed solutions from governistas tend to draw from the same wrongheaded playbook that ISS and Glass Lewis have preached for decades , recited on cue by the governistas: split the chair and CEO roles, encourage more so-called independent board members, tally the committees, and count board diversity. As we have argued in Fortune , this tired and trite playbook has never been able to tell a good board from a bad one. Consider how Nvidia was an ISS and Glass Lewis box-checker’s showpiece . Every director but Huang was technically independent. It had an independent lead director who was a former CEO of a respected law firm; independent audit, compensation and governance committees and committee chairs; annual elections for every board position without any staggered terms; and the ‘one vote per share’ principle so beloved by governistas. Huang was not even chairman of his own board: Nvidia had no chairman at all until he left, so Nvidia even fit the technical separation of roles box with a separate lead independent director. In June, shareholders re-elected all ten directors , the CEO with 99% of the vote, with ISS supporting the entire director slate this year, as it has each year for many years now . But the Nvidia crisis reminds us all just how misleading are the metrics of ISS and Glass Lewis’ checklist. This ‘check-the-box’ approach does absolutely nothing to actually weed out genuinely responsible boards from boards asleep at the switch operating on a bedraggled autopilot. Indeed, it is ironic that many of the worst corporate governance crises this century have been at companies which were darlings of the governista community. For example, Enron had 12 independent directors among its 14 directors , split the chairman and CEO roles in its final year, and had a former dean of Stanford’s business school, an accounting professor, chairing its audit committee, winning widespread praise from governance advocates with one governance publication even naming the Enron board one of America’s five best boards in 2000 – right before Enron blew up, exposed as a fraud. events.title: ‘If you don’t act now, it will be existential’: Defense tech CEOs say Pentagon’s ‘Industrial Age’ bureaucracy must adapt
events.summary: As AI-enabled drones transform the way wars are fought in Ukraine and Iran, two leaders of military tech startups warned on Tuesday that the Pentagon has to move faster to keep up with modern warfare.  “There’s a growing realization that if you don’t act now, it will be existential in the near future,” Tyler Sweatt, CEO of defense software deployment company Second Front Systems, told Fortune ’s Allie Garfinkle at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum . While venture money is pouring into defense tech at record levels, the Pentagon hasn’t sped up to match, and investors want returns. Sweatt said that pressure means defense tech companies will likely consolidate in “a tranche of deals” in the next six months. Shield AI, the autonomous weapon developer whose CEO Gary Steele joined Sweatt onstage, has already started: It announced Nov. 5 that it’s raising $2.5 billion to support its acquisition of radar systems company Echodyne in a transaction valued at $5.3 billion. Sweatt and Steele said the Pentagon’s lengthy approval processes and outdated systems could keep new tech from reaching troops quickly enough. Sweatt described the Pentagon as an “Industrial Age organization” bogged down with “big long bureaucracies” and “antiquated technology production lines” that will have to change.  “We’re at the beginning of this journey, not the end of this journey,” Steele added. “It will take time because things move slowly; the technology is not moving slowly.” Sweatt and Steele’s concerns echo those of a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published in July, which found the average time needed to deliver a capability across the Pentagon’s major weapon acquisition programs rose to over 12 years, and the watchdog predicted this average “will likely increase in the future.”  Steele contrasted those delays with Shield’s autonomous fighter jet, which the company designed to fly alongside aircraft piloted by humans using its Hivemind software. He said his company expects the time “from conception to first flight” will be less than two years. By comparison, Lockheed Martin’s F-35 started development in 2001 and flew in 2011 , and in total took 23 years from being awarded the Pentagon contract to being cleared for full-rate production.  But Steele said Shield can develop its aircraft faster because it being autonomous means it’s not endangering pilots in the testing process. In separate tests last month , Shield’s Hivemind software executed directions from a F-22 pilot and enabled the coordination of multiple uncrewed aircrafts called CCAs.  “We can go faster because we’re not putting people’s lives at risk every single day,” Steele said. “We can think about that iterative development cycle to get very different outcomes at speeds that never could have happened before.” VC appetite for defense tech Venture capitalists are now keen on investing, though that hasn’t always been the case. They deployed a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in Q3 2026, up 117.5% quarter over quarter, according to Pitchbook data . “Defense tech was in the same category as porn and gambling, and that’s all changed,” Steele said.  But Sweatt, whose company is valued at $1.2 billion per Pitchbook data , added that the influx of funding and increased defense spending by U.S. allies doesn’t mean new tech will reach the military immediately. “It takes a minute for that tail to really reach the tooth,” he said, referring to the lag between investment in defense tech and its actual implementation in the battlefield.  That delay could also test whether defense tech companies can justify their valuations , with Shield doubling its valuation to $28.8 billion from $12.7 billion in March . Anduril CEO Brian Schimpf, whose company is valued at $61 billion , even said at the Fortune Brainstorm Tech conference in June that defense tech could be in “a bit of a bubble.” “I think the next 24 months are probably going to confirm or deny the bubble hypothesis,” Sweatt said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: DOJ says it hasn't yet found any evidence of Saudi espionage in case against OpenAI engineer
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan and his lawyer David Rizk speak to Judge Peter Kang in a courtroom sketch from Friday, November 3, 2026. Vicki Ellen Behringer Abdulrahman Alfozan is making another attempt to get out of jail. The Saudi national and former OpenAI employee is facing a wiretap charge. A US prosecutor said they haven't yet found evidence to charge him with espionage. Federal prosecutors say they haven't found any evidence yet that the Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI's San Francisco office committed espionage or stole trade secrets. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested in mid-October, appeared in court on Tuesday as his lawyer sought his  release from jail . "Government counsel acknowledged that if there were supporting evidence, new charges would have been brought when Mr. Alfozan was indicted," David Rizk, his attorney, wrote in a filing ahead of the court appearance. "Instead, Mr. Alfozan was indicted solely on the Wiretap Act count that was the subject of the Complaint." During Tuesday's hearing, Rizk demanded that the prosecution turn over discovery documents more quickly, saying they had floated the idea that Alfozan was a "spy," yet provided nothing to substantiate it. He also said he plans to return to the magistrate judge who ordered that Alfozan remain detained. When asked by Business Insider how Alfozan is doing in custody, Rizk said, "He doesn't like it." Federal prosecutors in San Francisco arrested Alfozan in October, accusing him of planting a listening device in a conference room at OpenAI's office, where he worked as an engineer. The criminal complaint accused him of the interception of oral communications. Prosecutors brought a grand jury indictment against Alfozan later in October and didn't include more severe charges, such as espionage or theft of trade secrets. He pleaded not guilty in early November . The prosecution is still looking through evidence, including footage from OpenAI On Tuesday, US District Judge Vince Chhabria expressed concern that the prosecution might have overpromised during the October hearing that resulted in Alfozan's continued detention. The prosecution had said at the time that more charges might be brought. Nick Parker, the assistant US attorney leading the prosecution, said his team is still going through the evidence gathered for the case. That includes 160 hours of audio recordings, which he said appear to be from meetings at OpenAI. They are looking through Alfozan's and his wife's computers, as well as video footage from OpenAI. A power outage at an FBI facility locked Alfozan's cellphone, Parker said, so investigators hadn't yet been able to create a full forensic image. Alfozan agreed to provide the password after the hearing. Parker said also said that the recording device alleged to have been placed by Alfozan was encrypted, so the prosecution cannot access its current contents. Parker said he wasn't yet aware of any evidence that Alfozan committed economic espionage, stole trade secrets, or acted as an unregistered foreign agent. If the threat of those charges can be fully removed, Rizk said, "this case is going to completely change." He said that the prosecution had been moving too slowly in delivering him the evidence that he and his client need to fight the case. An agreement on AI use Judge Chhabria said that the prosecution should move quickly to provide additional material, including the contents of the laptops, the footage from OpenAI, and any reports prepared by FBI agents working on the case. Parker said that since there's OpenAI data on Alfozan's devices, there's reason to worry about Rizk using a competitor's AI model to look through the discovery documents. "I'm a lot less concerned about that than you are," Chhabria said in a deadpan. "You need to figure out a way to satisfy yourself on this, and you need to do it quickly." He told Parker and Rizk to reach an agreement on the use of AI by midday Friday. They also scheduled another status conference for December 8, a final deadline to submit discovery for December 11, and trial to begin the week of January 19. Parker said he suspects Rizk will delay the trial after getting the evidence. A different federal judge had earlier ordered that Alfozan must remain in jail while awaiting trial, ruling there was a high risk he would flee if released because the Saudi government offered to pay his bond and because his wife and son had already flown to Saudi Saudi Arabia . Photos included in Alfozan's criminal complaint show images of a USB device plugged into the back of a conference room TV and wrapped in toilet paper. The complaint also included what prosecutors said was a photo of Alfozan checking on the device a week after another OpenAI employee found it hidden there. Have a tip? A Tasmanian cheese and chocolate producer has entered voluntary administration, following what its director has described as prolonged "difficult trading conditions". Coal River Farm was established in southern Tasmania in 2015 by Daniel and Melanie Leesong. On Wednesday, Apex Advisory's Adam Johnston was announced as administrator of the business. It follows what Mr Leesong, the business's director, said had been "sustained efforts to find a solution" following difficult conditions in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. "We have undertaken an extensive process with the shareholder group, working through the available options to secure a lifeline for the business," Mr Leesong said. events.title: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The US-led board has decried continued fighting in Gaza and delays in implementing the terms of a 2025 ceasefire deal. The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza. In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse. list 1 of 3 Palestinian baby dies from cold in Gaza amid Israeli restrictions on aid list 2 of 3 With every rainfall, Gaza risks losing access to power and healthcare list 3 of 3 Who can force Israel to implement Gaza ceasefire deal? “The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained. The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza. Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. In recent weeks, Israel has continued to carry out deadly air strikes, and its ongoing restrictions have prevented the delivery of life-saving aid into Gaza ahead of the winter season. “Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the board said in its report. According to the board, the widespread devastation in Gaza has left Palestinians facing “another winter in tents and rubble”. Trump first proposed the Board of Peace in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace. The board’s mission was laid out in a 20-point Gaza peace plan , as well as the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire formally began on October 10, 2025, though attacks have continued since. The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood. But in Tuesday’s report, the board said Israel and Hamas have fallen far short of their commitments in the ceasefire deal. “A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.” The board also noted that Israel has blocked the technocratic civil administration body created to run Gaza on an interim basis. “The absence of decisions by the government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan,” the report said. “The Board of Peace calls on the government of Israel to take these decisions without delay.” To break the deadlock, the board called on the UN Security Council to press both sides to fulfil their agreements. “Neither party may treat the other’s delay as license for its own inaction, and together these obligations are the only route to Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction at scale,” the report said. It also added that the outcome must establish a credible path towards Palestinian statehood and self-determination, warning that no unilateral actions should be permitted to derail that ultimate goal.

events.title: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Crew says their boat was attacked by drones launched from US-operated vessel as part of ‘manifestly unlawful’ campaign. A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March. The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just. list 1 of 3 Families of Trinidadian men killed in US boat strike demand accountability list 2 of 3 Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court? list 3 of 3 US says it killed five people in strike on alleged drug boat It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador. “We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.” The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months. A report from the Washington Post in August, however, suggested that the vessels were targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission. Other reports have raised the possibility of the attacks being conducted by a US government contractor or a regional ally. The attacks appear to be similar to an ongoing campaign the US military has claimed credit for. Since September 2025, the US government has publicly undertaken a series of boat strikes, with the aim of killing alleged “narcoterrorists”. At least 244 people have been killed as part of that campaign, which experts have described as extrajudicial killing , in violation of international law. The lawsuit filed on Monday alleges that two drones were launched from a vessel operated by the US in March and proceeded to attack La Negra Francisca Duarte II. The boat was set ablaze, resulting in “serious burns” for two of the 16 crew members. “All of the Plaintiffs ended up jumping off the ship and into the sea. They then found their way onto small emergency boats,” the filing said, calling the strike part of an “unprecedented and manifestly unlawful US military campaign”. After the strike, the crew members say they made their way towards what they believed was a tuna fishing boat nearby but were met by armed men speaking English dressed in military uniforms. Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he has launched a hardline campaign to combat drug trafficking into the US. That push has coincided with a policy of expanding US military operations across Latin America, often in collaboration with right-wing political allies in the region. But critics have raised concerns over transparency and potential rights abuses during such operations. No suspects have been identified in the boat strike campaign undertaken by the US military, for instance, nor has any evidence been presented to the public. Families, however, have stepped forward to claim the dead as their loved ones. Many have argued that the people killed in the boat strike campaign were not drug traffickers but fishermen and informal workers. In December 2025, the family of the missing Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza filed a complaint about the boat strikes through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, claiming his right to life had been violated. A few weeks later, in January, the families of two workers from Trinidad and Tobago – Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo – filed a wrongful death lawsuit in a US federal court in Massachusetts. The men had reportedly been travelling home from Venezuela after taking work abroad. But experts say that efforts to hold the US government to account will be difficult, given the lack of transparency surrounding the boat strikes. The lethal boat strike campaign has continued in recent weeks, with a recent attack taking place on October 27. The US government has also been involved in non-lethal interception efforts, stopping suspected drug-trafficking boats. The watchdog group Human Rights Watch said that the US and Ecuador intercepted at least eight vessels between late August and mid-September, on the basis that they were being used to supply drug trafficking groups. Of the 160 crew members on board those vessels, Human Rights Watch says that 56 were released without charge by court order, 40 were acquitted for lack of evidence, 50 are awaiting trial, and 14 were not formally charged.

events.title: Recent AI cyberattacks are part of a ‘short period of transition,’ says Yann LeCun
events.summary: The world is “probably” going to enter an era of “unprecedented safety of software systems,” AMI (Advanced Machine Intelligence) founder and chair Yann LeCun said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I’m worried about very few things when it comes to AI,” LeCun told Semafor’s Shelly Banjo. LeCun predicts a short period “where AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor the attacker over the defender,” but that will be “just a short period of transition.” Future software, he suggested, will be “hardened” by AI. LeCun, a winner of the 2018 Turing Award, has long been skeptical that scaling large language models will usher in superintelligence or artificial general intelligence. He left Meta to found his world-model company AMI in 2025, which raised more than $1 billion in seed funding, the largest ever for a European company. He told Banjo that “I think it’s called a coconut when it’s that big.” He spoke on Tuesday about world models’ practical application in physical AI, but acknowledged there is a long way to go in their development. “We’re going to need a few conceptual breakthroughs in AI to make domestic robots that are useful,” he said. “We can use humanoid robots for very narrow tasks in well-controlled environments at the moment,” but domestic robots are “not for tomorrow.” He said he and his peers working on world models are gravitating toward physical AI because it’s a “complete blind spot” of LLMs. When asked about open source models, he remarked that “it made a lot of people really sad in the US, including people who are in the current government, that the most powerful open source systems are Chinese.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: DR Congo’s rival peace efforts fail to halt violence in the east
events.summary: Diplomatic efforts struggle to end fighting in eastern DRC as civilians continue to bear the cost of conflict. Bukavu, DRC – For residents of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the succession of diplomatic initiatives meant to end years of conflict is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the violence unfolding around them. In North and South Kivu provinces, fighting between the Congolese army and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), an armed and political coalition led by former President Joseph Kabila, has continued despite international efforts to secure a settlement. Civilians remain exposed to attacks, displacement and the disruption of essential services. The latest escalation has raised questions about whether negotiations in Washington and Doha can deliver security on the ground, and whether the separate diplomatic efforts are sufficiently coordinated to make progress. “One meeting follows another, and they all end up being much the same,” said Blaise Chasumba, a resident of Bukavu, the provincial capital of South Kivu. “But the real peace that the warring parties are dangling before us is far from becoming a reality on the ground. We continue to lose our loved ones and our homes.” A conflict with deep historical roots The Washington Accords, signed in December 2025, seek to address tensions between the DRC and neighbouring Rwanda. The Doha process, by contrast, is intended to resolve the conflict between the Congolese government and the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which includes the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group. The distinction is important: an agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali cannot, on its own, resolve the confrontation between the Congolese government and armed groups operating inside the country. The Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed by the DRC government, the AFC and M23 on November 15, 2025. In August 2026, representatives of the two sides, alongside Qatar, the United States, Togo, the African Union Commission and Switzerland, agreed on a road map to advance negotiations and establish a mechanism to review implementation. Fighting has nevertheless continued. The roots of the conflict stretch back decades. The 1994 genocide in neighbouring Rwanda and the flight of former Rwandan soldiers and militia members into what was then Zaire helped create the conditions for successive wars. The presence of armed groups linked to the genocide, and the emergence of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), became a persistent source of tension between Kinshasa and Kigali. The First and Second Congo Wars, which began in 1996 and 1998, drew in several neighbouring countries. Although the conflicts formally ended, disputes over land, political representation, citizenship and control of natural resources continued to drive violence in the east. M23 emerged in 2012 after a mutiny by former members of the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP). The group had been integrated into the Congolese army under a March 23, 2009 peace agreement, which its leaders later accused the government of failing to honour. The United Nations and conflict researchers have documented the movement’s origins in the breakdown of that integration process. The diplomatic landscape has since become more complicated. Established in October 2026 under Kabila’s leadership, the FRN says it has succeeded the AFC and assumed its commitments. The precise relationship between the new coalition and the earlier AFC/M23 structure remains important when assessing who is represented in the negotiations. On the battlefield, an offensive in early November underlined the fragility of the diplomatic process. FRN fighters advanced through Kahuzi-Biega National Park and along National Road 3, a strategic route linking Bukavu with areas farther north. Conflict monitoring reports said the fighters captured several localities, including Bitale and the centre of Bulambika on November 8 . The Congolese army said it had halted the advance at Bulambika and was preparing a counteroffensive. Local and military accounts differed over the extent of the fighters’ territorial gains. Diplomatic commitments, limited progress The fighting has driven further displacement and placed additional pressure on communities already struggling with years of conflict. Humanitarian organisations have warned that conflict is also making it harder to maintain essential services. Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said it had reduced its staff presence in the Bunyakiri health zone, relocating some personnel to Bitale and Bukavu as the security situation deteriorated. “We remind all parties to the conflict of the importance and the obligation to respect and ensure the protection of healthcare facilities, civilian populations and humanitarian staff, in accordance with international humanitarian law,” MSF said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera.
