events.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
events.summary: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation. "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end." Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. " A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy." Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not. "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added. What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.). Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?" Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support." Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical." What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles. Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation. He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error. The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," the senior CPC member told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

events.title: Jeff Bezos has tips for the Nvidia board in choosing a successor for Jensen Huang
events.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says Nvidia's board should look internally for Jensen Huang's successor. Kimberly White/Getty Images for Semafor Jeff Bezos advised Nvidia's board to look internally for Jensen Huang's successor. Bezos said outsiders have a "vanishingly small chance" of succeeding at complex companies. Bezos said that whether Huang returns as CEO, he "deserves admiration and respect no matter what." Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia's board as it searches for a permanent successor to Jensen Huang : The Amazon founder told Semafor's Liz Hoffman during the Silicon Valley & The World conference that Nvidia would be wise to look inside the company. "If you don't bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider," Bezos said. "NVIDIA is too complicated. "I think outside CEOs in complex companies have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding," Bezos added. "And so I would always think that's a last resort." Bezos, who stepped down as Amazon's CEO in 2021 after nearly three decades leading the company, said Nvidia's situation was different from Amazon's carefully orchestrated leadership transition, adding that his departure was the result of a "multi-year planned transition." Bezos's advice comes as Nvidia faces the challenge of replacing a founder whose leadership helped turn it into a central player in the AI boom. Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs and questions about a possible foreign intelligence effort, broke his silence Tuesday, saying he would be "honored" to return if the board determined it was in Nvidia's best interest. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him. Nvidia Executive Vice President and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent replacement. The board is also investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang's potential return has drawn support from employees and industry figures. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has garnered more than 190,000 signatures. When asked whether Bezos thinks Huang should be brought back, he declined to weigh in, saying he didn't know enough about what had happened behind closed doors. "Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company with a lot of hard work and foresight," Bezos said, "And he deserves admiration and respect no matter what, and that will never go away." events.title: Japan exports in October surge 20.5%, beating estimates on robust chip shipments
events.summary: Shipments of semiconductor equipment jumped 49.7% by value. Shipments to China rose 13.3%, while they climbed 23.9% for the U.S. Import growth in Japan for October came in at 21.6%, sharply missing analysts' estimates of 25.8%. Japan's exports in October surged 20.5% from a year earlier, snapping a two-month slowdown in shipments, official data released Wednesday showed. Exports growth beat expectations of economists polled by Reuters that had pegged it at 20%, and it was sharply higher compared to a revised 16.5% in September. Shipments of semiconductor equipment that have been propping up Tokyo's exports jumped 49.7% by value. Exports of motor vehicles climbed 19.9% year on year. In terms of destinations, shipments to China rose 13.3%, while they climbed 23.9% to the U.S. Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth, although a surge in the value of imports of petroleum due to the Iran war has offset some the impact of the exports surge on its economy. Import growth in Japan for October came in at 21.6%, sharply missing analysts' estimates of 25.8%, with petroleum imports climbing 60.5% by value, even as volumes slipped 0.7%. Analysts previously told CNBC that the surge in value was because Japan was attempting to switch sources to more expensive American oil as shipments from the Middle East stalled. Imports of petroleum from the U.S. jumped more than 1,100% year on year by value and 738% by volume. In contrast, shipments from the Middle East dipped 16.5% by volume, while higher prices pushed up import value by 37.7%. The country posted a surprise contraction in its third quarter GDP, which shrank 0.1% on an annualized basis. Following the data, Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 0.91%, while the yen traded at 159.50 to the dollar.

events.title: Top IRGC commander in Iraq for talks amid Kataib Hezbollah tensions
events.summary: Esmail Qaani, head of Iran’s IRGC Quds Force, has meetings over alleged oil smuggling linked to pro-Iranian armed groups. The commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, has arrived in Iraq to push for a solution amid simmering tensions near the town of Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the pro-Iranian armed group Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi official has told Al Jazeera. The Iraqi official explained that Qaani met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and held meetings with forces within the Coordination Framework—an umbrella for Shia Iraqi parties in the Iraqi parliament—in an effort to reach an agreement amid rising tensions over an investigation into suspected oil smuggling. list 1 of 3 Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah list 2 of 3 Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’? list 3 of 3 Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know A leaked intelligence report last week had said two strategic oil pipelines running through the town of Jurf al-Nasr, located near Baghdad in the centre of the country, had effectively been tapped into. Iraq recently launched a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries. While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, some analysts say they believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of pro-Iranian armed groups that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus. The Iraqi source told Al Jazeera that the judicial committee has not yet reached an agreement with the factions to enter the area. At least three leaders of the Coordination Framework also expressed their rejection of any armed clash or entry of federal forces before reaching a political understanding with Kataib Hezbollah, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Iraq. On Monday, al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group. Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area. A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr. A Kataib Hezbollah commander told AFP, “I can state decisively and with absolute certainty that the dream they dream of the Kataib withdrawing [from Jurf al-Nasr] will not come true, not even over our dead bodies.” Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of armed groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines. The group has recently issued several statements criticising Iraq’s prime minister, accusing him of corruption and threatening his government. It accused the government of “fabricating lies” about oil smuggling and of waging “the largest blackmail operation aimed at forcing” it to abandon its weapons. Since coming into office, al-Zaidi has pledged to ensure that armed groups will hand over their weapons to the state.

events.title: Maybe all the outages are because of AI. Maybe not. We're in for a confusing time.
events.summary: Markwayne Mullin, the head of the Department of Homeland Security, says new AI software might be to blame for a spate of computer outages. Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images Hey! What's up with all of these tech outages ? Are they related? It's a reasonable question, even for people who avoid conspiracy theories. The federal government doesn't really seem to know. That's frustrating to hear — and something we should get used to hearing. Did AI cause the US government to shut down all air travel Friday? Could be, says the US government. Also, maybe not. Who knows? But don't worry. That's the confusing answer from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He went on Fox News on Monday and said that the nationwide grounding last week — as well as other recent high-profile outages at places like JPMorgan, Microsoft , and United — might have all stemmed from organizations introducing new AI software into their IT stacks. Why does he think that? Because "one guy that's very smart with tech," — not Elon Musk, Mullin specified — told him that. And "that kinda makes sense to me." I mean, it also kinda makes sense to me? Maybe? But I'm not running a federal agency with more than 200,000 workers and an annual budget of more than $100 billion. But Mullin said he really doesn't know. He does know that "we just have a lot of technologists [sic] thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems. And the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now." Then Mullin told Fox viewers that they should "breathe." And be assured that the US is probably not under a cyber attack — something he felt "98%" confident about. I would very much like to live in a world where a top federal official doesn't muddle through national news interviews about outages. I would very much like to live in a world where the administration hadn't spent much of last year telling us the federal government was incompetent and should be radically downsized . Because sometimes we really want the federal government — not "one guy" — to be able to tell us what's actually happening inside these complicated systems, and what should be done about it. But I also think we'd have these exact same problems if we had the most competent, well-meaning public servants in charge right now. That's because all of this stuff is gnarly and complicated. Long before the AI boom, we've had technologists pointing out how rickety and poorly maintained much of America's digital and physical infrastructure is — and how seemingly isolated problems can have enormous ripple effects. Perhaps you recall the giant blackout of 2003 , where big swaths of the country, including New York City, lost power because of a software glitch in Ohio. Now we've added AI to the mix —a technology so new and head-scratching that the people who are building it frequently say they're not really sure how it works , and aren't exactly sure how to control it . Which is why people who have talked to more than "one guy" often tell us to buckle up for more instability. "We should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time," as journalist Josh Tyrangiel put it in The Atlantic . What can you, a normal person, do about this? Here I agree with Markwayne Mullin: You shouldn't do anything. There's nothing much you can do, aside from the digital equivalent of making sure you have some soup cans and water bottles handy, just in case. But if you're a member of the media — that is, anyone with access to a keyboard and an internet connection — things get a little trickier. It is reasonable to cover all of these outages, ask why they're happening, and not accept the hand-wavy answers you often get right after an event. But also be ready to accept that sometimes things break because things break, and that sometimes a coincidence is a coincidence. Or that maybe it's all a squirrel's fault . That's not an easy balance to pull off. Ring the bell every time there's a possible threat, and you'll end up with a country that's permanently on edge — or worse, doesn't pay attention to any warnings at all. Wait too long before ringing the bell, and people may be woefully unprepared. It's a real challenge . That said, one very easy step is to just stay mute when you don't have anything helpful to say. Tuesday morning, I got asked to come on an interview show to discuss "the November 17 blackout," which confused me since I was unaware there had been a blackout Tuesday. Turns out it was a reference to a made-up thing on social media , and I'm not going to spend more time discussing a non-thing here. Except to say that it's one thing for your uncle to pass along a hoax email to his friends and family. And it's another to go on TV or the internet and give the hoax that much more oxygen. Even if you're ostensibly going to debunk the hoax, you're still spreading the particulates around. But Markwayne Mullin? I'd definitely like you to ask a few more people — perhaps there are still technology experts in your organization, for starters — for more information. Then come back and tell us what you've learned. We'd love to know more. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia promises that revenue will keep soaring — for now
events.summary: Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang , the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop. On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations. “We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases. Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading. Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Nvidia chair closes the door on Jensen Huang comeback; analysts don’t push on China/Singapore black box
events.summary: Nvidia’s board ended the talk of a Jensen Huang comeback on Tuesday. On the company’s first earnings call without its cofounder, chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” He then ruled out any discussion of why Huang left. “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” Jones said. None of the eight analysts who got on the line pressed the point. None asked about Singapore or Megaspeed or about a report earlier Tuesday that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating whether Nvidia misled investors. It was a bit tense. That left the biggest open question about the world’s biggest chipmaker unasked: where some of its revenue really ends up. Nvidia beat Wall Street’s estimates by about $7 billion on $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, as Fortune’s Alexei Oreskovic reported . Nvidia stock was up nearly 5% in after-hours trading to roughly $163. The board’s line Jones said Huang “voluntarily resigned” on Nov. 12 “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” The board accepted the resignation unanimously, he said. It has hired a search firm and will consider internal and external candidates. Huang had said earlier Tuesday on X that he “ would be honored ” to return as CEO. “I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote. Jones tied the search to the national security questions around the company. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully,” he said. On Tuesday the board also created a national security and export control oversight committee. Jones said it “will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies.” What didn’t get asked The call had a one-question limit. Bank of America’s Vivek Arya came closest to the scandal, asking about talent retention and the leadership transition. Interim CEO Colette Kress said that among employees, “there are diverse opinions,” and that “from a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” Other analysts asked about margins, vendor financing and next year’s outlook. The question they skipped is a downright national-security scandal. In the quarter that ended July 2025, Nvidia attributed $10.2 billion in sales, 22% of its revenue, to customers billed in Singapore, according to its 10-Q filing . “Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere,” the company wrote in that filing. It added that over 99% of its controlled data center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for orders from U.S.-based customers. The next quarter, Nvidia began reporting revenue by the location of customers’ headquarters. It said that change “provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue.” Singapore no longer appears as a line. On Monday, the Commerce and Justice departments confirmed a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company suspected of helping shift Nvidia’s most powerful technology to China, according to AFP . Commerce began probing the company in 2024. The departments said Nvidia put Megaspeed on a “no sell” list in June 2025. Huang resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. She is not related to him. Megaspeed has said it will work “constructively” with the government. On Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is opening a civil probe into whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors. What Nvidia did say about China Kress gave one new China detail: sales of licensed Hopper data center chips to China were $2.4 billion in the quarter. “We are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China,” she said. The company’s forecast for next quarter assumes no data center compute revenue from China. On new Commerce Department export rules released this week, which tighten access to advanced chips through other countries, Kress said Nvidia is “still going to spend some time studying those.” She also said “demand far exceeding supply” would keep performance strong. Nvidia raised its outlook for fiscal 2028 revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%. Kress also put a number on customer concentration: frontier AI labs are expected to make up about 15% of Nvidia’s data center revenue this year. Kress said Nvidia will file its 10-Q “in the coming weeks,” the first regional revenue breakdown since Huang’s exit. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to transcribed interviews with three House committees, and Huang’s is expected before Thanksgiving. Kress ended the call with: “We’ve got this.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Citi settles sexual harassment claims by managing director
events.summary: Ardith Lindsey alleged that a senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her family with violence after she ended it. Citigroup settled a lawsuit by managing director Ardith Lindsey, who said the bank allowed years of sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination in its equities division. Lindsey, a Citi employee since 2007, alleged an abusive relationship, threats to her family, and a sexual assault by a superior. She described a “boy’s club” culture. The deal was finalised after months of talks and a June “settlement in principle”. No terms were made public, and Citi said no one should be “discriminated against or harassed in the workplace”. Citigroup has settled a high-profile lawsuit by a managing director who claimed the bank had for years tolerated sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination against her. Ardith Lindsey sued Citi three years ago, claiming she had been the subject of “prolonged, pervasive and outrageous mistreatment” during her 16 years in the bank’s global equities markets division. Lindsey had spent her entire Wall Street career at Citi, starting as the most junior member on the electronic sales trading desk, before later taking charge of the desk in 2021, when she was promoted to managing director. A lawyer for Lindsey, Jeremiah Iadevaia, told the court in a letter on the night of Nov 13 that they had finalised a deal to resolve the case, after months of negotiations. No terms of the agreement were made public. The two sides announced in June that they had reached a “settlement in principle” after engaging in mediation. Neither Citigroup nor Iadevaia immediately responded to phone messages seeking comment. “Our values and expectations are clear – no one should ever be discriminated against or harassed in the workplace,” Citigroup said in an earlier statement. Lindsey, a University of Virginia graduate, joined Citigroup in October 2007. She alleged that another, more senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her and her family with violence after she ended it in October 2022. Lindsey’s suit also alleged a sexual assault by a superior when she first started at the bank and claimed there was a “boys’ club” culture at Citigroup’s equities group, including suggestive comments, traders mocking the firm’s sexual harassment policies and frequent outings to strip clubs. events.title: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn
events.summary: Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050 Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero. The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets. In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years. Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO 2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade. The electric vehicle rules are the single biggest contributor to those climate goals , meaning the government will have to find other major carbon emission reductions, unless it amends the budgets to allow more pollution. Carmakers must sell a bigger proportion of electric cars each year under the rules, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle. However, the industry has lobbied intensively for months to cut the headline targets from 80% electric by 2030 to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing that the mandate was putting them under too much financial pressure. Electric cars were 26.6% of UK new car sales during the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target. However, carmakers are expected to comply with the mandate using a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”. The committee’s chair, Nigel Topping , wrote to Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, to oppose any reduction of the targets. Such cuts would, he said, “put the government’s commitment to tackling climate change at risk, miss an opportunity to reduce costs for a typical household by about £800 a year, increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels of oil a year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as our main export markets rapidly transition to electric vehicles”. Some in government have become alarmed in recent months about the impact the government’s various changes could have on the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments. The government has just cut funding for installing heat pumps, the second-biggest decarbonisation policy. Burnham has also alienated some Labour MPs by waving through gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield , and considering approval for the massive Rosebank oilfield . MPs voted earlier this year to approve a new set of carbon reductions for the years 2038-42. However, the Guardian has learned that one cabinet minister in the Keir Starmer government wanted the government to go back to parliament to scrap those planned reductions and enact a more conservative target instead. The idea did not come to fruition though, with other cabinet ministers mostly opposed. An industry source with knowledge of discussions in government said that serious consideration was still being given to changing the carbon budgets in the run-up to the UN’s Cop31 climate conference, subject to parliamentary approval. The source said it was not clear if the proposal was still being discussed. A government source strongly denied that it was under consideration. The changes to the mandate also mean the UK is unlikely to meet the carbon budget covering 2033 to 2037. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emissions reductions elsewhere, given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans. The policy could also face opposition from the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each of which have their own carbon budgets. Burnham on Thursday told Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey , that he was “proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification” and urged people to choose electric cars and heat pumps. Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK, said: “The Burnham government cannot talk of climate leadership on the international stage while doing a U-turn on ZEV targets at home.” Topping added: “Weakening the zero-emission vehicle mandate would miss an opportunity to reduce the cost of living for people, undermine Britain’s competitiveness and leave us more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices. “People are buying electric vehicles in record numbers because they are cheaper to own than the alternative. “The mandate gives those up and down the supply chain the certainty they need to invest, supports thousands of jobs, and keeps the UK on track to meet its climate commitments. “British drivers deserve better than a backtrack on such critical policy.” The car industry criticised the CCC’s analysis.

events.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
events.summary: CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips. A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit. But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China. Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility. “Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire. EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat. McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations. He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains. “Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel. “If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said. Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts. “There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said. While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study. “It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat. But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty. The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit. Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away. events.title: Stripe backer Atomico calls for Europe to own its success stories
events.summary: Europe is home to many of the world’s fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report . The report, for instance, notes that the likes of Black Forest Labs and Microagi have reached $100 million in revenue in months, not years. “I think we can put to bed the idea that there’s a fundamental reason or constraint on the ability to scale a breakout company from here in Europe,” Atomico partner and head of intelligence Tom Wehmeier (pictured) told TechCrunch. Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer. But there’s also a sense that this success hasn’t been acknowledged enough, perhaps obscured by louder calls for improvements. Wehmeier, the report’s lead author, was quick to opine that “policy, procurement and capital are not moving at the same speed as our founders.” But he said the tech sector should advocate for itself in an inspiring way. “When it comes to policy, I think the language needs to be, ‘Hey, this is not us complaining. This is us saying here is an opportunity to make the magnitude of impact even greater,’” Wehmeier said. “When we frame it as problems, that becomes harder.” This reframing may also help European tech improve its image abroad, where complaints around overregulation may have overshadowed Europe’s potential to leverage its deep tech talent and growing pool of repeat entrepreneurs to have even more of success stories. Plenty could be still done to fully unlock this potential, and Wehmeier said that “the next few weeks are going to be a really important test, with EU Inc .” Also known as the 28th regime, this initiative would create a unified European corporate regime akin to the Delaware C Corp. If the last stretch of EU Inc’s grassroots campaign achieves it goal, it will become much easier to create and operate businesses across the EU. It would also show that the tech system got itself heard, which could open the door to the kind of endorsement Atomico is hoping to see more of. Politicians have strong incentives to give the tech sector what it wants. If it is Europe’s second largest sector, biggest contributor to growth, and biggest job creator, “Do we not want more of that?” Wehmeier asked rhetorically. But it is unclear whether it will win them any votes. To make the answer more straightforward, the tech sector will have to work on having public opinion on its side. For Wehmeier, one key is to “demonstrate that this is translating into value for citizens.” The report is supporting this endeavor with a mix of high-level data and examples from its portfolio; for instance, it notes that ICEYE ’s satellites monitor severe weather, flooding, and other hazards; and Daniel Ek’s Neko Health has now done more than 100,000 body scans, some of which helped identify severe or life-threatening health conditions. One limit to this argument is that Neko Health’s scans will seem pricey to most Europeans, who largely rely on collective, public health insurance. But Atomico seems to hope that its report will give readers FOMO not just as potential customers, but also as potential shareholders. There’s more to be done for this to happen. Beyond joining the sector’s push for an EU capital markets union, he hopes more of Europe’s institutional investors will invest in the region’s own tech companies. “We must get to the place where Europe and European beneficiaries are the biggest shareholders in the success that we create,” Wehmeier said. Before that can happen, the industry must overcome anti-industry beliefs like fears of AI-induced job destruction. But Wehmeier is a believer in the power of proof. “I think that trust is going to be earned through showing results to the public — be that lower energy bills, better healthcare, more homes built for cheaper and faster, and having infrastructure that we can rely on.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
events.summary: Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data "Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO. If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger. The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical. They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre). Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips. Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s. "With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago." American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology. Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips". "Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme. "We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing." Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently. "[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol. His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven. It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol. "That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious. "In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it." Netherland's based ASML is a crucial supplier of chip-making equipment Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML. The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors. Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters. "The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol. "You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology." ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer. "Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team. Peter Wennik says TNO's pilot production line is a "launchpad" for European tech ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips. The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity , external , which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years. In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy". "By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said. Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

events.summary: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

events.title: Banks pause US$480 million chip loan tied to China’s ByteDance
events.summary: The latest US curbs on access to its AI chips have frozen work on a US$480 million (S$618 million) loan to purchase advanced Nvidia hardware that would be used by Chinese technology giant ByteDance. US chip curbs have frozen a US$480 million loan for Nvidia GPUs linked to ByteDance, after banks feared the deal may breach the new rule. Aolani Cloud says it is working with regulators and financing partners to keep the Malaysia data centre project in compliance. Banks are waiting for clearer licence rules before moving ahead, and some now see the loan as too risky to continue. The latest US curbs on access to its AI chips have frozen work on a US$480 million (S$618 million) loan to purchase advanced Nvidia hardware that would be used by Chinese technology giant ByteDance, according to people familiar with the matter. Bankers at five lenders evaluating the deal said that they had internal discussions about pulling out or not joining the loan amid fears that the deal might violate the new US rule, they said. Singapore-based neocloud Aolani Cloud recently began inviting banks to join the loan, which would fund the purchase of GPUs (graphics processing units) for a data centre in Malaysia. But on Nov 16, the US announced a rule requiring data centre operators in countries including Singapore and Malaysia to get a licence to buy advanced AI chips. The step is aimed at curbing Chinese companies’ remote access to such technology, which is how TikTok parent ByteDance would use the Nvidia GPUs. The pause in work on the loan illustrates how the Trump administration’s surprise move has caught many dealmakers in Asia off guard. Across the region, lenders scrambled on Nov 17 to work out what the new regulations would mean for billions of AI debt in the pipeline and deals that have already been done. “We have spent significant time with our banking and financing partners to assess and anticipate regulatory risk ahead of this recent new ruling,” a spokesperson for Aolani said in response to questions about the loan being paused. “We are proactively working with regulators and our financing partners to ensure the project delivery goes ahead in full compliance with the new ruling.” There was no immediate reply from DBS Group, which is the mandated lead arranger and book-runner on the deal. It is not yet clear how exactly the licence approval process will work, and which firms will be required to apply for these. That has prompted a barrage of questions from potential lenders, one of the people said. It is unlikely that there will be progress on funding the Aolani deal until bankers can fully evaluate the new rule, the people said. Internally, some bankers have described the facility as dead given the risks banks could incur if it was found to violate the new US rule, they said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
events.summary: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfortable reality I think we're grappling with is that attackers don't always have to break our systems. Sometimes, our systems are already capable of breaking on their own.” For people who couldn’t withdraw money from their bank, board a flight, or use email at work on Friday, “the disruption was real regardless of the cause,” she said. “Cybersecurity has spent decades investing in detecting threats, identifying vulnerabilities, and generating reports,” according to Kollender. “Yet we still allow for these preventable weaknesses and configurations that can bring entire systems down.” Cynthia Kaiser, senior VP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told The Reg that the recent disruptions show “how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems.” AI has entered the chat Then we go and add AI to this already delicate balance, and everything essentially blows up. AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit development has surfaced more than 100,000 CVEs so far this year, with Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday disclosing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in each of the past two months. AI has also shrunk the elapsed time between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits . “We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organizations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” Kaiser said. “Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyberattack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.” Even when attackers aren’t using AI to facilitate intrusions, the technology itself has become a source of risk to organizations. “Autonomous agents can execute actions, change configurations, access sensitive information, and interact with critical systems at machine speed,” Kollender said. “When those systems lack proper governance and safeguards, a mistake can develop just as quickly as an attack. Former US Department of Defense network exploitation and vulnerability analyst Mike Wiacek, when asked if these regular system outages are the new normal, told us: “The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in.” After the DoD, Wiacek founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. He's since founded Stairwell, a threat-intel firm he serves as chief technology officer. “The idea that we are going to patch ourselves to security is, dare I say, an antiquated concept,” he told The Register . One of Stairwell’s engineers was doing regular, daily software development tasks on an open source library with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, and the model told the engineer about a buffer-overflow vulnerability in the code. “We weren't even looking for it,” Wiacek said. “It found a vulnerability in open source software by accident. You used to need specialized bug hunters and really, really technical security folks to discover and develop vulnerabilities and exploits. Now, it’s almost too easy to do it.” This new reality, he said, necessitates a total rethink of how we build and maintain digital infrastructure. “How do we get to a world where we assume compromised by default, and continuously recompromised, and then develop the architectures and the systems necessary to make what was the expense of incident-response investigation really fast and cheap? Because we will not be able to patch our way out of it.” It requires vulnerability managers and system administrators to patch as soon as software updates become available. events.title: AI companies lost voters on narrative and execution, Alphabet's Porat says
events.summary: Alphabet’s longtime investment chief acknowledged that Google — and AI companies generally — have come up short convincing US voters that the trillions of dollars being plowed into data centers across the country are worth the cost. A bipartisan backlash against data center building galvanized voters, who almost uniformly moved to block expansion across the country in local measures earlier this month, and elected lawmakers in the midterms who largely backed a slowdown in the AI buildout. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta have been at the center of that expansion — either directly financing massive projects or signing up as the anchor tenants there. “I’ve been traveling the country quite a bit and the pain you saw reflected in polls, I’m hearing firsthand around affordability,” Ruth Porat told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Like many executives at the heart of the buildout, Porat argued that most Americans are willing and excited by the job opportunities that the AI frenzy presents. “What’s most potent is when I have these conversations across the country,” she told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, “what I hear time and time again is, ‘This is creating opportunity that I hadn’t seen in my town.’” Porat also defended the dilutive — and expensive — capital that Alphabet and other big companies have been using to finance their ambitions. “It’s expensive, but the reason we’re investing is we see the extraordinary opportunity,” Porat said. “None of us have lived at a time like this.” Google is expected to spend up to $205 billion in capex this year, and has forecast even higher numbers for 2027. The company’s free cash flow has turned negative in recent quarters, worrying investors who believe that the company — and Big Tech generally — may be getting ahead of its skis. “We want to make sure we’re showing up with a full-stack approach that delivers value and a balance sheet that’s a fortress balance sheet so that we can continue to deliver in a high-quality way,” Porat said. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
events.summary: Iran claims drone strike on US radar was retaliation for alleged airspace violations by US military drones. Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive. The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”. list 1 of 3 Vance calls out ‘neoconservatives’ over Iran war list 2 of 3 Vessels on fire after naval mine hit in Hormuz Strait, Iran says list 3 of 3 Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’? The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain. “The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday. He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening. A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain. US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency. It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran. Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions. It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage. Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines. Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait , which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers. Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard. Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday. events.title: A string of tech outages disrupted flights, banking, and major apps. Here's what officials have said about the causes.
events.summary: Major tech outages have caused issues for Americans traveling, banking, and at work. Apu GOMES / AFP via Getty Images There has been a wave of major tech outages over the past five days. Thousands of Americans have run into issues at work, while traveling, and when making payments. Here's what we know about all the major incidents. There's no indication they're related. If you feel like the digital world is ending , you're not alone. A string of high-profile technology outages over the past week has disrupted the lives of many Americans trying to travel, transfer money, or make purchases, and caused speculation that something bigger and more nefarious could be going on. There has been no indication from government officials or the companies affected that cyberattacks or AI were responsible. And despite the uncanny timing, there are no signs the incidents were connected. "At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort," Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence committee, said in a statement Tuesday, adding that the evidence suggested the outages were due to "legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity." Warner said AI was allowing vulnerabilities to be identified faster and creating pressure to fix them immediately, "putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change." "These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call," he said. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences." Here are the major outages reported and what we know about each one. Microsoft Microsoft 365 tools experienced outages last week. Zamek/VIEWpress/Getty Images Microsoft experienced  a major outage last week that impacted its 365 tool suite, affecting products such as Outlook, Teams, and Copilot. By late Friday morning, the company said services were stabilizing. Microsoft said the cause of the outage was "technical" and "not related to cyber or AI / agents." Federal Aviation Administration The FAA nationwide ground stop left thousands of travelers delayed. Joe Raedle/Getty Images The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday, citing issues with its air traffic control systems. Flights were grounded for over four hours, leading to thousands of delays and cancellations on Friday and Saturday. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the outage on aging air traffic control infrastructure. Mullin said they did not believe the outage was related to cybersecurity or an AI attack. JPMorgan Chase JPMorgan Chase said a "software bug" had caused disruptions. Gary Hershorn/Getty Images JPMorgan Chase said Monday said it experienced service issues related to a "software bug in on-premise hardware systems." Customers had reported issues accessing account information and delayed transactions. Customers of other banks also reported issues, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and US Bank, with the latter saying customers attempting to use Chase's Zelle may have been affected. "There is no evidence this is cyber-related," Chase said. United Airlines United Airlines said a technology issues causes delays to departing flights. KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI / AFP via Getty Images United Airlines on Monday said it fixed a "technology issue" after a system outage caused delays to departing flights. The airline said flights in progress and United Express flights weren't affected. United had 945 delayed flights on Monday, according to the flight tracking site FlightAware. "There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," United said. Charles Schwab Charles Schwab said it had a brief website disruption. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Charles Schwab experienced issues with its website on Tuesday. Some users were unable to access the site, which temporarily displayed a message that said its server "encountered an internal error or misconfiguration and was unable to complete your request." The spokesperson for the brokerage firm said a "brief webpage loading issue has been resolved." Apple Shoppers pass by the Apple Store at the Porta di Roma shopping mall in Rome, Italy, on November 13, 2026. The illuminated Apple logo hangs above the store interior, where customers browse Apple products at wooden display tables. Colorful promotional graphics line the walls inside. (Photo by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images Apple said an "internal update" caused outages to some of its services after users online said they were having issues accessing Apple Pay and iCloud. "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple said in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Apple said the incident was not a cyberattack. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
events.summary: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. events.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
events.summary: Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster. Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown. In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday. Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter. “We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.” When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”. When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”. Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions. Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”. Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.” A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO . “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”. “While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.” Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. The company is also facing an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China in the wake of Huang’s resignation, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

events.title: Lutnick must answer questions from Congress on Nvidia, Sen. Kelly says
events.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., demanded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before Congress as questions mount over his role in delaying restrictions on AI chip exports to China. “He needs to come to Congress,” Kelly, who serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee, told Ashley Gold at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I would like to hear answers to a lot of questions that we have about why he made the decisions he made.” Kelly also alluded to Lutnick’s family business interests in the AI industry, saying they raised additional questions that the commerce secretary needs to address. The Arizona senator added that he believed Lutnick should have been removed from his position at earlier points during President Donald Trump’s second term, saying there had been “multiple times” when his “expiration date in this job had already expired.” Kelly also said he wants answers from Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week amid revelations about his reported extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. “We haven’t received answers to the questions that I have and my colleagues have,” Kelly said, noting that Huang had volunteered to testify before Congress. “What we need is answers.” Kelly also expressed skepticism about the Justice Department’s ability to conduct an impartial investigation into the matter, citing his own experience with the department. The senator said the department had been “weaponized” against individuals — including himself, noting that Trump called for his prosecution over remarks he made reminding military personnel they must refuse unlawful orders. “I might be a little biased here, but I do not have a lot of faith in the folks that are currently running the Justice Department,” Kelly said. Kelly also voiced support for three bipartisan provisions in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation that would strengthen restrictions on exports to countries of concern, including China, saying the US must be careful about transferring its most advanced technologies. He specifically called for more “guardrails” on AI technologies and argued that companies and individuals should face penalties when those standards are violated. Liability, he said, “depends on the outcome,” but in cases involving particularly egregious conduct, “individuals could be held accountable.” — Lauren Morganbesser
