events.title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks
events.summary: The U.S. has lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The director of the Pan American Health Organization made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates help to fuel outbreaks that have sickened thousands and led to a string of preventable deaths. The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday. It's a devastating step backward for American public health , as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated. More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania , one in New York and two in Wisconsin . The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be " doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post , said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment." CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

events.title: US Fed’s Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House hearing
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? US President Donald Trump has been trying to fire Cook since August 2025. United States Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has declined, through her lawyers, to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration of US President Donald Trump initially demanded for November 6. list 1 of 4 China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting list 2 of 4 US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces list 3 of 4 Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided list 4 of 4 ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money Administration officials have called on Cook to appear before the committee to address allegations that she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies. Cook has not been charged with any crime. Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs. “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook”, the letter said. In June, the US Supreme Court blocked Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design”. Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a November 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating. The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Department of Labor secretary. The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire Cook if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions. Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause”, but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.

events.title: LeBron James sues AI sports-betting analytics app over alleged bogus endorsement
events.summary: LeBron James is suing PlayVision. Mitchell Leff/Getty Images LeBron James is suing PlayVision, saying its Bron app illegally used his name and likeness. The lawsuit says PlayVision illegally traded on James' identity to unjustly enrich itself. "Defendants selected the name 'Bron' precisely to evoke Mr. James," the lawsuit alleges. NBA legend LeBron James is taking an AI sports-betting analytics app dubbed Bron to court, accusing the startup behind the tool of stealing his name and likeness to make consumers believe he endorsed it. James' lawsuit, filed Tuesday in Manhattan federal court by celebrity attorney Alex Spiro , alleges that PlayVision, the Y Combinator-backed company behind the app, illegally traded on the basketball star's identity to unjustly enrich itself. "Defendants selected the name 'Bron' precisely to evoke Mr. James, to trade on his fame and goodwill, and to falsely suggest to the public that Mr. James endorsed or was affiliated with the Bron App," the lawsuit says. In addition to PlayVision, the company's founders, Mark Zogby and Anish Gupta — the CEO — are also named as defendants in the lawsuit. Representatives for PlayVision did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Business Insider. The lawsuit points to a November advertisement that it says was built around an AI-generated version of James in a No. 23 jersey bearing his "Bron" nickname and sporting tattoos that mimicked his. "Speaking in Mr. James's voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in Defendants' Bron App. The Ad then urges viewers to 'Scroll to bet,'" says the lawsuit, which alleges trademark infringement. The ad "catapulted the Bron App from obscurity to controversy, with the Ad gaining a million views within a day—exactly as Defendants intended. But Mr. James has no affiliation with Defendants or their product," the lawsuit says. The complaint alleges that the defendants violated James' rights and treated the violation as a "marketing expense." When James' attorneys sent the company a cease-and-desist letter, the lawsuit says the startup used it as an opportunity to "gin up additional publicity, taking down the Ad while teasing 'a new name' without delivering one and daring Mr. James to file a lawsuit." The lawsuit, which seeks a jury trial and an unspecified amount of monetary damages, said James is "one of the most recognizable identities in the world" and that he commands tens of millions of dollars in fees for endorsing a product or venture. "His endorsement is uniquely valuable," the lawsuit says. "And that is why Defendants decided to steal it all for themselves." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skeptcism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

events.title: Europe the natural location for Mistral IPO, CEO says
events.summary: French AI champion Mistral will likely go public in Europe, and is in preparations to do so, CEO Arthur Mensch said Tuesday. “The natural place to list is Europe,” Mensch said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re not going to do this this year, but we’re definitely getting ready for it.” Mistral, which mostly makes open-weight AI models, aims to carve out a lane as a sovereign AI provider, pitching it as an alternative to closed US models or open Chinese models. That’s especially salient in Europe: Mensch said most of the investor base and half of its customer base is European. A US IPO, though, could offer the company access to more capital: Other European tech companies including Arm, Spotify, and Klarna have listed in New York, drawn by higher valuations and a bigger pool of investors. Mensch also said that regardless of who wins the French presidential elections next year, “we’re very confident as well that in Europe we will still have a lot of support. Support is needed.” He said he has met with most of the candidates to explain how AI and the industry works. “Many of them are not technical, and so they need to get a little more technical because that’s going to be five years of very technical discussions,” he said. He tied the country’s recent protests to young people’s anxiety around AI: “The youth need answers to what they’re going to do. So I think part of the unrest and part of the anguish that the youth is having is because of AI changing the way their jobs are going to be.” He criticized companies’ decisions not to hire young people because of AI. “You can invest in them, they will use AI much better, and they will create a lot of value,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nvidia posts strong outlook as board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above estimates on Tuesday in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang 's resignation as chief executive. The chip maker, which said it has launched the search for a new chief executive, announced that it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, compared to analyst expectations of $125.5 billion, according to LSEG data. It posted an earnings per share of $2.68 on revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter, up 20 per cent for the quarter and 103 per cent from the same period last year. Estimates compiled by LSEG data projected an EPS of $2.47 and revenue of $109.15 billion. "Our momentum is real, with the market-leading multi-year roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand. We are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position," interim chief executive Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call. Addressing the company's leadership vacuum during the call's question-and-answer segment, Ms Kress said Nvidia wants to install its next chief executive "as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person". With Mr Huang out at the company at the heart of the AI buildout, investors were turning attention towards the company's outlook. The earnings come amid growing negative sentiments towards chip makers and the AI buildout , and rising concerns over financing to build AI data centres . Data centre revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21 per cent from the previous quarter and 110 per cent from a year ago, Nvidia said, compared to an anticipated $101.85 billion. Ms Kress said the company expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow roughly 75 per cent year-on-year. The company's cloud industry backlog currently sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months ago. Nvidia said it is "not assuming any data centre compute revenue from China in our outlook". Ms Kress also said Nvidia's total CPU revenue will at least double in fiscal year 2028. Coreweave , Meta, NScale and Open AI have since adopted the Vera Rubin processing platform, joining AWS, OCI and SpaceX. The earnings cap a frenetic week for the company and a widening fallout after Mr Huang left the company. Shares in the company are down more than 17 per cent this year, while the S&P 500 is up 8 per cent. Nvidia was up nearly 5 per cent during after-hours trading, after closing 0.48 per cent lower at $155.39 a share in Tuesday's trading session. The S&P 500 declined 1.03 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 per cent, while the Dow Jones dropped 848 points, or 1.64 per cent. Nvidia not considering reinstating Huang as CEO Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said the company does not intend to reinstate Mr Huang as chief executive. Nvidia has retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search for Mr Huang's replacement. "While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," he said. The company has lost about $410 billion in market value since Mr Huang's resignation last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for China. In his first public comments since his resignation, Mr Huang on Tuesday said he would be open to returning as Nvidia chief executive if the company's board asked him to. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he said. President Donald Trump said he would support Mr Huang's return as chief executive, while a petition calling for his reinstatement has received more than 178,000 signatures. Mr Huang has agreed to testify before three US congressional committees on December 1. Nvidia's general counsel will testify on December 2. The Wall Street Journal reported the Securities and Exchange Commission is reporting the chip maker after Mr Huang's resignation last week, quoting people familiar with the matter.

events.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
events.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives." Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows. "Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella. AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world . Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software. "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot." Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, " Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365 ," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric. He also talked up Microsoft IQ , the company's new enterprise context management platform. "The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot. Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion , its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench , a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal. Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model. Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available. "We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it." He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available. It's a question of trust After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust. "Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted. "And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable." Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative . The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative." Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®

events.title: Nvidia raised next year’s sales target by tens of billions of dollars, signaling confidence in its future without Jensen Huang
events.summary: Nvidia raised its sales forecast for its next fiscal year, and reported stronger-than-expected results in its most recent quarter, in a striking signal of business confidence by the AI chipmaker following the resignation of longtime CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang . “Our momentum is real,” interim CEO Colette Kress said on conference call with analysts on Tuesday, citing strong demand for the company’s products, Nvidia’s ongoing technological advances, and the commitment of its employees. Kress, Nvidia’s longtime finance chief, made her debut as interim CEO on Tuesday’s earnings call, flanked by newly appointed chair of the board Harvey Jones . The pair took pains to project a business-as-usual attitude—even using the phrase—while seeking to put Huang in the rear-view mirror . The board of directors “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the call, noting that the company has retained executive recruiting firm Hedrick & Struggles to search for a permanent CEO. The comments were a direct rebuttal to Huang, who is seeking to reclaim the CEO throne just days after resigning amid revelations of multiple affairs, one reportedly with a Nvidia employee who reported to him and another with a woman some believe may be a Chinese spy. Shares of Nvidia were up more than 5% in after hours trading on Tuesday. The company’s stock has plummeted more than 36% in the past month, shedding more than a trillion dollars in market value. Investors have been spooked by the loss of Nvidia’s longtime leader, Huang, as well as by general concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Kress doused both concerns at once on Tuesday by raising sales expectations for Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 year, which is roughly equivalent to the 2027 calendar year. “We had originally indicated that we would be at about 70% growth year-over-year, and now we are are increasing that to 75%” growth,” Kress said, citing improvements in supply and ongoing strength in demand. The guidance was particularly striking because Huang himself had delivered the 70% growth forecast three months ago, framing it as an usually far-reaching forecast that reflected the exceptional strength in the business. In raising the annual revenue forecast by the equivalent of $20 billion or more, Nvidia’s message seemed to be that Huang was not so essential after all. “We got this,” Kress said during the call. “The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him,” Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors on Tuesday. Revenue in three months ended October 25 totaled $115.8 billion, roughly twice the amount Nvidia generated in the year ago period, and above the $109 billion expected by analysts. Net income increased 105% to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per share. The world’s leading maker of AI chips said it expects revenue in the fourth quarter to come in at $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—besting the $125 billion expected by analysts at the low point and potentially exceeding the target by billions of dollars. Nvidia said it would file its official 10-Q report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in “the coming weeks,” rather than on the same day as its earnings announcement as it traditionally has done. Chip exports in the spotlight Jensen Huang’s affaire with Alice Huang (no relation) a former executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed has raised questions about whether Nvidia’s advanced AI chips were being diverted to China, in violation of U.S. export controls. On Monday, U.S. Department of Justice announced that it was pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed for potential export control violations. The Trump administration also announced stricter rules Monday around chip exports to companies like Megaspeed. (Megaspeed has said its business is “legitimate and lawful,” and that Alice Huang, who some U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe is connected to Chinese intelligence, left the company in August 2025). Kress said the company was in the process of assessing the new rules around chip exports, but stressed that the company remained confident of overall demand and of its revenue forecast. Another overhanging question in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure are the billions of dollars in equity investments and financial guarantees that Nvidia provides to other companies in the AI industry such as neoclouds building data centers and startups developing AI software. Kress said that Nvidia would continue to financially support companies in the AI ecosystem but said Nvidia might not as supportive as it has been in the past. Nvidia will take a “very strong look” at the types of companies that get help, as “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter,” Kress said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
events.summary: United Kingdom authorities have passed the investigation to the United States ‘in line with existing international protocols’. A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said. The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”. list 1 of 3 UK sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements list 2 of 3 Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University list 3 of 3 Who is behind Habibi UK, an X account that targeted critics of Israel? The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023. Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service. “These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said. He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.” US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.” Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK. Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”. The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

events.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
events.summary: Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard . As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems. The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users. The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions. However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.” Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before. events.title: Optum’s CEO still works weekends as a pediatrician. What he sees ‘should not happen in America, but it does every single day’
events.summary: On his last couple of weekends working as a hospital pediatrician in Boston, Dr. Patrick Conway saw three patients he can’t stop talking about. One was a 14-year-old girl who had called more than 100 people trying to get mental health care before she ended up in his hospital with broken legs. Another was a 21-year-old with meningitis. “She wakes up. What’s the first thing she says? I’m a single mother. I can’t afford this. I got to get out of here,” Conway said. The third was a 15-year-old on Medicaid who needed complex rehab for a neurologic disorder, and the hospital was struggling to find anywhere to send her. “That should not happen in America, but it does every single day,” he said. During the week, Conway runs Optum, the health services arm of UnitedHealth Group, which he said employs about 300,000 of the conglomerate’s roughly 400,000 people. That makes him one of the more unusual witnesses to American health care’s failures, because his company sits on the other side of many of them. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, he told Fortune’s Diane Brady that the weekend shifts are the point. “Those stories could be anywhere in America,” he said, and Optum’s job is “to prevent those stories from occurring in the future.” Brady put the tension more bluntly. Optum, she said, is a bit like the cable guy: people need it, and they don’t always love it. Conway didn’t argue with that. He said Optum’s business customers (health systems, payers, employers) are “generally quite positive.” On the insurance side, “people have concerns,” he said, listing access, prior authorization and whether their doctors are in network. Conway took over Optum in 2025, a year in which UnitedHealth replaced CEO Andrew Witty with former CEO, Stephen Hemsley, and said it was cooperating with federal investigations into its Medicare business. Conway has seen the system from most of its angles. He joined Health and Human Services as chief medical officer late in the George W. Bush administration and held several roles at Medicare and Medicaid, mostly under Barack Obama, “which is a little less common these days.” He has also run a Blues plan. His first week as an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, he said, a child arrived with a 1,000-page paper chart after years of bouncing between community hospitals. On page 487, he spotted a rare mitochondrial disorder. “In today’s world, that child should be diagnosed anywhere in America … within seconds, minutes,” he said. His case for Optum is that scale and AI can close those gaps faster than a fragmented system can. On affordability, he pointed to Optum Rx’s Savings IQ tool. He said it brought the median copay for specialty drugs down from about $88 to $5 and saved consumers more than $1 billion out of pocket over the past 12 months. One patient with cancer emailed him to say he’d been going on and off his medicine because it cost about $300, and he hadn’t told his wife. “Now it’s $5,” Conway said. “I’m on my medicine. I’m doing better.” He also pitched OptumReal, which digitizes benefits and connects payers with health systems. Conway said it can approve a service with “99 plus percent accuracy,” so the payer, the provider and the patient all see the same number at the point of care. “That’s how healthcare should work,” he said. Asked when it would be the norm, he said it “may become faster than you imagine,” because payers and providers “know the system doesn’t work as it is today.” Brady also asked about Mark Cuban, who has spent years arguing that pharmacy benefit managers like Optum Rx are what’s driving drug prices up. Conway noted he once debated Cuban in Washington: “I think he was a little surprised. I accepted the debate.” He called Cuban’s model “a niche solution for some number of drugs” that helps people, and said the system needs something more comprehensive. Brady raised Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla’s argument that cancer will one day be as manageable as diabetes. Conway, who lost his father to cancer, said he hopes Bourla is right. “It may take a little longer,” he said. He closed on time. He’s been trying to fix health care for 20 to 25 years, he said. “I don’t know if I’ve got another 20. I hope so. It’s got to go faster.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City, on Nov 17. US stocks fell sharply as investors worried about Nvidia’s earnings, AI spending and Anthropic’s planned IPO. The S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow all closed lower. Tech shares led the drop after scandal around Nvidia and concerns over data centres, Chinese equipment bans and weaker AI enthusiasm. Intel, Microsoft and several software stocks also fell. Strong retail sales and stubborn inflation added pressure, while Fed officials signalled possible aggressive rate hikes. Markets now expect a 25-basis-point rise in December. NEW YORK - US stocks extended their tech-driven slide on Nov 17 as investors braced for Nvidia’s earnings, expected just after the bell. Scandal and controversy have surrounded the chip giant in recent days, fuelling worries over the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure and risks associated with the nascent technology. Those jitters intensified ahead of Anthropic’s mammoth IPO, expected on Nov 18, which is targeted to raise as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion). All three major US stock indexes closed sharply lower. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq notched their first four-day streak of declines since September. “Every sector in the S&P is down,” said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors, in New York. “So clearly, it is a reflection of overall investor nervousness as opposed to being driven by a specific set of stocks, whether they’re AI-related or not.” “It’s a confluence of all of the events that are there, and it seems to be speculation-driven as opposed to fact-driven,” Pursche added. “It’s not all about Nvidia.” The AI trade was already contending with popular opposition to large data centres when tech shares were rocked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster following revelations of his relationship with an alleged spy. Investors are also impatient to see returns on hyperscalers’ massive expenditures. The Trump administration’s plans to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment gained momentum in the wake of Huang’s departure, despite opposition from Amazon, Alphabet , Meta and others. Expectations leading up to Nvidia’s results were sky-high. The company was projected to post 90.4% year-on-year earnings growth on revenue of US$109.11 billion. The stock ended the session in negative territory. Enthusiasm over artificial intelligence helped send the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index’s year-to-date gain as high as 106% in June, but that fervour has since lost steam. The index’s gains so far this year have shrunk to about 34%. Economic data released early in the session showed strong underlying retail sales, weakening industrial output and rising import prices, largely driven by spiking petroleum costs. Homebuilder sentiment plunged to its lowest level since April 2012. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 75.96 points, or 1.02%, to end at 7,341.23 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 180.42 points, or 0.74%, to 24,329.34. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 859.71 points, or 1.67%, to 50,748.46. On the sector level, software and services, airlines and banks were clear underperformers. Intel fell after Nvidia cut its stake in the company by 25%. Software shares were broadly lower, with Salesforce, Workday, Intuit and Adobe all losing ground. Microsoft also declined on the day. JPMorgan shares dipped after the company said insider Bregje de Best would succeed Jeremy Barnum as chief financial officer in early 2027. Fed officials are increasingly suggesting that stubborn inflation has made the central bank more open to an aggressive US rate-hike path. Markets are pricing in a near-certain 95.4% likelihood of a 25-basis-point increase in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. On Nov 18, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting could help illuminate the central bank’s approach to near-term monetary policy. REUTERS

events.title: 7 smart reasons to sell a stock—and my ‘golden rule’ for offloading shares, says hedge fund CEO
events.summary: Money Use 5 phrases to gracefully decline an invitation you can't afford, says financial therapist Leadership Jared Diamond: What makes leaders successful Raising Successful Kids Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist Leadership The RealReal CEO’s No. 1 leadership lesson How to Talk to People When someone talks down to you, use Dolly Parton's simple trick to 'maintain your dignity and disarm' them, says expert Nobody is born knowing anything innately about the stock market. And if you feel like you've missed the investing class, you didn't. Usually there isn't one. So responsible people who are trying to do the responsible thing by building a portfolio for themselves and their families often find huge gaps in their knowledge and don't know where to turn. As the co-founder and CEO of the hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money, I know that there's no shortage of advice when you're getting started about great investments to buy. It can feel easy and gratifying, especially when your portfolio is doing well. But then things get tougher. One of the hardest things to do as an investor is to figure out when to sell. You buy a stock because you believe it will go up in value. But the decision to sell is rarely so straightforward. Personally, I've made just about every selling mistake. But over time, I've developed a framework for knowing when to sell — and when not to. Selling decisions are often rooted in emotion and cognitive bias rather than logic. One major culprit: anchoring to past performance , a flawed reference point that clouds clear thinking. Behavioral economics, particularly prospect theory , shows that we experience the pain of a loss more intensely than the joy of a gain. This leads investors to cling to losers ("just need to get back to even") and sell winners too early ("lock in the gain"). We also place too much emphasis on recent events, a phenomenon known as recency bias . If your last tech stock soared, you're more likely to chase another. If your last trade flopped, you may avoid the market altogether. And when recent trades go well, people tend to trade more — often to their detriment. Finally, selling triggers a storm of second-guessing and rationalization. Here are my responses to common excuses: "What if I'm wrong and it goes up?" What if you're right and it keeps going down? "What will I do with the cash?" You don't always need to put it to work right away, or you can buy a little more of what you already own. "If I double down and it rebounds, I'll make it all back." But if it continues to go down from here, your losses will double. "I don't like having a loss, so I'll sell once it gets back to even." What you originally paid is irrelevant. Yet for many investors, it becomes the most important factor in their decision-making. To assuage their fragile egos, they risk even bigger losses. These biases and emotional landmines are why you need a clear, disciplined plan for when to sell, including when: The original thesis no longer holds. If the fundamental reasons you bought the stock are no longer true — if earnings slow, revenue shrinks, margins deteriorate or the company loses market share — it may be time to move on. There's a regulatory risk. Legislative changes can dramatically shift a company's prospects. For example, the outlook for solar-related companies can decline dramatically when tax credits are cut for installations. Management loses credibility. Frequent earnings misses or misleading guidance suggest deeper problems. One-off surprises happen; recurring surprises reflect poor leadership. It becomes too big a slice of your portfolio. A stock that grows from 10% to 25% of your portfolio due to the superb performance of its underlying business, which fuels a soaring stock price, increases your risk from a diversification standpoint. Rebalancing is smart and necessary. The maximum I would have in any one position in my own portfolio is 20% — and that's probably too much! The stock becomes overvalued. Sometimes the hype drives prices beyond what fundamentals justify. If valuation detaches from reality, it's okay to take some profits. If it really goes nuts, I will sell enough to take my original investment off the table. You need the money elsewhere. Selling to fund a home, college tuition or retirement is perfectly valid. Opportunity cost matters. You have tax reasons. For example, tax-loss harvesting may allow you to offset capital gains or deduct up to $3,000 of losses against ordinary income. When you've decided to sell for a solid reason — especially the first, second, or third outlined above — don't hesitate. Don't wait for the perfect price. Just sell. Just as important as knowing when to sell is knowing when not to sell. Avoid emotionally driven decisions that sabotage long-term gains. Don't sell just because it went up.

events.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so. "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands. "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. events.title: Sheehy, Klobuchar look to solve hemp dispute
events.summary: Sens. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., are introducing a new, far-reaching hemp regulatory bill that could smooth over a major point of contention in the government funding negotiations, according to details shared first with Semafor. The bipartisan proposal would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people under 21, ban “gas station” marijuana products derived from hemp and copycat advertising for those products, and also restrict synthetic cannabis products from China. The bill would also require hemp products be produced in the US, preserve access to CBD products, and empower the FDA to inspect hemp facilities. The timing of the compromise is crucial: A new federal definition of hemp goes into effect on Dec. 11 — the same day as the government funding deadline — and without action could upend the industry in the US. Internal Republican disagreements over the issue complicated the last funding bill. Sheehy has made solving the hemp issue within his party a major priority; he’s holding a hemp roundtable on Tuesday afternoon with veterans to discuss the issue. In a statement, the Montana Republican said the compromise with Klobuchar will put “every bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating [productsout of the hands of children,” while shielding farmers, cancer patients, and veterans from criminal penalties. Klobuchar, who will leave the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, touted her state’s hemp industry and warned that the “looming federal ban on hemp products is threatening farmers, brewers, small businesses, and consumers across Minnesota and the country.” A coalition of veterans groups is also asking congressional leaders to support the bill, according to a letter shared with Semafor . Republican Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., is a leading opponent of delaying the new hemp definition deadline and is gearing up for another push ahead of the December funding deadline. Sheehy and Klobuchar’s bill would go into effect on Dec. 11 if passed.

events.title: Data center industry should repurpose older infrastructure, SambaNova CEO says
events.summary: Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach “disrupts the communities less,” he told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be “much more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,” Liang said. Still, he said, it’s good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. “To distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem — it’s not a bad way to do it,” he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that “compute constraint” in the near term is a real possibility. — Jake Angelo

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters But the new chairman shot that idea down on the company's earnings call GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs 3 hours ago Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit 10 hours ago The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors 1 day ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 1 day ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 4 days ago No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. The US Department of Justice made the rare point of commenting on one of the pillars of the Jensen Huang story on Tuesday when it confirmed that it’s investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean company formerly helmed by Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), the alleged Chinese spy. The DoJ has been checking the company out since 2024, when Alice Huang was still in charge, over potential export control violations. In other words, the DoJ is hinting that even if Alice Huang isn’t a spy, Megaspeed may have still been moving illegal chips. The DoJ added that Nvidia blacklisted Megaspeed in 2025, and that the Department of Commerce previously interviewed Alice Huang around the same time.

events.title: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says
events.summary: Europe must enact more innovation-friendly regulation if it wants to compete in the AI race, Germany’s director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization said Tuesday. There are “a lot of things we need to do to catch up in the race,” Marco-Alexander Breit said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “One of these is actually having a more innovation-friendly regulatory framework, especially in Brussels.” Germany also needs to “step up” its capacities and capabilities, he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, adding that the country hopes to quadruple its data center capacity by 2030. Steve Jurvetson, managing director and founder of Future Ventures, who joined Breit on stage, went further, saying Europe is “trapped in a sort of regulatory doom loop” that smothers innovation. Jurvetson said “regulation is the elephant in the room” that “is stifling European innovation at every step of the way.” While Breit pushed back, saying, “it’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” he acknowledged that red tape and regulation needed to be cut, arguing that change would ensure European AI leaders “don’t need to leave Europe to work on AI and change the world and make a lot of money.” Breit said he agreed with the vast majority of the EU AI Act, for example, but continued on to say that “it actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world,” he said. “So it actually hurts our economy, even more than people maybe think in Silicon Valley that it hurts the US companies.” Speaking earlier at Silicon Valley & The World, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act, saying “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, Sunak said he supports some regulation, because despite being bullish on new AI technologies, “they bring new risks with them.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Medical practice squeezed as business confidence slumps in SA
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Business confidence takes hit in SA amid cost and profitability concerns Clinical psychologist Quentin Black is among those dealing with rising business costs. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Business confidence in SA has again been dented, according to the latest snapshot produced by the state's Business Chamber. The group's CEO says confidence has slumped to levels "we haven't seen since COVID". The most recent quarterly survey found almost 75 per cent of respondents felt the pressure of wage, energy, rent and other costs. Quentin Black helps people deal with life's pressures, but he himself knows what it's like to be under the pump. The clinical psychologist manages a not-for-profit practice in Adelaide, which he said was currently being squeezed. Dr Black said the practice was too big for small business support, but too small to qualify for other forms of financial assistance. "There's a lot of pressures on businesses at the moment," he said. "Small enterprises like PsychMed that employ a lot of South Australians actually don't get any assistance whatsoever. In fact, we end up paying a lot of the burden. "Even though we're running not-for-profit programs, we pay payroll tax to the state government for employing people on the programs." Dr Black's comments reflect a mood that is corroborated by the latest snapshot of business confidence in South Australia. According to the September quarterly survey produced by the South Australian Business Chamber, confidence has again been dented, slumping to its fourth-lowest level since 2001. Among the factors driving that result — which reversed an uptick in confidence in June — were cost pressures and government policies, the chamber's CEO Andrew Kay said. "Business confidence in South Australia is back to levels we haven't seen since COVID," he said. Andrew Kay says businesses are feeling the pressure of rising government charges. ( ABC News: Daniel Litjens ) About three quarters of survey respondents listed costs — including wages, energy and rent — as major obstacles to confidence. Dr Black, who is a long-time member of the ALP, said he was all-too-familiar with those challenges. "There's been regular increases in wages as part of the inflationary spiral. That's a yearly event now," he said. "Also, insurance costs have gone up significantly along with energy costs which have really skyrocketed for businesses." More than two thirds of respondents to the confidence survey were anxious about profitability, while more than 60 per cent highlighted government policies and legislation. "Government needs to find ways to reduce cost pressures on businesses, to reduce red tape, and to find ways to encourage investment, rather than detract from investors coming to this country," Mr Kay said. "We're seeing at the moment government putting pressure on businesses through increased credit card surcharges, through changes to trusts on businesses — these are simply additional costs or additional taxes on businesses." The SA opposition said the pressures were being exacerbated by inflation caused by excessive government spending. "Inflation and red tape are absolutely hammering small businesses right across South Australia," opposition leader Ashton Hurn said. "They're being squeezed in every direction because they've got their costs that are going up, but we also know that families at home are really feeling the pinch in their own hip pockets." Ashton Hurn has been critical of government spending. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) But business confidence in South Australia nevertheless remains higher than it does nationally, according to the survey. "The national economy is clearly under a bit of strain, and under a bit of pressure, yet South Australia is outperforming the rest of the nation, with the exception of maybe Western Australia," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said. "That doesn't change the fact that we are subject to the national economic headwinds which are clearly under strain at the moment.

events.title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
events.summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated. Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week. Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives , a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election. Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift. Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday. The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.” Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently. “It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge. Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case. “It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied. Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act. ___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report. events.title: Nvidia closes lower ahead of earnings as company reels from Huang resignation
events.summary: Nvidia reports earnings after the bell Tuesday. Investors have been weighing the fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. Nvidia shares closed marginally lower Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell. The stock move Tuesday marked Nvidia's fourth straight daily decline. In the statement, Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation." "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee. Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025. Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2. An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday. The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips. Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.
