events.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
events.summary: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared. But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy. "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey. State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities. A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather. Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer. Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year. Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick: An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity. A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood. Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring. And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change . Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed. By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly. Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place. Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems. How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police. This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data. Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments. Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab. Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification. Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts. The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035. Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic. In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises. Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said. Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year. Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead. Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey). Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement. Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then. In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels. The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

events.title: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
events.summary: The FAA said it would pause work to install new routers after problems with the technology in recent days. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said an overloaded router led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for more than four hours on Friday, but the cause of the tech problem is still unclear. Democratic senators have asked the FAA, the Department of Transportation and the companies involved in the work for clarity on what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause. The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic. Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong. "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety." The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat. The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage. CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment. Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years. Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization." Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. — CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

events.title: Wall Street's fear gauge is surging again and this time it's not just about AI jitters
events.summary: Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide tech outages to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering, traders on Tuesday piled into protective put options on the S&P 500 Index at a rate that suggests fear beyond just an AI-specific correction. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged nearly 5 points to a high of 27.7 at the worst of Tuesday's selling and the ratio of put to call volumes on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) hit 1.5, the highest since the first week of April, according to Barchart data. The 'VIX' was last still hovering above 26. With the VIX climbing four days in a row, the volatility gauge hasn't traded under 16 since Oct. 16, arguably trending higher as the S&P 500 slips below this month's lows, trading under 7,300 for the lowest price for the benchmark equity gauge since June. Cboe's three-month volatility gauge, VIX3M, briefly touched the highest since April. While Nvidia earnings are contributing to the uncertainty – the stock's options currently imply more than a 7% move after its report, the biggest in almost two years – volatility in the S&P 500 jumped more than in the Nasdaq 100 Tuesday, pointing to a more widespread fear among investors. "SPX vol is expanding faster than NDX vol, as SPX vol is coming from a lower base," Eric Metz, CIO, SpiderRock Advisors for BlackRock, said via email. "Today, the market is pricing acute near-term stress in large-caps broadly, but tech-specific fear is still notable. Even within the technology cohort, Tuesday's laggards took on a different tone. Software stocks declined the most ahead of Anthropic's IPO, with options volume on the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) surging to almost four times the 30-day average, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Salesforce was hardest hit, with put contracts outpacing calls on twice the average options volume. "There's a lot of reasons to be risk-off," said Noel Smith, co-CIO of Kai Asset Management. "This is a market-wide phenomenon today that's not just AI stocks." To be sure, bulls weren't totally absent from the session, with the Nasdaq 100 Index holding its November low and VIX still under its Nov. 5 high of 28.4. "While vol is now at a relatively elevated level, we have not seen much fear in the options market," said VolSignals' Matthew Nadel, citing fixed-strike volatility in S&P 500 options, which measures volatility changes across specific options strikes. "We have seen a pretty decent move higher in SPX fixed strike vol, however the move up in vol has been mostly orderly."

events.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
events.summary: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said. A view into parallel Python Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol ) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds. To kick off a debugging session , a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions. The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release. And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun . TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®

events.title: What smart people are saying about Jensen Huang's new statement
events.summary: Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jensen Huang said he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia. The ex-CEO broke his silence on Tuesday after resigning in the wake of affair allegations. Here's what business leaders think of his new statement. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang finally addressed his resignation publicly — and he'd be happy to undo it if invited back. In his statement, Huang said he owned his "mistakes completely" and that he was cooperating with an internal investigation. The statement adds new pressure to Nvidia's board and interim leadership hours before the company reports quarterly earnings after the closing bell. Here's what business and tech leaders and personalities are saying about Huang's statement: Travis Kalanick, Uber founder Travis Kalanick Zak Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty Images Kalanick, who's pushed publicly for Huang to be reinstated, celebrated the statement on X. The Uber cofounder was famously pushed out of his own company in 2017. "Let's bring Jensen back!!! LFG," he wrote . Dan Ives, tech analyst and partner at Yorkville Ives Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Nvidia's board could now face increased pressure, Ives and his colleagues wrote in a research note for Yorkville Ives. "Clearly Jensen wants to come back as CEO, and the statement moves the fight from a petition to the board," the note reads. The research note said Nvidia's bylaws allow a critical mass of shareholders to call a special meeting — and with President Donald Trump , Elon Musk, and many employees on board, "that coalition is no longer unthinkable." But the fight over Nvidia's next CEO will play out in Washington, where federal authorities will want an outsider and compliance with export controls, according to Yorkville Ives' note. "The board's decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a President open to his return and a Treasury Secretary demanding an outsider," the note says. On X, Ives posted, "This could be next step in Nvidia saga." Jason Calacanis, angel investor and "All-In Podcast" co-host Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Huang's got a fan with at least one of the All-In Podcast hosts. "Bring @JensenHuang back 🫡," Calacanis posted . Gavin Baker, chief investment officer at Atreides Gavin Baker predicted $100 billion in annual recurring revenue. Bloomberg/Getty Images Baker, an Nvidia shareholder who co-wrote a letter to its board urging it not to rush to judgment with its CEO search, praised Huang as an "exceptional" CEO during an interview with CNBC's Sara Eisen on "Squawk on the Street." Huang put out his statement moments before Baker appeared on TV — and Baker was glad to see Huang say he would cooperate with investigations. "I think this is all good," he said on CNBC. "I think this is good for America. I think this is good for Nvidia." Baker said he wanted to see Huang back at Nvidia. "America loves comebacks and second chances and I would like to see Jensen, if he is cleared of these charges, given a second chance as to be the CEO of Nvidia," Baker said. Ruben Gallego, US Senator U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego Finn Gomez/Getty Images The Democratic senator from Arizona warned Huang not to get too ahead of himself. "Slow your roll there," he replied to Jensen's post . "You have to answer some questions first. We need to know if you allowed Blackwell chips to be siphoned to China? Where you ever told the Megaspeed was a problem. Did you know that Megaspeed was under investigation in 2024 and if so why did you allow the sales to go forward?" Huang has agreed to testify behind closed doors before three House committees on December 1. Gallego's questions hint at the investigations Huang and Nvidia might face as Democrats — who were swept into power during the midterms in part due to backlash against tech companies — regain majorities in Congress starting in January. Casey Newton, "Machine Gods" podcast host and founder of The Platformer Casey Newton Jerod Harris/Getty Images for Vox Media Newton cracked some jokes at Huang's expense. "This man's commitment to delivering chips to Alice Huang is simply inspiring," he said on X , referencing the Megaspeed CEO whom Huang allegedly had an affair with. Newton later had an idea : "Instead of coming back to Nvidia directly, Jensen should try to route himself through a holding company in Malaysia or Singapore." events.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
events.summary: Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines. National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge. The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract. Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this. "If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have." In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer". The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14. A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval. The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement". It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate." The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment. Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols. But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year. Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about." There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network. In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways. For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit. The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year. Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed. As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances". It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement". Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations". It said it would put further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites. events.title: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations
events.summary: Home Depot named Richard McPhail as its new CEO effective next week. McPhail currently serves as CFO. CEO Ted Decker had been on a temporary medical leave of absence but has since returned, according to Home Depot. The company made the announcement as it posted earnings and revenue that beat expectations. Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week. Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail. Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said. "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan." McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles. "We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick. He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market. Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects. The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount. Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expected Revenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expected The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86. Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period. "We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts. In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric. The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth. For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase. Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

events.title: Microsoft’s Satya Nadella praises Jensen Huang, says return as CEO is ‘up to the Nvidia board’
events.summary: Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella praised ousted Nvidia founder Jensen Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, but he stopped short of calling for Huang’s reinstatement to the chipmaker’s top job. “I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it’s not up to me. It’s up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next,” Nadella said Tuesday at a media roundtable in San Francisco during Microsoft’s Ignite conference. He added that he had “all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he’s done for Nvidia,” noting that he has known and worked with Huang for a long time. Huang, who turned Nvidia into the dominant maker of AI chips and owns about a 3.56% stake, on Thursday stepped down as CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago, amid revelations of multiple affairs, including one with an executive whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. On Tuesday morning, Huang broke his silence and said he would be open to returning as CEO . Later in the day, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the company did not intend to bring Huang back. Nadella, who said he texted Huang over the weekend to say he was thinking of him, said that Nvidia has a deep bench of talent. “I think Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership,” Nadella said, noting that interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress once worked at Microsoft. “I’m making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we’re scaling Rubins as we speak,” Nadella said, referring to Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin line of processors. “It’s a pretty critical project for us.” As one of the world’s largest cloud computing providers, Microsoft is a major purchaser of Nvidia chips, and the two companies have a longstanding relationship. Nadella appeared with Huang last month at a Microsoft Windows event. Nvidia is navigating its most tumultuous period in company history, as Huang’s ouster has raised numerous questions about how one of the world’s most valuable companies can continue to operate without the all-powerful executive who was critical to its decision-making and deals, including agreements with Microsoft and other major tech companies. Speaking about the recent midterm elections and the overwhelming rejection of AI data centers by communities throughout the U.S. that voted to restrict data center development, Nadella said that building data centers requires earning support “one community at a time” by delivering long-term local value, rather than attempting to lobby in Washington. He acknowledged community skepticism, such as concerns that data centers create local nuisances or drive up electricity bills, and emphasized that companies cannot resolve this through public relations alone, but must physically prove the benefits. “I don’t think the public is getting it wrong,” he said. Nadella also stated that election results have not altered Microsoft’s plans for building data centers, and he noted that the constraints on data center growth are more about the availability of power, chip wafers, and memory, rather than election cycles. Nadella also addressed a massive outage of Microsoft’s systems last week that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide. And he spoke about the company’s recent buyout offer to 60,000 employees, which is nearly 30% of its workforce. Nadella said that the outage was not caused by AI code or AI deployments, and that the incident was a “perfect storm” in which a bug surfaced under specific web traffic conditions during routine testing. In fact, internal AI tools helped engineers solve the problem more quickly, he said. Nadella said that the voluntary buyout offers were designed for employees to “have some agency on how they decide what to do with their careers,” and that rather than leaving employees with the anxiety of something happening to their jobs, the offers gave people a clear option. He did not say whether the offers were a prelude to layoffs. “There are some teams that are changing faster, some teams that are in a different place,” he said, speaking about the different speeds of teams that are part of the company’s workplace transformation. events.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
events.summary: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face . Google did not respond to The Register 's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255 , a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident , Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register . Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

events.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order
events.summary: Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns. California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order. The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco. Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities. The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch. The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies. Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025 , a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets. That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour. In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones. Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones. events.title: Hyundai will start delivering Waymos in December in autonomous push
events.summary: Hyundai Motor CEO José Muñoz said the company will start delivering cars to Waymo next month, part of an autonomous push by the South Korean carmaker. Hyundai’s all-electric IONIQ 5 will supply Waymo’s self-driving fleet, starting in the US and expanding globally. It’s part of a deal the companies struck in 2024. “It’s not only going to be for the United States. It’s going to be also for export,” Muñoz said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re talking about significant volume and it’s just the beginning.” Hyundai also has a partnership with Uber through its self-driving platform Motional, which struck a 10-year agreement with Uber in 2022. Despite Hyundai’s push into self-driving cars, Muñoz emphasized the need to maintain jobs for their current workers and to bring employees along during the massive AI transition. He said he believes “those who still want to get a job within the mobility industry will have it,” noting the company has started listing new jobs like robot technicians in its big Georgia plant. Muñoz said Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a key partner to Hyundai, will have a big impact on the industry, but that the chipmaker remains “very strategic, very important for all the activities that we are doing in robotics, in autonomous driving, and in many projects which are strategic for South Korea … whether it’s with the same CEO, with a new one.” When asked whether Muñoz, a rocket scientist by training, was interested in the top job at Nvidia, he deflected: “I’m very happy here.” — Shelly Banjo

events.title: Universities, public sector are ‘priced out’ of AI, Fei-Fei Li says
events.summary: Fei-Fei Li, cofounder and CEO of AI company World Labs, said the public sector and universities are missing out on the fruits of the AI revolution. “I don’t think universities and public sectors are keeping up because we’re priced out,” Li told Semafor’s Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson at Silicon Valley & The World, speaking on the pace of change of AI. “The resource[s] we have in terms of tokens and compute are extremely limited.” Before founding AI research firm World Labs, Li was a professor at Stanford, where she continues to work, helming Stanford HAI, one of the US’ most elite AI research centers. She was recently named executive vice president and chief scientist at the chip company AMD. Li argued that lawmakers in Washington should allocate resources to the public sector to allow it to reap the benefits of AI given the high costs of using it. Universities are also responsible for holding society accountable by researching and benchmarking AI, Li said. “It would become one of the biggest failures of our time if we don’t, as a society,” Li said, “if we don’t resource [the] public sector in a serious way.” — Jake Angelo

events.title: Altria CEO says ‘responsibility needs to be at the heart’ of its FDA-regulated nicotine business. It’s part of why it sued the regulator
events.summary: As Big Tobacco companies pivot away from combustible products to less harmful nicotine alternatives, they’re finding new challenges in their relationships with regulators. Sal Mancuso, the CEO of Altria Group, which owns cigarette and cigar brands like Marlboro and Black & Mild,  explained at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday that competing in a Food and Drug Administration-regulated industry brings with it both an added sense of responsibility to consumers, and hurdles in competing with other businesses in the space. Mancuso said that Altria’s On! nicotine pouch brand is a key innovation for the company, but regulations have slowed growth. The Marlboro-maker announced its Moving Beyond Smoking initiative in 2023 as more consumers move away from cigarettes, putting a renewed focus on smoke-free alternatives to cigarettes such as NJOY vapes and On! nicotine pouches, which are competing with Philip Morris’s Zyn.  “You can call us the underdog in the pouch category today, but our intention is to lead the pouch category over the long term,” Mancuso told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “When you think about what’s maybe getting in the way, there’s a couple of factors: One is just the misperception that nicotine is what causes harm from tobacco use. Most of the harm is from combustion, so clarifying that misperception is important. And then we are regulated by the FDA. When you’re in the nicotine business, responsibility needs to be at the heart of everything you do.”  Altria, through its subsidiaries Helix Innovations and NJOY, sued the FDA in September, claiming the agency blocked newer nicotine products from reaching the market through its review process, which the nicotine company is seeking to overhaul. Through the Premarket Tobacco Product Application (PMTA), the FDA is legally required to review new tobacco products before they reach market and decide if the product provides an overall public health benefit within 180 days of submitting an application. Altria claims the FDA has failed to meet that deadline, and that the regulator’s red tape and bureaucracy stalled newer On! products from reaching the market, while foreign competitors flood store shelves.  The FDA said it would consider revisions to the PMTA and consider new rules as the market continues to change, and last month, U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas granted a joint request from the FDA and the plaintiffs to pause litigation.  Mancuso explained that Altria sued the FDA because it needed enforcement against illicit products. Reiterating what was in the lawsuit, he said what should take the FDA six months to review was taking six years in some cases, allowing illegal products, particularly from China, from not just taking market share, but also skirting standards Mancuso believes the FDA should keep in place to protect the safety of the consumer. He claimed competing overseas products are marketed in vape shops as made in the U.S.A, but are mislabeled. “Quite frankly, the regulations are broken,” Mancuso said. “There’s too much information. We still want a high standard, but it should be streamlined.  “Guidance is not durable,” he added. “It can be torn up immediately. What we want is more rapid authorization, so that consumers have product choices that they can choose from.”  The regulatory landscape of nicotine is similar in some ways to how cannabis is being introduced and regulated in U.S. markets, Mancuso suggested, such that the substance is legal in half of U.S. states, but there’s no federal standard, creating a “hodgepodge” of regulations. “Regulations are hard for any business,” Mancuso said. “At the very least, it should be an even playing field, not a playing field where bad actors are in a better position than responsible companies like ours. events.title: Paralympians surprised infrastructure authority has no employees with disability
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane 2032's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority has no employees with disability Brisbane will host the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2032, with planning underway for 17 new and upgraded venues. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority's (GIICA) latest annual report shows it has no employees with disability. Paralympians say it is a missed opportunity as the state prepares for the 2032 Games. GIICA says it has established a reference group to ensure accessibility requirements are met for the venues. The independent authority responsible for key 2032 Olympics and Paralympics venues has no employees with disability. Para-athletes say it is a missed opportunity. The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) was established in late 2024 to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of 17 new and upgraded venues for the Games. GIICA's employment headcount grew by 50 per cent in the 2025-26 financial year compared to the previous year. Its latest annual report showed its workforce, of 81 employees, included no people with disability. Brisbane Stadium at Victoria Park is one of the venues GIICA is overseeing for the 2032 Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) Dual Paralympic medallist Karni Liddell said that was "surprising". "Zero per cent is not reflective of how many people with disabilities are in Australia," she said. Ms Liddell, who lives in Queensland, said planning for the Games was not just about making stadiums accessible. She said getting to the venues was always the hardest part for people with disability. Paralympian Karni Lidell says people with disability should have a positive experience at the Games. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato ) "We don't want them showing up to Brisbane and having a really negative experience," she said. In 2018, the Gold Coast hosted the Commonwealth Games' largest para-sport program, but the international event's transport to and from the venues was not accessible. How Brisbane's 2032 Games can learn from the past A report highlighting the "missed opportunities" for people with disability at past global sporting events hopes to create a "road map" for Brisbane's 2032 Games. Gravel car parks were used for disability parking, and people in wheelchairs could not use the toilets in the trains or move between carriages, a Queenslanders with Disability Network and Urbis 2024 report found. Fellow Queensland Paralympian Marayke Jonkers said the Games won't be the most inclusive and accessible if people with lived experience aren't in the rooms when decisions are made about venues. "It's a missed opportunity," she said. "Very few people with a disability are ever going to be a Paralympian, but we all do need a job." Ms Jonkers said she has been unsuccessful in applying for jobs connected to the 2032 Games. Paralympian Marayke Jonkers says an amazing legacy for the Games would be improved employment outcomes for people with disability. ( Supplied: Marayke Jonkers ) "I did not want to get a job because I was disabled," she said. "What I have experienced trying to find work after having two university degrees, started a charity, being the president of the board of very big ASIC-registered companies … it's still really hard to actually get employment." Ms Jonkers said people with disability are more than twice as likely to be unemployed compared to those without disability. She said changing that statistic would be a "pretty amazing" legacy for the games. "If we really want to do well in 2032 as a country, it's not just about the athletes for 10 days," Ms Jonkers said. GIICA was established to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of new and upgraded venues for the Brisbane Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) A GIICA spokesperson said the venues will be accessible, inclusive and welcoming for everyone. They said the authority has partnered with Queenslanders With Disability Network (QDN) and Paralympics Australia to establish an accessibility reference group to ensure requirements are met across venue design and construction. The group met for the first time in September and included people with lived experience of disability, para-athletes and accessibility advocates. "Their insights will help GIICA test ideas, identify opportunities and make informed decisions as we deliver venues that are accessible," the spokesperson said.

events.title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
events.summary: Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results. events.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
events.summary: President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled. "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says. The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC. Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast. What would happen if one exploded in Washington? Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats. The Department of Homeland Security 's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors. DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks. The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials. Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site. The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off. Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says. Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says. Has a dirty bomb ever been used? No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports , though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts. The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia. In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice . The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized. The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

events.title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns
events.summary: Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s youth unemployment report? Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights. The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham , called a “watershed moment” for young people. But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government. In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage. “ A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government : employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.” Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups. “The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said. Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work. He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”. Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work. It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people. The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim. People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”. The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said. Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments. The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office. Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals. Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo. ” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts. McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.” On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate. And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences.

events.title: Food relief takes election back seat but cost of living front of mind for voters
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cost of living bites hard across regional Victoria as voters head to the polls Susan Naveed visits Whittington Neighbourhood House weekly to help feed her and her nine-year-old son. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Regional Victorian food relief centres fear funding that expires next year will threaten their ability to supply 100,000 meals a week. The relief centres are also struggling with food shortages due to supermarkets reducing waste. The food centres are calling on Victorian election candidates to commit to further funding. Susan Naveed never thought she would need food relief. But after leaving her job due to personal reasons a year ago, Ms Naveed is now a frequent customer of Whittington Neighbourhood House's Foodbank relief centre in Geelong. Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog. "Sometimes if it wasn't for Foodshare I don't know if my son and I would have food," Ms Naveed said. But a looming food shortage may become a reality for Ms Naveed and thousands of others, with six regional food relief centres due to run out of state government funding in July. A Foodbank hunger report in October found 69 per cent of households experienced food insecurity for the first time in the past year. A volunteer packs food at the Bendigo Foodshare centre. ( Supplied ) In the 2025 state government budget, Regional Food Security Alliance received $6 million over two years for its relief centres in Wodonga, Bendigo, Geelong, Shepparton, Mildura and Warrnambool. Neither Labor nor the coalition have committed to extending the grant. Alliance chair Cathie Steele said $12 million was needed for the next four years to meet demand. "Everyone could do with more but it's a tough time so we can't ask for more. We just need to keep our services going," Ms Steele said. "We've got to ensure that there's ongoing support for people." The Victorian government did not respond when asked by the ABC about whether funding would be continued from July 2027. A Victorian Liberals spokesperson said it was up to Labor to explain why future funding had not been secured. One Nation at the weekend committed $14 million over four years for the alliance's six relief centres if it formed government. Alliance chief executive Jacqui Watt said she had met with election candidates and current sitting members, including Carers and Volunteers Minister Luba Grigorovitch. Ms Watt said the response from all had been non-committal. Michelle Murphy says produce supplies have dropped in the past year. ( Supplied ) Bendigo Foodshare chief executive Michelle Murphy said her centre had experienced a 21 per cent drop in fresh food supplies this year and was struggling to keep shelves stocked. "We've seen less fresh produce coming through our warehouse as supermarkets continue to reduce their food waste and less produce becomes available through our statewide food relief partners," she said. Ritchies IGA supermarkets chief executive Fred Harrison said supermarkets were cutting food waste, which meant less was available to donate. "Business being tough, one of the areas you try to minimise is the amount of waste and throw-outs you might have," he said. Mr Harrison said short shelf-life products such as milk presented challenges for distribution. Fred Harrison says supermarkets have cut food waste in the past year. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) "Dairy products or small goods products are used by three or four days and logistically it's hard to do much with it once you get down to those short use-by dates." Coles told the ABC it had contributed $151 million in total community support "to promote health outcomes and build resilience". Woolworths said it had provided more than 44 million meals nationally in the past year through Foodshare and community organisations. "Our five local supermarkets in the Bendigo region donate excess food every week, rescuing an average of more than 800kg of food per week," the supermarket said. Ms Steele said the alliance was now focusing on getting supplies direct from food producers rather than supermarkets. Whittington Neighbourhood House in Geelong provides a vital service for people dealing with food insecurity. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Shoppers switch to cheaper alternatives According to Foodbank, more than half of food-insecure households have swapped to cheaper food alternatives, such as tinned food instead of fresh products, in the past year. Supermarkets have also seen a trend towards customers buying cheaper cuts of meat and moving to products such as minced meat to make meals go further, according to Mr Harrison.

events.title: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
events.summary: Kalshi has paused trading on several of its "mention" markets related to statements by President Donald Trump. A spokesperson for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission told CNBC it has placed holds on some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets' certifications. A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on Kalshi. Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday. Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast. Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments. Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month. The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk. A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025. "The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson. In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order. In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied. A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000 . Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets. In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues. As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: Gina Raimondo criticizes Trump admin chip policy
events.summary: Gina Raimondo, former commerce secretary and CEO of RAISE US, said that when it comes to selling chips to China, the US government has to put national security above corporate revenues. Raimondo said that when she was running the Commerce Department under the Biden administration, she spent a lot of time with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, going over the rules and what they could and could not sell. “They weren’t always happy,” she said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. But she added that she always put national security first and that you couldn’t “put a price” on America’s national security. “This administration hasn’t been like that,” Raimondo said. She described the ever-changing message on chips as: “‘No, you can’t sell chips.’ ‘Yes you can, if we can get a 25% cut.’ You’re either for America’s national security or you’re not — it’s not at a price.” Referencing new export rules to crack down on China’s ability to rent compute, she said she started work on that two years ago, but then the “buzzer rang and the game was over,” she said. “Why did it take two years for that to happen? I don’t know, but I’m glad they’re moving in that direction.” She added that China “wakes up every day” thinking “how do we beat America?” When asked whether she would run for president on the Democratic ticket in 2028, Raimondo deflected. “My next job is my current job.” — Ellen DiMauro
