events.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
events.summary: An aerial view of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in September Jae C. Hong/AP Photo A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found. A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided. Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters. Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph. Guests ride the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California, in 2023. Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades. Christopher’s is a third. A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents. “How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.” CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle. Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”  Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said. When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.” Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain. The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel. That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4. Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later. It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America. Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections , and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency. But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2. events.title: Trump has arrived in Asia. Here’s what he said about Iran and Deutsche Bank
events.summary: Trump has arrived in Manila ahead of meetings with regional leaders and a trip to China for talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. He threatened Iran after CNN reported a possible dirty bomb or chemical weapon plot in Washington, D.C. Trump said Deutsche Bank “shouldn’t have” leaked his tax details, after the FT reported the bank mistakenly disclosed them in 2017 and didn't tell the White House. U.S. President Donald Trump has arrived for his high-stakes trip to Asia, and took a range of questions on subjects from Iran to Deutsche Bank leaking details about his tax. The president landed in Manila, Philippines, for the initial leg of his trip on Tuesday and answered rapid-fire questions from the press while meeting with other leaders. Asked about a possible Iranian threat to Washington, D.C., he said that, if there were an attack, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before." The question was about CNN reporting that U.S. intelligence suggested the country was planning to target senior members of Trump's administration with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the U.S. capital. "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," Trump said. CNBC has not independently verified CNN's report. But the president also said he believed his administration was "very close to getting it done" when it came to the Iran war. While Trump was airborne, the Financial Times reported Deutsche Bank had mistakenly leaked details of his taxes in March 2017, during his first presidential term. The mistake was kept from the White House at the time, according to the FT. In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years. "Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said. Asked about the situation in Manila, the president said, "I paid a lot of tax." "They shouldn't have done it. It's illegal for them to do it," he added. Trump was also asked about Nvidia 's announcement on Tuesday of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company, which reports earnings later on Tuesday, is reeling from the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned last week after having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. "It's a great company. It's a great idea," Trump said. Trump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. He is also due to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Xi. Asked by a reporter if he would have a separate meeting with only Putin, Trump said: "I don't know, but I would, if it's available, I would do that. He's coming. I mean, it's really with the guests. I am the guest of President Xi." Trump met the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping in the Philippines and the prime minister of Thailand. He is due to China on Wednesday. Speaking at a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders as the event wrapped up for the day, Trump touted his record during his second term, citing investment into the U.S., trade deals made with countries represented by attendees at the dinner, energy infrastructure buildouts and America's AI industry. Trump, who has led a campaign to rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence," or "SI," told leaders around the table that the U.S. is "leading the world" in the technology. "We have the world's most powerful SI ecosystem," he said. "We're leading everybody by a lot, and we hope to keep it that way, and we will keep it that way." He added that the U.S. has "the strongest and most capable military on the planet," pointing to investments in the armed forces and the country's defense sector. "We make the greatest equipment. You saw that in Venezuela. You see it in Iran. You see it everywhere," Trump said.

events.title: To appoint the next comptroller general of the United States, follow the law
events.summary: The new approach being employed to appoint the next Comptroller General of the United States should raise a red flag. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), which is headed by the Comptroller General, plays an important role in helping Congress discharge its responsibilities under Article I of the U.S. Constitution, particularly in connection with oversight of the Executive Branch. We were shocked to learn that U.S. Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), Chairman of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (HSGAC), recently and spontaneously requested that names be submitted to him, under a short time constraint, to be recommended to the President for nomination as the next Comptroller General of the United States. Under the GAO Act of 1980, a 10-member statutory bipartisan and bicameral Comptroller General Selection Commission was created. Chairman Paul is a member, since he is Chair of the HSGAC, but he is not the Chairman of the Commission. That Commission is required to jointly develop and transmit a list of at least three qualified nominees to the President. That is the law, and that is how the process of appointing the Comptroller General has been conducted since 1980. The current vacancy for Comptroller General of the United States began on Dec. 30, 2025, and yet the Commission and its members have never met. Equally shocking is that Sen. Paul took the liberty as HSGAC Chairman to insert an empty placeholder for an unnamed nominee for Comptroller General of the United States for a Nov. 19, 2026, Committee confirmation hearing. Again, Sen. Paul did so even though the statutorily required Comptroller General Selection Commission has never convened or submitted a list of candidates. Then, on Nov. 16, President Trump submitted a nominee for confirmation. The General Accounting Office Act of 1980 included a revised method for appointing the Comptroller General. It recognized that the position was in the Legislative Branch and that GAO was the primary agency the Congress uses to conduct oversight of the Executive Branch. Therefore, it provided for a bipartisan and bicameral commission to recommend candidates to the President for possible appointment. It also provided for a 15-year non-renewable term with extremely difficult removal requirements to help ensure the independence of the Comptroller General. This 15-year term is the longest for any appointed position in the federal government. To be clear, the 1980 law doesn’t say in so many words that the President must pick from the Commission’s list. The Senate report on the bill said he could, “in his discretion,” look elsewhere, but should give the Commission’s recommendations “great weight.” You can’t weigh a list that doesn’t exist. Every Comptroller General nominated since 1980 came from a Commission list, and the law’s answer to a President who wants other options is to ask the Commission for more names, not to skip it. Henry Wray, a former GAO attorney who helped develop the 1980 law, says the current unprecedented process “violates both the letter and the spirit of the law.” It is extremely important for Congress to follow the statutory process. Dave Walker and Gene Dodaro (two of the coauthors of this piece) were unanimously confirmed under this process in 1998 and 2010, respectively. Both of these appointments were made under the statutory commission method, which has worked like a charm. With regard to potential candidates, any Comptroller General should be a highly qualified executive with relevant past experience who will operate in a professional, objective, fact-based, non-partisan, non-ideological, and non-personal manner. The Comptroller General must be independent from the Executive Branch, which the GAO audits, investigates, and evaluates on behalf of the Congress and the American people. In addition, any Comptroller General must have broad bipartisan support. In fact, every one of the past eight Comptrollers General was confirmed with overwhelming bipartisan support. All of these factors are of critical importance for the Comptroller General to be credible and for him or her, and the GAO, to be effective. Since Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Paul and President Trump have not followed the statutory requirements for the appointment of the Comptroller General, the Nov. 19, 2026, confirmation hearing should be canceled, and the normal appointment process should be adhered to. events.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust T he gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate. Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work , he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit. While cuts to some benefits are part of the package, this doesn’t look like a rerun of the Starmer government’s ignominious failure to cut £5bn from the welfare bill. Its fiscal impact claims to be largely neutral, with spending on employment support offset by savings. Higher workforce participation is not expected to significantly reduce working-age benefits for a decade. Instead, the plan is to face down demands by the Tories and Reform UK to cut welfare spending and a poisonous narrative about workshy “snowflakes” , by persuading voters that what young adults need is help. Of the hundreds of young people he met, said Mr Milburn, “I have not found a single one who wanted to be Neet”. A Youth Opportunity Service will be the new system’s “engine room”, offering wraparound support, including with health issues, to those who need it. Legislation will ensure that access to an adviser, and a job or training place, are guaranteed. Mayors will be responsible for delivery, making the new Neets service a core element of the devolution project . Mr Milburn says that jobs must be created for the scheme to succeed, and draws unfavourable comparisons between the UK and countries that spend more on employment support relative to benefits. While he stops short of demanding that employer national insurance rises should be reversed, there is implied criticism of earlier decisions taken without sufficient regard to their impact. Presumably, his unit will take charge of a proposed “youth opportunity test”, whereby every new policy is examined from this perspective. Ministers should expect the principle of age-linked entitlements to be challenged. Mr Milburn makes a good case for treating young adults without significant work experience or higher education as a distinct group. But 18- to 24-year-olds are adults, and there are legitimate objections to drawing lines in this way. Nor can people be expected to take it on trust that the new opportunities and allowances will be an adequate replacement for what they lose when they are moved off existing benefits. The Department for Work and Pensions has frequently failed to assess need fairly in the past. And while the proposal for waiting-time limits for mental health support is welcome, it points to a challenging reordering of NHS priorities. This is not the only commitment that will be difficult to deliver. The need for cross-department cooperation will stretch Whitehall to its limits. But the emphasis on young people’s long-term prospects is positive, as is the decisive rejection of welfare cuts to bolster fiscal credibility. Youth participation is an overlooked form of inclusion. Increasing it is a sound principle for a Labour government. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: US-China AI race causing global ‘alarm,’ UN's top tech envoy says
events.summary: The rest of the world is looking at the AI arms race between the US and China with “some kind of alarm,” the UN’s top tech envoy said Tuesday. Other countries “don’t want their agency taken away with this attention just on this competition between two players,” Amandeep Singh Gill, the Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies of the United Nations, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “The rest of the world wants to build up its own models, its own infrastructure.” Gill told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie that while other countries are not trying to compete with frontier labs in the US and China, they still want to innovate. “So this also translates to some alarm in terms of guardrails, because if you have a race, then you tend to ignore the rules,” Gill said, adding that recent incidents around AI safety have sparked concerns among several countries that “shortcuts are being taken.” Building out Africa’s AI infrastructure Gill also emphasized the importance of addressing Africa’s AI shortfall, saying more capacity needs to be built to bridge the AI divide and guarantee the continent access to emerging technologies. Gill said a country like Ethiopia, with a population above 130 million, needs significantly more GPUs. “You need a massive infusion of capacity, but capacity alone is not enough,” he added. Connectivity and energy availability are necessary, too. Investing in African AI would be “creating a market,” Gill said, and could improve AI’s reputation by showing how it can be used to improve water scarcity, public health, and public services issues. “It’s easy to say AI will solve cancer, but if you can point to these useful applications that work at societal scale, then it reinforces the case on the beneficial side of AI,” Gill added. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability T he catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation. With US interest rates rising, the cost of borrowing dollars for developing nations is seeing more cash paid to creditors. Between 2021 and 2024, the debt of such countries increased by just 2%, but debt repayments rose by 28%. The UN’s latest figures show that in the global south, excluding China, external interest costs reached $125bn in 2024. The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, was right when he said that developing countries faced a “downward loop”, where climate risks raise borrowing costs, disasters increase debt levels and mounting repayments leave governments with little to invest in resilience. This makes them more vulnerable to future shocks. Climate finance, he argues , “must help countries break free”. But is the world failing to tackle climate change because governments lack the political will? Or because climate action, among other development objectives, is being pursued within a global economic system whose rules entrench the inequalities inherited from colonialism? That is the question posed by Fadhel Kaboub , an economist at Denison University, Ohio, and adviser to the UN. His answer is that those structures never truly disappeared, but have evolved into today’s rules governing international finance, trade, investment and taxation. The upshot is that the countries least responsible for global warming have the fewest resources to confront its consequences. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential At Cop31, Dr Kaboub was among a group of experts arguing for the least developed countries to emulate Mark Carney’s middle-power strategy and employ the same logic of collective bargaining in a world of great-power rivalry. Poorer nations should seek not just strategic autonomy but economic sovereignty. The experts suggested that they pool resources and build regional common markets as well as green industries together. The aim was to negotiate as a bloc with western powers – and China – for technology transfer and investment without racking up further debt. Half a century after developing nations demanded a new international economic order , the climate crisis may be giving that unfinished struggle a new purpose.

events.title: Salesforce sets AI budgets after employees spent 'thousands of dollars per month on tokens,' memo says
events.summary: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Salesforce is setting AI budgets for employees. Some spent thousands per month on tokens last quarter, according to an internal memo. Other companies have introduced similar spending limits to rein in climbing AI costs. Salesforce is setting AI budgets for employees after some spent thousands per month on tokens last quarter, according to an internal memo viewed by Business Insider. "Starting this month, every role has a monthly token budget, so we can focus our AI spend on the work that matters most for our customers and business," Salesforce Chief Operating Officer Miguel Milano wrote in an email to employees. The budgets reflect a delicate balance for companies adopting AI. They want to control spending for the expensive technology without discouraging employees from using it. A Salesforce spokesperson said the company does not have companywide individual token budgets, leaving it up to team leaders to manage AI usage. "Our focus is always to ensure that our AI investments deliver the greatest impact for our business and customers," the spokesperson added. Salesforce piloted the new AI budgets on one team for a month and found that group "was operating well under budget by month two with no drop in output," the memo stated. The sales organization under President and Chief Revenue Officer Alexa Vignone will have a budget of $1,000 per month for technical roles, and $100 per month for non-technical roles like sellers. Salesforce Customer Success, under Jim Roth, and Salesforce Global Professional Services and Forward Deployed Engineering, under Lori Steele, will have budgets of $500 per month for technical roles and $100 per month for non-technical roles. Other companies have introduced similar spending limits. As Business Insider recently reported , Coinbase has weekly AI spending caps ranging from $500 to $5,000 based on employee roles and seniority. JPMorgan Chase introduced a $2,000 monthly limit for some engineers using Anthropic's Claude Code. In May, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said the company expected to spend roughly $300 million on Anthropic tokens this year, largely for coding agents. Read the memo Team, As we scale our AI capabilities, we're getting smarter about how we manage them. Last quarter, some individuals spent thousands of dollars per month on tokens. events.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
events.summary: Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware. Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat. Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy. Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices. KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker. KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added. The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns. Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said. That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people. AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said. By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data . In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours. Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4. The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

events.title: Anthropic forges ahead with its IPO even as AI fears mount and markets wobble
events.summary: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies NEW YORK -- Investors fearing an AI bubble are getting jittery. Financing costs are rising. Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry. It's not an ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock, but Anthropic is pressing ahead with its blockbuster initial public offering anyway. No ordinary sale, the Claude chatbot maker's IPO could raise more than $60 billion on Thursday, a massive haul that, depending on the ultimate pricing and other issues, could rival SpaceX's in June . But Anthropic is facing headwinds as it prepares for its coming-out party . Tech stocks have done well so far this year, but the path higher has been rocky, especially for AI-related companies. That's not a reassuring setup for the IPO. One particularly volatile AI stock, CoreWeave, plunged 15.5% on Oct. 14 over fears it wouldn't be able to borrow enough, cheaply enough to fund its growth. The stock then swung wildly. On Wednesday, the company, which buys chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, surged 25% after an encouraging earnings report, only to plunge 7% the next day. Most stocks move no more than 2% on the average trading day. Adding to the sector volatility recently has been the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, a high-profile AI booster, built Nvidia into a linchpin of the industry and a major financial backer of other AI companies. Stock in the AI chip designer dropped 4% Monday, dragging the broader S & P 500 down for a third day in a row. Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the IPO. It also sells chips to Anthropic but the latter also buys from AMD and others. As to whether the gyration in AI-tied stocks argues for an IPO delay, note that volatility can cut both ways: It might be signaling the much debated AI bubble could burst soon so it's better to sell stock now, fast. And history shows demand for IPOs can disappear quickly. In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public in the U.S., but then investors got scared of a possible recession the next year and demand dried up with only 71 making market debuts. Another reason to sell stock now is that the other way to raise money — borrowing — has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting its resources are limited to pay interest and principal. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech On the plus side, it has ample cash, although it will likely run through it quickly if it can't raise more soon given its outsized spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion in computing and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. Higher interest rates are not the only problem. Politics threatens to slow growth, too. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democrat governors vowing to stop new construction. It wouldn't be unprecedented for Anthropic to postpone its IPO at the last minute. After a bout of volatility following President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, several companies postponed their initial offerings, including the online ticket marketplace StubHub and Klarna, a buy now, pay later business. And an Australian data center company, Firmus, called off its IPO last month because of jitters in the market. But newly elected Democrats don't take office until January. Anthropic could be betting that selling now is best before the feared crackdown begins in earnest. If the company does go ahead as expected, it will beat rival OpenAI to the market. That's an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don't want to buy stock in the next public AI company. And despite the jitters, companies on public markets are still fetching top prices. One measure of investor enthusiasm shows they are paying nearly as much as ever to buy stocks.

events.title: Nvidia tells robotics startups they have its support as questions swirl about its investment strategy
events.summary: Nvidia's headquarters. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Nvidia reassured robotics startups that its support would remain after Jensen Huang’s exit. Interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to pursue deals more slowly than Huang. Nvidia has backed more than 35 robotics and physical AI companies. Nvidia is reaching out to robotics startups with a message after Jensen Huang's sudden departure: The chipmaker still has their backs. Since Huang's resignation, the company and its venture capital arm, NVentures, have contacted at least three robotics startups they back to reassure them of its support, Business Insider has learned. The calls began last Thursday, shortly after Huang's resignation , with startups assured that business would continue as usual. The outreach comes amid uncertainty about Nvidia's broader investment strategy under interim CEO Colette Kress, who is not expected to pursue deals as quickly as Huang and has sometimes pushed back on investments he championed. Nvidia declined to comment on the calls. Under Huang, Nvidia became a major backer of robotics and "physical AI," the term he popularized for AI that can act in the real world. At the company's conferences, he often appeared onstage flanked by humanoid robots. Huang described robotics as the technology industry's "first opportunity to address a $50 trillion industry that has largely been void of technology until now." That enthusiasm translated into investments in more than 35 robotics and physical AI companies, according to PitchBook data. Of these, 29 have disclosed funding rounds totaling nearly $11 billion. Nvidia's portfolio includes humanoid makers Figure AI and Neura Robotics, robot foundation model developer Skild AI , self-driving software company Wayve , and autonomous trucking startup Waabi. The robotics investments are part of a broader push that made Nvidia a financial backer of much of the AI ecosystem. At the end of July, it held $48 billion in stakes across 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress Nvidia Deepu Talla, an Nvidia robotics vice president who worked on some of the company’s investments, told Business Insider that Nvidia intends to "continue to aggressively cultivate the ecosystem.” Nvidia's robotics products brought in $11 billion in the first half of this year, 30% more than in all of 2025, Talla said. Some of that revenue comes from companies Nvidia has invested in. The company's robotics strategy has two parts: developing the simulation tools, software, and chips that power robots, and investing in startups building them. The investments can turn startups into customers while giving Nvidia a stake in their success. "If you look at any cap table of a company that is compute-heavy, Nvidia is probably there, because they knew much of that money was going to flow back to them," one investor whose firm has backed multiple startups alongside Nvidia, told Business Insider. events.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
events.summary: Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper. Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant. How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so. In a blog post , Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill. Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands. events.title: Nearly $500k of underwater gear in limbo after shipping agent cancelled
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Goods in limbo after Australian Border Force cancels Top Logistics Australia depot licences Tim Hochgrebe says he has been waiting five months for his goods. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) Freight logistics experts say a crackdown on illicit products is slowing supply chains. Businesses awaiting the delivery of imported goods say the delays are creating trade and cash flow problems. Australian Border Force says owners of delayed goods, customs brokers, and freight forwarders should take steps to find to retrieve them. Importer Tim Hochgrebe has almost $500,000 worth of niche underwater equipment languishing somewhere within his supply chain, and no idea how to find it. The Byron Bay-based business owner is dealing with the fallout from the suspension of Top Logistics Australia, a Sydney-based company whose depot licences were cancelled in September by the Australian Border Force (ABF). He is one of a number of small importers left waiting on stock caught up in border delays as the Christmas trade period begins. Company director Peter Ping Xie is due to appear in Burwood Local Court on November 18, charged with dishonestly obtaining financial gain by deception. The ABC has confirmed the charges relate to the alleged importation of illicit tobacco and vapes into Australia. Mr Hochgrebe said the ABF cancellation of Top Logistics Australia had forced his Chinese-based shipping agent to find another freight logistics company in Australia. He said goods he had expected to receive within six weeks had still not arrived five months later. Tim Hochgrebe has been importing goods from China for over a decade. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) The company now handling his goods has an email address, but no phone number, and his efforts to contact it have so far failed. "There's no-one we can simply call and say, ' Hey, where's our stuff? Is it going to be a week? Is it going to be a month?'" he said. "It's just the limbo we are in that causes the trouble. "It's starting to affect our cash flow because we don't have the goods we long ago paid for." The ABC understands all consignments held by Top Logistics Australia have been cleared by ABF or transferred to other licensed depots for ongoing storage and processing. ABF recently published Australian Customs Notices advising the owners of goods, customs brokers, and freight forwarders to identify the location of their goods and take steps to retrieve them. The ABC has attempted to contact Top Logistics Australia for comment. Jane Laverty from Business NSW said small businesses were struggling to absorb the cost of delays and refunds, and the hit to their reputations and cash flow. "It's a lot of cost for a small business to be carrying," she said. Logistics experts say supply chains have been disrupted by a crackdown on the illicit tobacco and vape trade. Australian Border Force established Strikeforce Borderdale to tackle trade in illicit tobacco and vapes. ( Supplied: Australian Federal Police ) Industry body Freight and Trade Alliance represents the interests of importers, exporters, freight forwarders and customs brokers in Australia. General manager of freight policy and operations Tom Jensen said there were ongoing delays in the screening of cargo coming through Australian ports, particularly Sydney. Mr Jensen said, since December, border holds on some containers had blown out from one or two days to more than 30 days in extreme cases. "It's one of those things where at the moment a lot of innocent imports are being tied up because their containers are being flagged for inspection," he said. He said any significant delay added extra cost as importers had to pay for storage of the containers at the cargo terminal and container lease fees. Australian Border Force says it is clearing goods through customs within legislated time frames. ( ABC North Coast: Hannah Ross ) "ABF has thrown more resources at this, but there are still significant signs of delays here and there, so it definitely hasn't resolved the situation," he said. Data published in the ABF's 2025/2026 annual report shows sea cargo cleared within five days had fallen from its five-year average by almost 2 per cent, to 91.6 per cent. Victorian-based importer Phil Burn said he had nine remote-control lawn mowers worth $9,000 awaiting customs release. "Due to the excessive delays, I have had to personally refund the purchase cost of every mower," he said. Phil Burn has had to refund his customers due to delivery delays.

events.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
events.summary: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program , which can certify it and issue the certification mark. IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program . This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements. New industry connections group The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members. The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle. The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability. Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues. “The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.” Podcasts and blogs To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “ Ethically Aligned Design : 10 Years of Impact” podcast series . It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks. The episodes center around the vision for EAD , the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards. The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices. The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems. The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog art

events.title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
events.summary: After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues. The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates. Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail. On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues. Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues . Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches. So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems. Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read. After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program. By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved. This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages. events.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
events.summary: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models. Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump has a plan to limit student loans for nursing and other advanced degrees. A new bill would reverse those cuts.
events.summary: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand co-led the introduction of a new bill to expand advanced degrees that qualify for a higher student-loan borrowing cap. Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images A new bill calls to expand the list of programs that qualify for higher student-loan borrowing limits. Trump's repayment overhaul would allow 11 programs to qualify for the higher $200,000 borrowing cap. The bill calls for excluded programs, like advanced nursing, to qualify for the higher limit. Democratic lawmakers are pushing to expand access to higher student-loan borrowing limits . On Tuesday, Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand and Jeff Merkley introduced a bill that would expand the number of advanced degrees that qualify for a professional degree designation and thus a higher borrowing cap. President Donald Trump's student-loan repayment overhaul placed a $100,000 lifetime borrowing cap on graduate degrees and a $200,000 cap on professional degrees. The administration also planned to limit professional degrees to 11 programs, such as medicine and law, while excluding other programs like nursing, social work, and education. The limits were met with criticism by both Democratic and Republican lawmakers who argued that limiting borrowing for nurses would exacerbate the healthcare worker shortage. A lawsuit blocked the administration from implementing the new limits on July 1, and the Democratic lawmakers are now seeking to codify professional status for an expanded list of degrees . "Nurses, teachers, and social workers are dedicated public servants, and Congress must do everything it can to help recruit the next generation of these heroes," Merkley said in a statement. "We're already facing a shortage of these critical workers, and new limits on federal student loans for these professions and others threaten to further jeopardize the future of our workforce." The bill would maintain professional status for programs that already qualify while restoring professional status to additional programs, including nursing, public health, and physician assistant programs. It would also give the education secretary the flexibility to add more programs that meet the "professional degree" requirements. It follows a bipartisan bill earlier this year that called for the inclusion of advanced nursing degrees on the list of professional degrees, noting that tuition for some programs exceeded the borrowing cap. The Department of Education previously said that most advanced nursing programs borrow within the limits. After a blue wave in the midterms, Democratic lawmakers said they plan to bolster oversight of the student-loan industry and Trump's repayment changes through hearings, investigations, and legislation. Gillibrand said in a statement that students pursuing fields like social work or nursing "should not have to break the bank to serve their communities." "This bill would help our students, our universities, and our communities, and I'm determined to get it passed," she said. Have a story to share about student loans? events.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
events.summary: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits. Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits. He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures. The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms. But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation. "That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future." The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage. There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year. But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential". McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers". The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs. He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow. In his wide-ranging 250 page report , external , Milburn proposes: An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support. And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending. At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 14 hours ago Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 12 hours ago Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 13 hours ago Milburn has said his plans are not about saving money - and his report says the government will not see overall savings from reduced benefit bills and higher tax receipts until 2036/27, when it will claw back £200m. But by then, it assumes the share of 16–24-year-olds that are Neet will have gone down from 13% - one of the highest in Europe - to 5%, the lowest in the UK since records began. Launching his report earlier on Tuesday, Milburn said "half measures will not do" because "the scale of the problem is just too big for that". He added: "Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people, not because they lack talent, not because they lack ambition, not because they do not want to work. "This is not a crisis of aspiration; it is a crisis of opportunity.

events.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust Microsoft Source | 5 minutes One year ago at Microsoft Ignite, we introduced Frontier Transformation. The premise was simple: technology exists to serve humanity and deliver real business outcomes. Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. Ignite 2026 is the next milestone in this journey as we introduce new innovations that deliver on the promise of all three of these pillars. Our goal is to build a frontier ecosystem , one that lets every organization benefit from progress at the frontier while preserving what makes it unique.   “We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large,” said Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, in his opening keynote at Ignite. “For us, that comes down to three things: keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring you have ownership over your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.” Human ambition: AI should serve humanity, not the other way around It starts with the work people are trying to do, which is why we think of Microsoft Copilot as the new operating system for work.   New Copilot Workspaces gives people and agents a shared space to work together as a team. Autopilot, a long-running agent, can manage recurring tasks and move projects forward without being prompted at every step, and Copilot Code lets anyone build dashboards, trackers and apps in natural language with enterprise security and governance built in. Together with Office in Copilot, and features like Today, they make up the new Copilot, which is built to translate raw intelligence into real value. Copilot is already driving transformation at scale among our customers. Volkswagen Group is equipping more than 330,000 employees with Copilot and The Estée Lauder Companies has expanded Copilot to more than 14,000 people across its global workforce. Copilot is also connecting to the systems teams rely on most, including Dynamics 365, as well as announcing Salesforce in Copilot , a plugin available in preview with more than 38 pre-built sales skills. Intelligence: Compound your intelligence without giving away your IP Agents are only as effective as the context they work with. Microsoft IQ is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing and reusing the business knowledge apps and agents need. New business plugins let teams package that knowledge into reusable, trusted context, skills and tools that can be shared across the business.  Customers are already turning that intelligence into business outcomes. Publicis Groupe is empowering employees to build custom AI skills that combine Microsoft IQ with Publicis’ industry expertise and proprietary data, then test them against real-world client scenarios. The result is faster innovation, quicker decision-making and greater value for clients. In Microsoft Foundry , new continuous improvement tools help customers develop more powerful agents and even train models automatically based on real production signals: optimizing for quality, latency and cost-effectiveness. New models for coding, cyber image and audio are also being introduced, as well as the general availability of Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , a fast, low-cost decision model for tasks like routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control. Trust: Observability at every layer of the stack and for every person As agents move from answering questions to taking action, trust becomes the deciding factor. There should never be a choice between innovation and safety. Microsoft Perception , now generally available, brings together specialized agents to find, defend and remediate vulnerabilities — powered by models including our MAI-Cyber line — to help defenders stop threats at machine speed. Agent 365 Business Analytics gives leaders a clear view of what their AI is costing and what it is delivering, from task success to hours assisted. And Windows is expanding its operating-system-level protection for agents, with more granular containment with Microsoft Execution Containers, built-in agent identity with Entra support and Agent 365 policies enforced on every device, giving IT more control over agent activity in their organizations. Building on its use of Microsoft Defender, Entra and Purview, BNY is exploring capabilities in Project Perception to further strengthen security and governance. These efforts support BNY’s broader AI ambitions, including its collaboration with Microsoft to complete the first agentic negotiation of a U.S. Treasury trade. Infrastructure: A cloud built for AI at global scale Microsoft builds Azure as a single system, co-designing silicon, servers, networking and racks around what we learn running workloads at scale. As agents increasingly work outside the model, from running tools to compiling code, CPUs matter even more. Cobalt 200 virtual machines , generally available today, deliver up to 50% better performance than the previous generation. Cobalt will reach 23 regions by year end and becomes a significant share of new Azure compute capacity in 2027. Azure Catalyst brings Azure and GitHub agentic tools together in one connected experience for modernizing the applications, databases and infrastructure that AI depends on, and hybrid intelligence on Windows lets AI run wherever it makes the most sense, on the device or in the cloud, starting with GitHub Copilot for coding and Copilot for everyday work. Taken together, today’s announcements demonstrate that the organizations that pull ahead in this next phase are the ones that connect intelligence to their people, their data and their processes, with trust built in from the start. That is the frontier ecosystem we are building with our customers and partners. To see it in action, watch the Microsoft Ignite keynote and explore the full set of announcements in the Book of News . ( Getty Images: Steve Bell ) Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in buying into the Hobart Hurricanes and the Hobart stadium precinct. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement for the stadium would signal a change in policy. An updated cost for the Hobart stadium project is expected in the next few weeks. Cricket looms as a wildcard in the Tasmanian government's hunt for more funds to build the new Macquarie Point stadium. And at least one American billionaire has expressed an interest in investing in the stadium precinct , as part of a potential power play involving the Hobart Hurricanes cricket team. Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil wants to buy at least a 50 per cent share in the Hobart Hurricanes, following Cricket Australia's decision to green-light the privatisation of the Big Bash League. As part of a broader cricket and infrastructure play, Mr Govil is interested in a slice of the Macquarie Point stadium and precinct, envisioning a place where American college football-style parties may be held before future Hurricanes games. "I think it's going to be very, very exciting. And to be part of that? Imagine," he told the ABC. Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in the Hobart Hurricanes and Macquarie Point stadium project. ( Supplied: Eagle Team ) Mr Govil, who founded Infinite Computer Solutions and digital healthcare company Zyter, is worth upwards of US$2 billion. Liberals' vote hits 25-year low as One Nation continues Tasmanian surge Tasmanian brand Coal River Farm enters voluntary administration Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Multiple shots fired at Tasmanian home with person inside He owns the Welsh Fire, which plays in the UK Hundred competition, the Ricky Ponting-coached Washington Freedom in America's Major League Cricket competition, and is funding the construction of a 10,000-capacity cricket stadium for the Freedom in Frederick, Maryland. He wants a stake in the Big Bash League and has targeted the Hurricanes — and its prospective new stadium. "There are two elements to it, part A and part B," he said. "We would come in, and part A is the operations team, taking ownership of the Hobart Hurricanes team. The Hurricanes would then, in turn, lease the ground and facility from entity B, which would have different shareholders including us," he said. Sanjay Govil says it would be "exciting" to have a stake in the Macquarie Point stadium. ( Supplied: Cox Architecture ) The Auburn college football fan, who also owns a stake in entertainment and events company Mari, envisages a college football-style atmosphere and fan experiences before and after Hurricanes games at Macquarie Point. "That infrastructure would not just include the stadium, but a tailgating area, shops, restaurants, a whole experience centre," he said. "It's all about experience. That's the expertise I want to bring to the Hobart Hurricanes. More stadium money sought amid cost blowout concerns The Tasmanian government has begun the process of courting financial partners to help fund its Hobart stadium, as the $1.13 billion project faces a budget crunch. The prospect of cricket-induced private investment was floated with Premier Jeremy Rockliff at a September 8 meeting between him and Cricket Tasmania bosses. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement would signal a backflip. It had previously explored a public-private partnership for the stadium, commissioning reports by Perth consultants Paxon Group and Melbourne-based Infrastructure Advisory Group last year — but ultimately decided against the model, deeming it too high a risk to the state . But with a stadium budget crunch on the horizon, a cricket-flavoured public-private partnership might become enticing to a government desperately needing outside funds to help fund the build. The stadium looks set to exceed its project budget of $1.13 billion, with state funding constrained to $875 million, as part of a government agreement with upper house MLC Bec Thomas in exchange for her support for the project in Tasmania's parliament last year. BESIX Watpac won the tender to construct the Macquarie Point stadium.

events.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Harvard study claims emissions attributable to datacenters are two to three times higher than in 2018 GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs 3 hours ago Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade 5 hours ago REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant 13 hours ago Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 20 hours ago US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 1 day ago Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses.
