events.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
events.summary: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous I t’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Neets review has taken on a life of its own. ITV has commissioned a four-part docudrama on the writing of the report. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Neets: The Musical will be opening just before Christmas. And Mud’s classic, That’s Neet, That’s Neet, I Really Love Your Tiger Feet is the hot favourite to be the UK’s entry for next year’s Eurovision. At long last, a song we can all get behind and that has a realistic chance of winning. But Tuesday was the day. The day Big Al took centre stage at Google HQ to tell us he was about to tell us everything he had already told us. We just had to listen quietly and bathe in his reflected glory. And tick off all the review’s highlights as they were mentioned. Neets bingo. We were in danger of creating a lost generation. In fact we already might have done, as more than 10% of young people under 25 had been out of work, education or training for more than 20 years. It wasn’t that young people were lazy snowflakes. They had been let down. Time now to invest in this generation , not write them off. To invest in their futures like other northern European countries do. You couldn’t get hundreds of thousands of people back to work just by cutting benefits. That was delusional. Rather, a culture shift was needed. A recalibration of the way the state engaged with an abandoned generation. Almost seamlessly, the venue shifted to the Commons where Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, surrounded by Andy Burnham and most of the cabinet, was due to give his own 10-minute potted version of the Milburn review. First though, an intervention from the speaker, who wanted to put on record his concern that copies of the report hadn’t been laid before the house. Not that anyone needed a copy; we all knew it off by heart. Pat then repeated pretty much everything Milburn had said an hour earlier. The only difference being that McFadden managed to sound a bit gloomier about the whole thing. Not because he wasn’t enthusiastic, but because he was. The more engaged and upbeat Pat is, the more depressed he sounds. It’s just the way he’s wired. Gloom is his natural state of being. Even with McFadden’s rather downbeat delivery, this still felt like quite a moment. For the last two and a half years, many have criticised the government for its lack of vision. For lurching from one crisis to the next. Here, at last, was that vision. A major shift in the way the state would engage with a generation of young people who hitherto had been ignored or left on benefits. You couldn’t help feeling a bit sorry for Keir Starmer. He was the one who – albeit late in the day – had commissioned the review, but Burnham would get the credit. That’s showbiz for you. While Labour benches were packed, barely a dozen Tory backbench MPs had bothered to come for what might be a seismic shift in policy. Maybe they are the snowflakes. Or maybe they really aren’t that bothered that so many young people feel they have no future. Or maybe they couldn’t face sitting through the truly hopeless response of the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately. You really can’t blame so many Neets for feeling the odds are stacked against them when they see the rise and rise of Whately. Helen is everything the Tories believe Neets to be. Lazy, stupid. A woman without principle who has morphed into whatever shape is required to fit in with a Tory party sliding ever further to the right. If there were any justice, Whately would be one of the many people struggling to find a decent job. Or any job. Had she been born 25 years later, it would have been Helen claiming benefits. Her reply was one of the most half-witted imaginable. You can just about forgive the nastiness. That comes with the Tory territory. So of course she was demanding that billions more be cut from benefits. Because that’s the only language they think Neets understand. What was too much was the stupidity.

events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
events.summary: Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia. But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company. The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely. The company's board is investigating his conduct , which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive. The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang. Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead. The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life". Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal. Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics". "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added. Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company. Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return. Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement. On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course. While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law." events.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents Through the new AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to advance a common approach to AI transparency, security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft will also bring greater visibility into how AI models and agents interact with enterprise data across its products and services Microsoft Source | 5 minutes REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency. “For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.” Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. “As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.” From principles to practice The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. “Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.” Clear accountability Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential. Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions. “As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.”  See, verify, control Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. See: Know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took. Monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. Verify: Agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves. Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source (the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy) so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider’s account of its behavior. Control: Stay in charge of what AI is permitted to do. Clear evidence of each workflow’s purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with them when models and providers change. Organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider. Get involved Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency . events.title: Voters broke with Democrats on ballot initiatives
events.summary: The News PALO ALTO, Calif. — Democrats swept Republicans on Nov. 3, but some of their party’s progressive ideas didn’t make it with them, as a host of liberal ballot initiatives failed and conservative proposals passed across the country. In California, where Republicans lost every major race by landslides, voters rejected a billionaire wealth tax, made it harder to create one, and likely killed a measure that would have piloted public financing of elections. In Colorado, a deep blue electorate voted to ban gender surgeries on minors by 4 points and to bar trans athletes’ participation in female sports by 5 points. A similar sports proposal prevailed by 12 points in Washington, even as Democrats padded their state legislative majorities. And in Iowa, where Gov.-elect Rob Sand led a Democratic comeback, voters endorsed a two-thirds legislative supermajority for any income tax increase. The success of some conservative ideas down the ballot — largely focused on taxes and social issues — gave some hope to Republicans after a hopeless election night. Voters rejected their party, but took multiple opportunities to oppose tax increases and roll back progressive social policies.Democrats were not taking that as advice to their party. Instead, they believe that opposition money and muddled messaging overwhelmed them, and they could win if they made another run at the ballot. “The margin was narrow enough that if we do more education with voters, we could significantly narrow it and win this,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff at the union SEIU-UHW and a proponent of the California wealth tax. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful House candidate who was a top contributor to the wealth tax campaign, agreed. “When you have nearly half a billion dollars against you, and they spend it to spread straight-up lies about an issue, it’s hard to win unless you can get your own message out,” Chakrabarti said. “The campaign had a winning issue,” he said, “but failed to get its own message out.” Different ways to lose The Proposition 40 campaign was heavily outspent, with some of California’s wealthiest residents funding its opposition. According to state campaign finance records , $152 million went into the “no” effort, compared to a bit more than $33 million for “yes.” Spending for and against Proposition 42, which bars new wealth taxes, was similarly lopsided —nearly $128 million for, and nearly $35 million against. Some of the funding to kill the wealth tax also came from members of the Democratic Party’s coalition, like Planned Parenthood, which advocated for a long-term funding source over the proposed one-time levy. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it, as did Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, giving voters permission to support their ticket while voting against an idea backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. “Since it failed, I look forward to Gov. Newsom leading the fight by championing a national wealth tax, which he claimed he heavily supports,” said Chakrabati. The spending in other conservative down-ballot victories was more mixed. Supporters of Washington’s ban on transgender girls playing in girls sports out-spent opponents by a 3-1 margin. One of the coalition’s other priorities, which would have required schools to notify parents if their children identified as a different gender at school than at home, failed by 5 points. In Colorado, where transgender sports and medicine bans for minors passed narrowly, the “yes” side was heavily outspent by its opponents, the Families Not Politics coalition. “It’s unfortunate that this is an issue that’s been politicized,” said Erin Lee, the Democrat-turned-Independent whose Protect Kids Colorado coalition got the measures on the ballot. “Democrats have chosen this as a hill to die on, and Republicans have grabbed this as a political tool to wield. But when we started putting the team together, it became clear that this issue transcends the parties.” The Democratic Party in both blue states opposed the measures. Shasti Conrad, the chair of the Washington state Democratic Party, said that the sports measure “was very confusingly written,” while Republicans brought out their base to support it. Sources who worked to beat the measure told Semafor that their campaign was beset by bad planning and bad luck. The Gender Justice League, an LGBTQ+ rights group that was working against the measure, claimed to have “lost 80% of our foundation support and 35% of our government funding” as the Trump administration enforced its executive order on gender. The “no” campaign also resisted help from Third Way, the centrist Democratic think tank not beloved by progressives. Lanae Erickson, a Third Way vice president, shared research with campaigners in every state where a sports ban could appear on the ballot. “We found that most persuasive messages were around the gender checks component of the measure,” said Erickson, referring to language in the Washington initiative that required female athletes to prove their biological sex . Colorado campaigners used Third Way’s research; Washington campaigners opted not to until the campaign’s final weeks, when they ran some digital ads based on the information. Democrats in both states believed that their eventual messaging was not effective enough. “We had an extremely long ballot, and I think it was confusing to folks,” said Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo. “I think a lot of people didn’t know exactly what those provisions stood for. We have to make sure we’re protecting folks, and that we’re doing so clearly and specifically.” In no state where conservatives passed their preferred tax or social issue measures did Democrats say that their party’s position might change. Erickson, pointing to the margins in both Washington and Colorado, said that Third Way had been trying to find a winning path for trans rights for years, and that the results showed progress. “Funders kept telling us it’s an 80-20 issue, so they didn’t help us,” she said, referring to polling on trans participation in girls sports. “It’s not an 80-20 issue. But if the question is put to voters as the status quo or a blanket ban, people will say yes to the blanket ban.” David’s view Roughly speaking, there are two kinds of ballot measures – those designed to bring out voters for one of the major parties, and those designed to pass no matter what the parties do. For years, Democrats hoped that ballot measures raising the minimum wage would help them change the electorate. Two decades ago, Republicans thought the same about ballot measures that banned same-sex marriage. But in many cases, voters simply took the chance to separate their partisan preference from their issue preference. This is what happened on Nov. 3, when Republicans got no lift at all from measures that were most attractive to their hardcore voters. events.title: Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: AI Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences Microsoft Source | 8 minutes New integrations connect Salesforce with Microsoft Copilot, Teams and Fabric, helping enterprises turn Salesforce customer insights into action while maintaining existing security and permissions. New two-way Zero Copy integrations between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric enable organizations to securely query and analyze data across both platforms without maintaining duplicate datasets. Accenture is serving as design and implementation partner and pilot customer, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization. REDMOND, Wash., and SAN FRANCISCO — Nov. 17, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Salesforce Inc. (NYSE: CRM) today announced Copilotforce, a new partnership that helps employees get more done in the tools they already use by bringing Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences.   Unveiled at Microsoft Ignite, the partnership introduces new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin available in public preview with 38+ prebuilt sales skills. Together, these capabilities help businesses move faster, reduce manual work and get more value from their existing technology investments — while maintaining the security, governance and permissions they already rely on.   Bringing Salesforce workflows together with conversations, meetings and documents in Microsoft 365 means less time spent moving between systems and more time on the work that matters. Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with the work happening across the business so employees can make more informed decisions and take action without constantly switching applications. Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides relevant context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive. Work IQ and Salesforce help sellers understand not only what’s recorded in CRM, but what’s happening across customer conversations and collaboration — and what needs to happen next.  Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can securely retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within their existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies its existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Data, context and the apps where sellers work come to life in practical workflows across the sales cycle, including:  Grow Revenue . Use the Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills to decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a concrete path to signature. Customer priorities and deal context inform the proposals and business cases sellers develop in Word and PowerPoint, with clear owners, milestones and next steps.  Manage Risk. Connect Salesforce opportunity data with customer concerns raised in Outlook, escalations discussed in Teams and unresolved commitments. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to the customer concern in an Outlook thread, the escalation discussed in Teams or the unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal, helping sellers identify where to intervene.  Move faster. Turn customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities using the Call Follow-Up skill. Sellers can review and confirm next steps instead of manually reconstructing conversations and updating multiple systems.    With Copilot as the front door to business process, Salesforce in Copilot allows organizations to bring together Salesforce data, workflows, agents and prebuilt skills from the systems they already rely on through Copilot’s open and interoperable platform.  “AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it,” said Judson Althoff, CEO, Microsoft Commercial Business . “Bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with the work context delivered by Work IQ in Microsoft Copilot allows our joint customers to unlock actionable insights across their core business applications. Copilotforce will give sales teams the intelligence they need to make faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand.”  “Through Copilotforce, we’re bringing Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today, embedding trusted Salesforce context and intelligent sales workflows directly where sellers work,” said Miguel Milano, President & Chief Operating Officer, Salesforce . “By bringing together the #1 CRM with the #1 productivity surface, we’re transforming AI from a standalone tool into a powerful driver of productivity, smarter decisions and customer success.”  Expanding connection in the places people work   For many organizations, the work first starts in Microsoft Teams, where people share files, make decisions and hand work to each other. Sales Cloud in Teams, now available in pilot, brings Salesforce customer context directly into those conversations, so sellers can see pipeline and quota progress, get deal notifications and find briefing materials without leaving the place where decisions are already being made.   Across these Microsoft and Salesforce integrations, customer data remains protected at every boundary: Salesforce controls data access and governs supported business actions, while Microsoft ensures communications and documents adhere to existing enterprise compliance policies. Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules, so teams can act with confidence while customer records stay governed and auditable.  AI is only as useful as the context it can reach, and for many enterprises customer data lives in Salesforce while operational and financial data lives in Microsoft Fabric. Microsoft and Salesforce are bringing a two-way Zero Copy connection between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric, so teams can work with fuller context across both platforms without building pipelines or maintaining duplicate datasets.  With Data Federation, now generally available, joint customers can now directly query and analyze supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data within Salesforce Data 360. A service agent can see a customer’s recent purchases on their account, a marketer can build a segment from spending behavior and an AI agent can answer from current data, all without moving the source data out of Fabric. events.title: As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier?
events.summary: In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier. Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model. TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week). However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately. The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish , a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model. Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgement using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgement. “What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch. Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context. “The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said. The Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake. “What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.” For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs. “Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: My daughter made $100 selling homemade slime door-to-door. Two years later, she's running her own business.
events.summary: Karly Wrede's daughter started her own slime business. Courtesy of Karly Wrede Karly Wrede's daughter, Nora, made $100 selling homemade slime door-to-door in just 30 minutes. She turned her hobby into Bee Kind Slimes and has hosted 50 birthday parties this year. The business has taught her about money and confidence while bringing her closer to her mom. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Karly Wrede, whose daughter created Bee Kind Slimes. It has been edited for length and clarity. Two years ago, my daughter Nora wanted to buy something. She asked my husband and me for money. We gave her a list of chores she could do, and she asked us if she could sell her slime instead. She's always been a fan of making homemade slime. So she packed it all into a tote bag and started walking door to door in our neighborhood. We walked behind her. I was worried she wouldn't sell anything and thought we'd have to console her, but she came back 30 minutes later and had made $100. My husband and I were both like, "Wow, maybe this is a thing." And that's really when Bee Kind Slimes was born. At first, people bought from her because she was a sweet little girl at their doorstep, but then she asked if she could sell on social media . It kind of went from there - someone reached out and asked if we wanted to do a farmer's market; we got asked to do a holiday show; Nora started to sell her slime online, and she started doing birthday parties. Now we even teach other families how to start a slime business . We've just sort of kept saying yes, and it's been amazing to see what she can do in two years. My daughter designed her own slime cart At first, we were selling individual containers of slime , but it goes bad if you let it sit for too long. After a farmers market or show, we spent a lot of time emptying containers, reactivating the slime, and putting it all back in. I saw a collapsible charcuterie cart on Facebook Marketplace one day, and it gave us the idea to design a slime cart. Karly Wrede's daughter has her own business now called Bee Kind Slimes. Courtesy of Karly Wrede Now we can wheel it in and out of events and parties , and it's more of an experience. Kids love picking their own slime color and can choose charms and fake sprinkles to mix in. Every slime is unique, which makes it really fun and less work for us. She works 10-15 hours a week on her slime business Bee Kind Slimes is a part-time job for Nora at this point, involving making, packaging, and selling slime. Some days she takes the slime cart to back-to-back birthday parties. She's done 50 birthday parties this year. Right now, she works on the business about 15 hours a week, but during the holidays that will increase. Karly Wrede's daughter goes to birthday parties with her slime. Courtesy of Karly Wrede To make the slime, we tried making batches in a KitchenAid mixer at first, but they didn't work well. We went through five mixers in the first year. Nora applied for a grant through the Mason Makes Money Fund and received it, so we used the funds to buy an industrial mixer. Now she can make 10 times as much slime as she could in a small batch. She's still a kid, though. A big part of this is figuring out how to balance helping her learn and grow without burning her out, because this is something we get to do together for fun. My daughter has learned about money and so much more Before she started the business, Nora got $10 in allowance a week. She'd instantly go to the store to buy a toy. Now she gets paid $100 each month, but has to wait until the end of the month to get the money . It's really made her think about what she wants to spend her money on, and be proactive about thinking about saving. Now there are times when she doesn't spend much, or any, of her allowance. Karly Wrede says her daughter has learned so much about money. Courtesy of Karly Wrede I work for a nonprofit, and I also wanted to help her learn how to be generous, which she's been able to do in a variety of different ways. Her confidence has also really grown. It's never really been about the slime for me. It's been about how I can teach her things she'll carry with her for the rest of her life. If this business is something that helps Nora in some way, be ready to be an adult, and helps her learn kindness, it's all worth it. We teach other parents and kids how to run a slime business We were getting a dozen messages a week on social media from other moms asking how to start a slime business. I teach classes at my corporate job, and leading cohorts comes really naturally to me, so I put together a course with everything someone might need. Courtesy of Karly Wrede Since April of this year, Nora and I have taught over 130 parents and their kids how to run their own slime businesses. Two years ago, I was making slime with her on the kitchen counter, and it's really fun to think about how much the business has grown. We get to spend a lot of time together, and hopefully she wants to keep making slime. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Chase Home Lending CEO says he plans to 'go on offense' against non-bank lenders
events.summary: Total mortgage demand, including both refinancing and new purchase loans, is now down just over 39% from a year ago, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Despite all that, Sean Grzebin, the CEO of Chase Home Lending, the nation's largest bank mortgage lender, said he's hiring and bent on increasing market share. Grzebin said he is looking to take back market share from non-bank lenders, who flourished after the financial crisis, when banks were cleaning up from thousands of failed home loans. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Mortgage rates shot higher again last week, after four straight weeks of declines. A hotter-than-expected monthly inflation report, coupled with new headlines from the Iran war, had the average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage up 33 basis points to 7.5%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Total mortgage demand, including both refinancing and new purchase loans, is now down just over 39% from a year ago, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Despite all that, Sean Grzebin, the CEO of Chase Home Lending, the nation's largest bank mortgage lender, said he's hiring and bent on increasing market share. "For the last several years, we haven't really added a lot of salespeople," said Grzebin, who admits plainly that this is the worst market in decades. "We're going to hire a bunch of home lending advisors across the United States. We're going to focus on areas where we haven't had a lot of coverage, but there's a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place, and it really matches the expansion that we're having within the branch network on the consumer bank side." Grzebin said he is looking to take back market share from non-bank lenders, who flourished after the financial crisis, when banks were cleaning up from thousands of failed home loans. In August, JPMorganChase announced a 40% increase in home lending capital through 2035 to $750 billion. It will also hire 850 new lending agents. "I think the non-banks are all very formidable competitors. I think they've had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades," he said. "I think now you're starting to see the resurgence of the banks, and I think a lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this." He said he expects to see continued consolidation in the mortgage market, especially as artificial intelligence penetrates the origination part of the business. Chase is investing heavily in AI for underwriting, he said. "We're hiring mainly in our sales functions because we think we can grow by adding people that have relationships with existing customers today, as well as them taking advantage of our branch network to help grow their business on one side," explained Grzebin. "And we think we can achieve all this growth without adding any incremental headcount in our operation because of the streamlining of the process that's happening with AI." Chase just ranked highest in mortgage origination satisfaction in J.D. Power's annual U.S. Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study. While overall satisfaction was unchanged from 2025, just 58% of borrowers said they receive same-day responses from their lender when they ask questions, down from 62% a year ago. Fewer borrowers also say they have a main point of contact, down to 88% from 91% a year ago. "Borrowers appreciate being able to handle more of the mortgage process online, but they still want someone they can turn to when they have questions," said Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at J.D. Power in a release. "J.D. Power is seeing less recognition of updates and guidance that are important to keeping borrowers informed. Lenders have an opportunity to make the process more convenient while ensuring borrowers feel supported, especially as they approach closing." That appears to be what Chase is leaning into as so much of the process now moves to agentic AI. Grzebin said they focused first on the closing process, which customers said was most frustrating. Then they moved to digital tools. "There's a lot of opportunity there that we're going to be able to take advantage of in the next 12 to 24 months, just making it easier for customers to do more self-service through AI capabilities that we're going to also roll out over the next couple quarters, and so we are invested heavily in AI," he said. "We're going to see some real efficiency from it, and then on the sales side, adding salespeople, but then also figuring out a way to make them more productive.

events.title: Hank Paulson warns of ‘underestimating’ risk of AI unwind
events.summary: Markets are underestimating the risk surrounding AI, and governments worldwide must work more closely with private businesses in order to better mitigate the chances of a catastrophic or financial crisis, former US Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson said Tuesday. “I’ve never seen so much money chasing one opportunity with not a lot of earnings and ROI backing it up,” Paulson, a former Goldman Sachs executive, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “People are underestimating the risk.” “It boggles my mind … people just brush aside this catastrophic risk,” he continued, speaking to Semafor’s Gina Chon. Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak largely concurred with Paulson, adding that while regulatory efforts thus far — such as the EU’s AI Act — were “not the right approach … that doesn’t mean we do nothing.” “The worst thing would be if we had some type of catastrophic accident … then we will have, as we all know, an overreaction on the other side.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain
events.summary: Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly. On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world. The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments. In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further. CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.” Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic , launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics. As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t. events.title: GP clinic bought by Bupa encouraged doctors to bill expensive Medicare items
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bupa GP clinic urged doctors to bill costly Medicare items to lift revenue Topic: Doctors and Medical Professionals A Bupa clinic encouraged doctors to increase revenue by billing extra Medicare items. ( ABC News: Nic MacBean ) Bupa emailed GPs at one of its clinics to encourage increased billing of chronic condition management plans, which cost more than standard appointments. Senior doctors say they are concerned corporatised GP practices are prioritising profit over patient care, but Bupa has defended the email. The Department of Health says it is spending $147 million over four years to review the industry and improve compliance. A GP clinic operated by health insurance giant Bupa has encouraged doctors to lift their billing of more costly Medicare items. The ABC obtained a June email from a Bupa clinic to its GPs, which told doctors to ensure "revenue is increasing". The email asked doctors to do this by increasing the bookings of patients for costly Medicare checks known as "chronic condition management plans" (CCMPs). It further encouraged doctors to re-book patients, if they were eligible for further checks but Medicare rules prevented them from being claimed on the same day. CCMPs are personalised plans written by GPs, designed to create a structure to improve outcomes for people struggling with complex health conditions. The plans can be used for conditions ranging from eczema to heart disease, and while often beneficial to patients, they may not be essential for everyone with a chronic condition. The Medicare schedule fee for a GP to prepare a CCMP is $160.60, compared to $87.10 for a standard GP appointment lasting at least 20 minutes. The federal government's spending on the plans is rising rapidly and it is now spending nearly $1.3 billion a year on these chronic care plans out of the $35 billion Medicare budget. 'Need to explain' why items not billed In the email, Bupa told doctors their appointment books were closely scrutinised each day through the popular software portal Cubiko, for "possible service opportunities", and notes were left about what could be billed. Bupa operates 33 medical centres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The booking software includes a specific function to check for chances to bill patients for "possible service opportunities", including the costly chronic care plans. The email also detailed how the "ops team" had tasked the practice managers with "ensuring revenue is increasing by ensuring there is an uptick in billings of HA [health assessments]". Cubiko spruiks that its "QuickCheck" function can help identify opportunities for billing patients more Medicare items. ( ABC News: Screenshot ) Bupa's email went on to list the Medicare item numbers for these health assessments, including chronic condition management plans and a nurse item. GPs were reminded that practice managers need to "ensure" an increase in patients being charged for these more expensive Medicare items, otherwise practice managers "need to explain why these are not being billed". In a statement, Bupa said the email was sent at one clinic and was an attempt to remind doctors to consider preventative care. "Patient needs, clinical judgement and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first," it said. Bupa said practice managers provided "administrative support to our doctors. Patient needs, clinical judgement, and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first and we reinforce this through ongoing guidance and training". Do you know more? Share it with us here . If GPs coerced, that 'has to be stopped' Policy analyst Terry Barnes was a senior adviser to two health ministers in the Howard government. He told the ABC he was not surprised by Bupa's email, and it was a window into how much corporate owners of GP clinics "called the shots". Terry Barnes says optional extras like chronic condition management plans should not become mandatory Medicare billings. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "If corporates are putting pressure on their doctors to order health assessments or any other type of extra service, and the optional extras become mandatory, then there is a real problem there," he said. "If they are actually putting pressure on the doctors, coercing them internally to behave in a certain way in relation to billing services and generating services, then that has to be stopped." Are private health insurers moving to US-style model? Increasing partnerships among health insurers, GP centres, and telehealth services raise concerns about a potential two-tier system in which privately insured patients have more affordable access to GP consultations.

events.title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
events.summary: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers CHICAGO -- New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400. Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix's anniversary trip to Chicago. On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for. Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed. But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement. Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles. Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult. “A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.” When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago. “We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said. Dread lingers around such events because they're getting more commonplace, with no end in sight. Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday's ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide. It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life. Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021. The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money. Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That's about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure. More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Harder to measure is the loss absorbed by the population downstream from the airports, including hourly workers, freelancers and caregivers — in short, everyone affected by the ripples. Another cost: Trust in government, which has been low for years . The nationwide shutdown, the nation's longest in 25 years, could cost billions of dollars, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend. He blamed a contractor and aging infrastructure . President Donald Trump testily pointed to Democrats , who in turn demanded answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared to $50 billion. Downplaying the event as a glitch with a faulty router raised questions, if not suspicions, one communications expert says. “It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale,” Shannon A.

events.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
events.summary: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.  Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.  Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.  The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.  But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.  Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

events.title: Amazon CEO says US AI lead over China depends on building more data centers
events.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday it would be a “historic mistake” for the US to pull back on its AI infrastructure buildout following the data center backlash during the midterm elections. “I cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centers and allows another country like China to establish all the norms,” Jassy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The US would regret such a move “for a very long time,” said Jassy, who has directed hundreds of billions into data centers around the world. Still, he acknowledged that tech companies need to “do it better and partner more closely with our communities.” Given Nvidia is so central to the AI buildout, Jassy said he didn’t think Jensen Huang’s departure would impact Amazon and pledged to continue working closely with the chipmaker. The growth in AI stems from “more than one company,” he said. Nvidia GPUs help power AWS data centers and Amazon works with the chip giant on infrastructure and robotics. “They’ll have to work out how they move forward as a company, but we’ll be partners with them either way.” Jassy also said that Amazon, which currently doesn’t let Meta’s Muse and other consumer agents access its site, is still talking to companies like Meta about how to open up the e-commerce giant to consumers who want to use the agents. He said the company would open up the site to agents if it could find a “good exchange of value” and a positive experience for customers, which isn’t happening at the moment. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
events.summary: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers. Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The problems aren't just technical, or workload-related: there's also a delicate balance of how to refuse well-intentioned and technologically viable submissions that just won't fit for non-technical reasons, such as being too niche for the typical use-case of a sub-£60 gadget. The problem is that this FOSS firmware is making these cheap gadgets so much more useful that re-flashing them is an implicit part of the purchase. That introduces all kinds of unexpected side-effects, for the users and for the developers. Crosspoint Reader is a microcosm of the rapid growth of Linux and FOSS in general – and a taste of what will happen if it ever goes truly mainstream with mass-market consumers. One of his "what I got wrong about this job" points we particularly liked was: “The scarce resource isn’t code. We have more code than we know what to do with." Instead, it's… "Judgement. Trust. Responsibility." There are lessons for the whole IT industry in there, we reckon. Even for the biggest players . In the meantime, though, these tiny cheap e-readers are an interesting new thing. As Mitchell put it, paraphrasing The Atlantic , they're: "Fun in a way gadgets haven’t been for a long time." Just being fun is a goal that is far too often forgotten… Especially in FOSS. ®

events.title: Defect-Aware Chiplet Matching For Heterogeneous Integration Yield (ASU, Ampere)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Arizona State University and Ampere Computing published “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.” “Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.” Find the technical paper here . November 2026. Xuanyi Tan, Sanmitra Banerjee, Dhruv Thapar, Sreejit Chakravarty, and Krishnendu Chakrabarty. “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.” arXiv:2611.19544, November 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19544. events.title: US Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has sought to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook since August 2025. Lisa Cook has refused to attend a White House hearing on claims she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, saying the process is unfair and aimed at a fixed outcome. Her lawyer said she has “no legal obligation” to join what he called a “facade” to fire her, and warned it could damage the Federal Reserve’s independence. The dispute adds to Trump’s push to remove Cook since August 2025, while the Supreme Court has already blocked her firing during the legal fight. WASHINGTON – Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear in December before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov 6. Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs. “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing – and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Nov 17 to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.” In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.” AP

( AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson ) Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would be honoured to return to his role. His supporters have been attempting to pressure the tech company's board to reinstate him. Mr Huang will be questioned by several committees of Congress on December 1 . Jensen Huang says he would be honoured to return as Nvidia CEO if the AI chipmaker's board decides to have him back. In his first comments since resigning under pressure over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Mr Huang said he had been humbled by an outpouring of calls for his comeback. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he said in a statement. Mr Huang also said he had seen an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO". "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO." The statement follows a campaign, backed by tech titans including Elon Musk, calling for Mr Huang's reinstatement . According to a counter on the official Stand with Jensen website, more than 190,000 people have signed an open letter demanding the board re-employ him. However, Nvidia chair Harvey ​Jones has said that the ​board does ​not intend to ⁠reinstate Mr ​Huang as ​chief executive. In a third-quarter earnings call, Mr Jones said he would not take questions on the circumstances of Mr Huang's resignation and the ongoing investigation, but backed Mr Huang's interim replacement, Colette Kress. "We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity and ability to deliver as interim CEO," he said, according to NBC . The US has moved to tighten controls designed to prevent chip-smuggling in the wake of the scandal. Suspected Chinese asset Alice Huang, who Mr Huang had an affair with, worked for a company that US authorities believe may have circumvented those controls to send Nvidia's most powerful AI chips into China, according to multiple reports. Chinese economic espionage is in the spotlight after the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, and former intelligence officials say the US is not doing enough to combat it. Several congressional committees are investigating. On Monday, local time, US President Donald Trump said he "would certainly not mind seeing" Mr Huang come back to the role. "I think he learned a big lesson," Mr Trump told reporters as he prepared to depart for a trip to Asia . Yet some members of Congress on both sides of politics have voiced opposition to Mr Huang's return. "Slow your roll there," Democratic senator Ruben Gallego wrote in response to Mr Huang's statement on X. "You have to answer some questions first. We need to know if you allowed Blackwell chips to be siphoned to China?" Mr Huang has agreed to answer questions before Congress on December 1, according to a statement from the House Committee on Foreign Affairs. "The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," said the Republican chairs of the committees, which also include the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee.

events.title: Proton’s Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop
events.summary: Proton , the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations. The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions. Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data . Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do. Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models. The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira. The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources. Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation. In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval. Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act , which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers. The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland. Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations.
