events.title: Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia
events.summary: Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia , five days after he resigned from the company . In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang said that since stepping down he has received an “ outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote. Huang also thanked people who showed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week. Huang resigned four days after Nvidia launched an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the company’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice. The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest." Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation. The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation. WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement . It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours. A separate, public petition titled “ Stand With Jensen ” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.” Nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly said on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Building social media apps isn’t cool anymore RIP to the unloved, unwanted Cybertruck Want better search results? events.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it’s a game
events.summary: Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals. Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery. The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game. The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence. Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose. The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare. Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game. Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable. “The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.” Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds. OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated. “We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.” Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems. In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences. The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though. Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat. A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems. For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.

events.title: Disney+ and Hulu are fully unifying by the end of the year
events.summary: Hulu is merging with Disney+ under CEO Josh D'Amaro. Jeremy Moeller/GC Images; Aurore Marechal/Getty Images Hulu's features will be fully integrated into Disney+ by the end of the year. This project, known internally as Project Gemini, has been in the works for years. The unified streaming experience is part of CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan to build a super app. The Hulu-Disney+ marriage is happening right on schedule. Disney's plan to fully unify its streamers "is nearly complete" and will be finalized in December, the company told investors on Tuesday. It could be the beginning of the end for a stand-alone Hulu app, though Disney hasn't said when the current Hulu app would be discontinued or what will happen to the beloved Hulu brand. This initiative, known internally as "Project Gemini," was scheduled to be finished by the end of 2026, Business Insider reported in May. In the coming weeks, the Disney+ app is getting its last Hulu-specific features, including the ability to watch live TV and add-on streamers for users with qualifying subscriptions. Disney has spent years integrating Hulu's content and features into its namesake streamer in an effort to lift engagement and reduce cancellations. Merging the streamers can create "a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises," Disney said in its shareholder letter as it shared earnings . The decision to move Hulu fully onto Disney+ may make the stand-alone Hulu app obsolete. An internal document obtained by Business Insider in May said that "the Hulu tech stack and app will be decommissioned after all users have transitioned" to Disney+, though it didn't specify exactly when that would happen. A Disney streaming town hall presentation in early November said that "One App Milestones" are expected to last through the company's fiscal fourth quarter, which spans early July to early October. The slide deck referenced Project Gemini, but didn't list the "One App Milestones" or explain the implications of completing them. How Hulu fits into the super app strategy Putting Hulu and Disney+ under one roof is part of CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan of building a super app where streaming subscribers can play games and buy merchandise without leaving the app. Disney's ambition is "to connect Disney+ more closely with the whole company," D'Amaro said on Tuesday's earnings call. "That means our parks, our cruise ships, merchandise, and games." This all-in-one experience will begin to shape this spring, D'Amaro said last quarter. Some media analysts think a streaming super app could boost viewership and customer loyalty while driving more revenue; others think adding games and shopping to Disney+ could make it bloated. Disney said Tuesday that it's adding creator content to Disney+ in December after announcing a deal with TikTok last quarter. The town hall presentation in early November said that Disney was planning to integrate creator content in early 2027. Employees were also told at the meeting that Disney is putting more vertical clips on Disney+, including clips from sports, news, and short-form "micro series" expected to arrive this quarter. Disney is also exploring creating a free streaming product to bring in new users, as Business Insider first reported in July. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday. Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology. Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees. Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12 , requesting they appear. The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations. Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed. A representative for Huang did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2. Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies. The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China. events.title: Jensen Huang wants job back, as Nvidia to reveal first earnings since scandal
events.summary: Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang acknowledged in a post on X that he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life, after resigning on Nov 12 over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang said he may return as Nvidia CEO if the board thinks it is best, after quitting over an affair and saying he made “serious mistakes” in his personal life. His resignation has hurt Nvidia shares, while Elon Musk, other AI investors, employees, customers and Donald Trump have backed his return. Huang will face three US House committees on Dec 1 over concerns that China gained access to advanced Nvidia chips, and he will cooperate with an independent investigation. WASHINGTON – Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said on Nov 17 he wanted his job back, despite resigning over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, marking a new twist for the turmoil-hit AI chip giant hours before it releases a key earnings report. Investors will scrutinise the results for indications that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies. Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia – until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company – which is at the centre of an AI boom that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe. Nvidia has lost US$700 billion (S$900 billion) in market value since the scandal broke, and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on Dec 1 over national security concerns. But his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and other entrepreneurs for his return, and even President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the spy allegations. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said, in his first statement since his resignation. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” As the scandal deepened, Washington on Nov 16 announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing. The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes. The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips. The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in South-east Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China. While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice. His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls. Nvidia’s Nov 17 third-quarter results, which are scheduled for 5pm ET (6am on Nov 18 in Singapore), will be the first presented under Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO. “If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer. Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies. Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Nov 19. Huang on Nov 17 sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.” AFP

The company said the first hundred guests at each of its stores will get gift cards of $25 or more. One winner at each location will receive a $1,000 card. Target is going big this Black Friday . The bullseye retailer said Tuesday that it will give gift cards worth $25 or more to the first hundred shoppers at each of its stores when they open on November 27. In addition to $50 and $100 cards in the mix, one winner at each location will get a $1,000 grand prize. events.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
events.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders. What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed. Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research. (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.) Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups: Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder. The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses. Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said. Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains. " You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said. "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added. The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy. Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%. Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history. Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees. What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change. Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing." What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit exposes succession and governance risks for companies and boards
events.summary: To join the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, apply at cnbccouncils.com/wec . Apply to the Workforce Executive Council Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has put Nvidia's CEO succession planning and board preparedness under scrutiny. Leadership experts say Nvidia's unusually flat structure with concentrated decision-making, relationships and reporting lines around Huang created outsized risk. "Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical. The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time. But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing. In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him? With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason. "Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council . She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO." "What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added. Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions. In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive. 'All the risk centered on the shoulders of one man' Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO." "Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual." The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips. In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization. "This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says. "Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears." Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies." This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang.

Careful what you ask Google's AI, because it's storing it even if you ask it not to HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider 1 day ago Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help 1 day ago Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 3 days ago Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year 4 days ago Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view 5 days ago Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. events.title: I moved from California to Japan and make $90,000 a year. Salaries are lower here, but life is more affordable.
events.summary: Kaito Itokazu moved from California to Japan three years ago. Business Insider Software engineer Kaito Itokazu moved from California to Japan three years ago. He earns around $90,000 annually while living in Tokyo. His budget covers his $840 rent. He saves up to $3,500 monthly, spends more dining out than on groceries, and travels across Asia. This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation for Business Insider's video series, The Pay Check, with Kaito Itokazu, 25, who lives in Tokyo. It has been edited for length and clarity. I'm a software engineer living in Tokyo , earning around $60,000 a year as a salaryman, plus around $30,000 from side gigs. I'm originally from Los Angeles, and I moved to Japan three years ago. Salaries in Japan are much lower than in the US. When I tell my friends in America and Japan my salary, I get the exact opposite responses. My friends in the US are shocked and worry about how I make it work. When I tell my friends in Japan, they're like, "Oh wow, that's really good for your age." This is because it's much cheaper to live in Japan . Even with a lower salary, it's possible to live comfortably. Each year I tend to evaluate whether this coming year is worth the opportunities, experiences, and connections I can create — as opposed to when I was growing up in the US — and every year has been yes. In the past three years, I've switched jobs, moved apartments, and now I'm starting a side business. Compared to the national average, my salary is on the higher end, which gives me more opportunities and experiences and allows me to live in Tokyo. I am extremely grateful and fortunate for that. Side income and housing in Japan For my side business, I create websites and web applications and help businesses integrate AI into their workflows. I also teach kids basic computer programming. With my side gigs, I'm projected to make an additional $30,000 a year. That's around $90,000 a year in total. A lot of the money I get from my side business is expensed or reinvested into it. My base rent is around $840 — that's almost double my previous rent when I was living in Yokohama . The size is around the same, so what I'm really paying for is the prime location. Kaito Itokazu's base rent in Tokyo is around $840 a month. Business Insider Moving into a new apartment is pretty expensive in Japan. You have to put down a deposit that you don't get back — mine was $2,000. Because of the nature of my apartment, they wouldn't let me move things on my own, so I had to hire a professional company to move the furniture, which cost around $500. For utilities, I pay around $57 a month for gas, water, and electricity. I also spend around $250 on AI tools. In total, from housing to utilities to streaming, it comes to around $970 a month. Day-to-day spending in Tokyo Being in the city, I don't really need a car. Most of my transportation is by subway and bus. When I go to work, I get my transportation fee reimbursed. So I usually spend $120 a month on public transportation for fun outings. If you're not careful, the trains can add up. I spend $130 on groceries, $250 on eating out, $70 on cafés and coffee shops, and $70 on convenience stores. Those numbers are pretty embarrassing to admit; I could definitely spend more on groceries and less on eating out. Kaito Itokazu shops for groceries in a supermarket in Tokyo, Japan. Business Insider Yet, one of the things I really like about being in Japan is the amazing food . To me, it's worth a little extra money to try new places and eat out. The $70 for the convenience stores comes from items like snacks, rice balls, yogurt, and ice cream. I also tend to eat out with friends or coworkers most of the time. Compared to the average Japanese person, I spend a little more on food and groceries. I like to play soccer or futsal — that adds up to around $38 a month. Recently, pickleball and paddle have been trending, so I spend around $26 on them and $51 on my gym membership. After that, around $65 goes toward nightlife and bars, and I spend about $32 on a haircut every month. I also love to travel within Japan , Asia, and to America. If I happen to go home to the US, it can be around $1,000, but on average I spend around $470 a month. I recently went to Busan, South Korea, for a $200 round-trip flight; I visited my grandparents in Kagawa for a $120 round-trip flight; and I also went to Mount Fuji for around $31. Managing finances in Japan For health insurance, $212 is deducted from my paycheck each month for standard healthcare from my employer. I broke my wrist three years ago, and when I wanted to get it checked out in the US, it would take me around two weeks to get an appointment. While I was in Japan, my wrist started bothering me, and I was able to get it checked out immediately. I went in that same day for X-rays and scans. I initially paid for the surgery, but my insurance reimbursed 70% of the cost. The total came to around $300. On average, I save around $1,500 to $3,500 a month. Of that, 30% goes to investments, 30% to an emergency fund, and the rest goes back into my side business. In Japan, we also have a residence tax that applies to you a year after you move. You get taxed on your previous year's salary at around 10% of your salary, fixed. I went to Chapman University in the US and recently paid off my student loan debt . I was fortunate to be in a position to receive a scholarship and use money from my internships to pay off my student loans. Kaito Itokazu said that discussing one's salary is taboo in Japan. By sharing his story, he hopes to help others considering a move there. Business Insider Now, I'm trying to find a balance between being financially smart and being able to experience and spend money how I want to. I have a budget range, and I don't want to go over it. I also have money saved up in case something goes wrong with a fund or if I want to invest it — but I also have some money I use to travel or experience new things. If I decide to settle down in Japan, I think I'm on track financially. As I build a community and make more connections, Japan starts to feel less like a temporary place and more like a second home. That makes it much harder to leave. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest. Huang’s statement, posted in full on X , reads as follows: Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. Jensen Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1. In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance. Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick. “We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.” Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms. Reached by Politico , one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: My family history of cancer was giving me so much anxiety. I finally learned to stop turning to Dr. Google.
events.summary: The author said she used to let her health anxiety send her down an internet rabbit hole before her doctor's appointments. Courtesy of Linda Wolff. I have a family history of cancer, and every lump and symptom pushed me to turn to Dr. Google. Compulsive Googling of my symptoms only stressed me out, leading me to feel even worse. I now avoid self-diagnosis by focusing my time and effort on things I enjoy. My first real scare came at 36. A swollen lymph node on the left side of my neck during a routine checkup raised my doctor's concern. "How long have you had this?" he inquired. I held my breath as his fingers traversed the lump hovering above my collarbone. He jotted down the name of a surgical oncologist. The room began to spin. After several anxiety-ridden months of visiting the local cancer center to have my lump observed, the surgical oncologist insisted we remove it. During the weeks that led up to my surgery, I made the fatal mistake — no pun intended — of Googling "lumps on my neck." The information took me down a rabbit hole, from ordinary viruses to malignant cancer. Of course, I ignored the benign and focused on the worst. Lymphoma and Leukemia kept popping up in my nightmarish searches at 2 a.m. Naturally, I assumed I was dying. My parents and siblings have all had cancer. I fear I'm trying to outrun my fate. Each time I go for a checkup, scan, mammogram, colonoscopy, or blood work, I brace myself for devastating news. My worry was sucking the life out of me, overriding the voice in my head telling me that instead of taking each moment for granted, I should be enjoying my existence. My worry has lingered for a long time I was 16 when my beloved father first complained of stomach pain. My mother assumed it was from blue cheese dressing that turned. But when the pain became severe, his doctor suggested exploratory surgery. He found pancreatic cancer. I don't think I ever fully recovered from my father's devastating six-week-long decline from diagnosis to death. It's no surprise that I struggle with a PTSD-like fear whenever medical issues arise. When I was faced with having surgery to remove my lymph node, my children were small, and the thought of them growing up without me tore me to pieces. I told them I was having a "pimple-ectomy," which sounded silly so they wouldn't be scared. I held it together in front of them, but fear and anticipatory grief consumed me as I cried myself to sleep. Thankfully, it was benign. The worry sometimes felt like wasted time Over my decades, I've had a multitude of suspicious bumps, polyps, and cysts tested and removed. Each clean bill of health comes with tremendous relief, and a side of guilt for being one of the lucky ones and the awful awareness of the all-consuming time and energy I wasted that I'll never get back. Instead of going down a symptom rabbit hole, I could have been learning a new language, making a photo collage of my grandbabies, or at the very least, watching adorable puppy videos. Eventually, one of my doctors saw how my anxiety was affecting my health . I recall the tears streaming like the fountain of Bellagio as I hiccuped my worst fears during an abdominal ultrasound. The 24-hour information drip I did prior to my appointment, Googling my symptoms, didn't calm my fears; it amplified them. I can't help but think this must be contributing to my high blood pressure, IBS, insomnia, and vertigo. I knew my doctor was right when they told me I had to stop. And I finally did. I'm keeping myself distracted with more fun things I'm not saying I don't worry anymore. I do. But now I avoid the armchair analysis on my computer or phone and let the medical professionals do their jobs. Instead, I try to remind myself of all the instances my worrying was for nothing and did nothing but rob me of precious time and peace of mind. Now when I'm tempted to do a deep dive on an ailment, I take a breath and remind myself that the search will only make me suffer. Choosing instead to engage in something joyful or productive, like planting in my garden, playing with my grandchildren, or penning my novel. The distraction is wonderful. I feel better, too. events.title: Iraq resumes pumping crude oil for export through pipeline to Turkey
events.summary: Iraq has resumed pumping crude oil for export through Turkey in a move expected to boost the economy and revitalise an industry paralysed by the war in Iran . Crude will be pumped through the 960km Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline at an initial rate of 120,000 barrels per day, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said, the state-owned Iraqi News Agency reported on Tuesday. That will be gradually increased to hit a capacity of 500,000 bpd, after the “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests”, he added. “This achievement represents an important strategic step in enhancing Iraq's export capacity and diversifying crude oil export outlets.” It will also help in “generating additional financial revenues for the national economy, especially since exporting through the northern outlet allows for the marketing of crude oil without price discounts”, he added. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. More than 90 per cent of Iraq's budget is funded in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The regional conflict has led to a sharp supply collapse for Iraq. Exports fell from 3.36 million bpd in February to 131,000 bpd in April. The result was a drop in monthly oil revenue that previously hovered around $7 billion. Baghdad has also announced the start of work on a new pipeline linking Basra to Haditha with a capacity of 2.5 million bpd, as it seeks new routes to export crude. But the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline remains crucial. In August, Iraq and Turkey signed a ​one-year agreement ⁠to continue crude oil ⁠flows at an export capacity of 750,000 bpd. Iraq is also driving efforts to boost its standing. At September's UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans. Last month, the International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said it was advancing discussions with Iraq , as well as Lebanon , as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa. Iraq is also debating a draft federal budget for 2027 that would be the biggest in its history but the plan is also the most detached from the country's financial reality.

events.title: Daydream’s new AI agent acts as your personal stylist — and can shop for you, too
events.summary: Can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out. On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you plan a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more. The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million users and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily. In Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its users. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases. Now the company says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process. The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends. Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events. The tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases. However, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the company says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih , an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on. Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes ( exited to Pinterest in 2022 ), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine . The company, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch. events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honored' to return as Nvidia CEO in first public remarks since exit
events.summary: Ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said Tuesday that he would be ‘honored’ to return as CEO, in his first public remarks since resigning from the US chip giant after revelations of extramarital affairs. In a statement, Huang said he had witnessed “an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and would return “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” adding that he was cooperating with the Nvidia board’s independent investigation. “I love our country, and I love NVIDIA,” he said. The machinations surrounding Huang have overshadowed expectations for more sky-high profits in the chipmaker’s latest earnings Tuesday. Interim CEO Colette Kress, appointed in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation following revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, faces a raft of questions over the chip giant’s outlook . The company has already formed a new board committee for oversight of national security issues. Kress’ reported reluctance to support Huang’s strategy to backstop and invest in many of the companies driving the technology will also be of particular focus: Any sign Nvidia is pulling back will have huge ramifications for the sector, and the global economy. — Prashant Rao

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Ride-hailing biz says stolen credentials allowed crooks to help themselves to driver's license data GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs 3 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 1 day ago Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 1 day ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 1 day ago Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week . According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts.

events.title: UAE’s Al Tajir family sells Scottish ‘ghost’ golf course to Gleneagles
events.summary: A Scottish championship standard golf resort which has never opened to the public has been sold by its UAE owners to its neighbour, the Ryder Cup venue Gleneagles Hotel. Gleneagles West, known as gWest, in Perthshire, was put up for sale in September by the UAE’s Al Tajir family and has now been sold for an undisclosed sum. Mahdi Al Tajir, who in 1971 became the first UAE ambassador to the UK, was named the richest man in Scotland by The Sunday Times in 2013 and owns the Highland Spring water company which is based nearby. The family bought the land in 2007, completing its tournament-standard golf course two years later but barely a shot has been played at the private-gated resort in the years since. A combination of the financial crisis, the Scottish independence debate and referendum, Brexit and Covid-19 meant the family felt the time had never been quite right to take it to the next stage of investment. The 18th-century-inspired clubhouse remains a shell and development of the rest of the resort – it has permission for up to 170 residential plots, a hotel and spa, leisure and entertainment facilities and staff accommodation – was shelved. Gleneagles Hotel is owned by Mumbai-born London businessman Sharan Pasricha. He founded hotel company Ennismore in 2011, buying The Hoxton in London's Shoreditch in 2012 and Gleneagles in 2015. A Gleneagles representative told The Courier newspaper, which first reported the sale: “The Gleneagles Hotel has acquired a neighbouring expanse of Perthshire countryside, bordering the hotel and its iconic King’s and Queen’s Courses. “Surrounded by the rolling Ochil Hills and breath-taking scenery, this land shares the same natural beauty and character that has defined The Gleneagles Hotel for over a century. “Nestled within this landscape is a golf course quietly whispered about, one of the lesser-known treasures of Perthshire. The acquisition offers an opportunity to extend our stewardship of this remarkable landscape that has always been integral to the spirit of the hotel. “We look forward to sharing more as our plans take shape, guided by the same care and consideration that have shaped this special place for over a century.” At the time the resort went on sale, Euan Kelly, partner at Knight Frank Edinburgh, described it as a “once-in-a-lifetime asset: a substantial consented resort development site, with a golf course designed by a celebrated architect, in one of Scotland’s most prestigious leisure locations”. Course architect David McLay Kidd designed the championship-standard course and described the resort as “the best inland site I’ve ever seen for a golf course”. It sits in one of Scotland’s best-known golf and leisure corridors, to the west of Gleneagles between Perth and Stirling. The UK’s golf industry generated revenue of around £2.7 billion ($3.64 billion) in 2024/25, which is expected to rise to £3 billion for 2025/26. There are about 560 courses in Scotland – one fifth of the total in the UK. Speaking in 2020, Mr Al Tajir’s son, Mohsin, said: “You want to invest. The next phase of gWest is another £50, £60, maybe £100 million. And as a family we're not willing to put that sort of money in if we don't know what the future is.” He said with concerns that taxes would go up, rather than Scotland becoming a tax haven if independence were to happen, “maybe it's not the place I need to put my money”.

events.title: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing
events.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's attorney gave the strongest signal yet that Cook will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry." President Donald Trump's "decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf. The "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation" in a hearing, Lowell wrote. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook. The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf. "Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday. The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties. While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name." Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett . Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome." Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue." Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing. "Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote. "Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote. Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter. Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden . Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September. Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal. The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

events.title: Jensen Huang open to Nvidia return in first statement since resignation
events.summary: Jensen Huang on Tuesday indicated he is willing to return as chief executive at Nvidia if the company's board of directors ask him to do so. In his first public remarks since resigning last week, Mr Huang said he was aware of the push from inside and outside the company for his return, and said he would "be honoured to to answer to answer these calls and return as CEO". "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO," Mr Huang said. "Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. Nvidia is a once-in-a-generation company." Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026 US media have reported that Nvidia's board of directors has no interest in Mr Huang returning after his affair with a technology executive purported to be have ties to China's intelligence services, which has caused considerable fallout for the world's most second-most valuable company by market capitalisation. The woman, Alice Huang , was previously chief executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which is under investigation by the US for allegedly smuggling chips to China. Megaspeed denies the allegations. Adding to the harm were accusations that Mr Huang knowingly tried to circumvent laws designed to prevent certain US technology from being used in China. US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday he would like to see Mr Huang return. Mr Huang has also agreed to appear for transcribed interviews with three US House of Representatives committees on December 1, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said in a statement. Nvidia's general counsel will appear before the committees on December 2. "The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," said US Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford. Mr Huang said he is committed to co-operating with the Nvidia board's independent investigation. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," he said. Nvidia 's board of directors earlier on Tuesday said it had formed a committee to oversee its security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. Mr Huang's affair has rocked Washington politics, particularly among hawkish members of Congress who say such a relationship could have given China access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips . The US has banned the sale of those chips to China, citing national security concerns. Nvidia's existing national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the newly established national security and export control oversight committee, and to the interim chief executive, Colette Kress. "Nvidia recognises that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and super intelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges." The announcement came a day after the US Commerce and Justice departments revealed they had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for possible export control breaches. “While we don't typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the statement said. Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. pic.twitter.com/aAdtN9aDfF — U.S. Department of Commerce (@CommerceGov) November 17, 2026 The agencies said investigators at the Commerce Department in May 2025 requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to the Singapore-based company. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025. That same month, agents from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, along with law-enforcement officials in Singapore, conducted an in-person check at Megaspeed and interviewed Ms Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead in Megaspeed's criminal investigation, they said. Earlier on Monday, the Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule tightening access to advanced AI chips and servers. The department said the rule was designed to ensure existing restrictions on access to sensitive US technology would not be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries. “The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes, while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” the agency said. The announcement came as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced growing criticism his agency did not do enough to curb exports of advanced AI chips to China. Meanwhile, later on Tuesday controversies kept arising for Nvidia as the Wall Street Journal reported that sources close to the US Securities and Exchange Commission were investigating the company as to whether or not it misled investigators. During the company's third quarter earnings call on Tuesday, Harvey Jones, chairman of the board of directors said that Nvidia had no plans to reinstate Mr Huang as chief executive. In addition, he said board was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and retained Heidrick and Struggles, an executive search team to lead the pursuit. "While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders," Mr Jones said.

events.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
events.summary: Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country. The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence. Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment. It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym. “Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.” Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people , including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”. In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”. Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered. Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work. “I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said. “I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.” Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work. “We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace. “They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.” Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements. Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet. All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career. For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel. Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers. “You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in. “And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.” Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course. “I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.
