events.title: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time | Timothy Garton Ash
events.summary: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal E ver since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans. Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech. Cautious in diagnosis: his bold statement that “we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years” was immediately followed by “the hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain”. (So a soft Brexit would be fine?) Cautious in prescription: beyond the welcome modest steps to be agreed at this Friday’s UK-EU summit (easier access for food and agricultural products, linking our carbon emissions markets, creating a youth mobility scheme), anything this government does during the term of the current parliament will stay within Keir Starmer’s “red lines” (no rejoining the customs union, single market or freedom of movement). Burnham will, however, explore “options for our long-term relationship” with the EU, “to inform decisions in the next parliament”. Unless we have an early election, that means not before 2029. This caution is easily explained. Roughly half of his cabinet doesn’t want even to mention Brexit. Roughly half of his MPs are in constituencies that voted leave in 2016. The country at large thinks Brexit was a mistake but dreads the prospect of rerunning the debate and isn’t sure it would vote for rejoining if the UK didn’t have its previous opt-outs, including from the euro and the Schengen free travel area. For all the great expectations that were raised, Burnham himself had actually only said in interviews that he hoped Britain would rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He’s a robust 56-year-old, so that could take us to about 2060. More surprising was how old-fashioned his speech was, albeit delivered with demotic verve. Here, for starters, was the weary old trope of Britain always having to “lead” in whatever it does (nine references to leading, if my count is correct). Then there’s the curious way in which Britain’s commitment to European defence and support for Ukraine is totally divorced from all the other dimensions of European security and strength, which self-evidently involve the EU. Instead, there’s a relentless narrow focus on what’s good for Britain economically. At the heart of his speech was what he called the “Makerfield test” – that is, what would deliver economic benefits for the hard-pressed people of his constituency of Makerfield, which in 2016 voted to leave the EU. Oddest of all was the way he harked back to a 1948 speech in which Winston Churchill conjured Britain’s position at the intersection of three majestic circles. Gliding over the fact that the first circle Churchill mentioned was “the British Commonwealth and Empire ”, Burnham talked at some length about the Commonwealth before coming to Europe. For obvious reasons (don’t offend the egomaniac in the White House!), he also glided over the fact that Churchill’s second circle was “the English-speaking world”, with its superpower being the US. Yet if we are highlighting, as Burnham did, how the world has changed since 2016, then the drastic change under Donald Trump in the US approach to its allies, including Britain, should be top of the list. Oh, and by the way, Churchill’s third circle was “United Europe”, which he talked of in visionary terms long before it ever existed. Now, with something called the European Union , much of Europe is at least halfway there. Unlike in Churchill’s speech, in fact unlike in everything that great British and European leader said and did, here there was no sense of a wider European story in which Britain has always played an important part. Instead, Burnham spoke of Britain’s reset “with Europe”, as though Britain were not part of Europe and “Europe” only means the EU. The most European things in London’s Guildhall on Monday evening were the Polish vodka served by the Polish-South-African-British lord mayor of London, Bronek Masojada, and a few words in Dutch that he addressed to the prime minister’s wife, Marie-France van Heel. But enough about the words. What of the actions to follow? I’m not sure how long these conversations with EU partners about “options” need to last. An hour or two might suffice. For the EU has repeatedly spelled out the current ones as it sees them.

events.title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
events.summary: Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working. Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff. We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals. Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staff Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC). The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors. Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience. "My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says. "In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed" As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience. Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 14 hours ago Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation". But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses. It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths". Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away" Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers. Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000 There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled. Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed. She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away." Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible". Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset. The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week. Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it "One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us." He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier. Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 13 hours ago Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 12 hours ago One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report. Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work. Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year. Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.' The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure. It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue. Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed. This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.

events.title: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
events.summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6 . Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs. “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.” In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.” Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary. The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction. Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen. The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune." Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device. Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required). The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data. Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps. The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs. The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2. events.title: Tech titans attempt their own recursive self-improvement
events.summary: Shelly’s view It rarely rains in Silicon Valley, but when it rains, it storms. Perhaps it’s the sogginess in the Bay, the post-midterms soul-searching, or the ethical questions underlying the Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal (and the Save Jensen movement), but signs are emerging that the tech industry is — like its most famous product — developing the capacity for recursive self-improvement. “ Heroes have flaws, ” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti, when asked how he’s coming to terms with Nvidia’s chief resigning from the company he founded 33 years ago and built into the backbone of the AI ecosystem. Altman said he couldn’t answer whether he thought Huang should be allowed to come back to the helm at Nvidia, but admitted the whole episode has shaken the industry. He sounded similarly chastened about the AI referendum that swept over the US midterms: “There is this long-term question about what are people’s roles going to be in society, and what is the balance of power going to look like … between people and AI.” Altman and his peers seemed to share a new willingness to adapt to a volatile political environment — even as much of Washington turns hard on Huang and Nvidia, and US voters show little sign of laying down their pitchforks. We’ve been here before, of course: There were tech “reckonings” on everything from the #MeToo movement to social media and kids. But onstage and in unguarded moments, the most important people in the room here at Silicon Valley & The World seemed to be realizing that their problems are not just about optics or telling their story better. The question they face is whether they can build the next big thing with the people outside the Silicon Valley bubble. Notable Altman wasn’t the only CEO to defend Huang ; leaders from across the tech world defended the former Nvidia CEO at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World.

events.title: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes
events.summary: Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes , which it said were the highest in Europe. As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market. “I would hope that we’re able to bring those projects back to life,” he added. “But it’s a very real impact here in the UK, when those investments will go to other countries in Europe.” The planned investments were smaller UK stores, but the retailer declined to comment on exact locations. Ikea has been pushing further into smaller high street shops , rather than its traditional out-of-town outlets. Ikea’s UK arm pays the most business taxes of its operations in Europe, and the third highest in the world, after the US and China, he said. The retailer’s UK sales edged 0.5% higher to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Sales rose 4.7% in the first four months of the year but fell in the second half as weak confidence and “sustained pressure” on household budgets led consumers to pull back on big purchases. McCabe said he had talked to customers in stores in recent weeks who were planning to replace an entire bedroom, but then decided to just buy one or two smaller pieces of furniture and a refresh with new textiles to save money. “We are seeing a change in the way that customers shop and we do anticipate a difficult period going forward,” he said. “We don’t think that there’s going to be a sudden, miraculous turnaround in confidence.” McCabe described John Healey’s recent budget as a “missed opportunity to back retailers under real pressure”, but said Ikea continued to talk to the government. The company has spent £54m on reducing prices by an average of 20% on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcase , Hemnes daybed and the cantilever Poäng armchair. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ikea is using seasonal offers to pull in customers, for example discounts on extendable dining tables, folding chairs and soft toys in the run-up to Christmas. McCabe said smaller stores, between 1,000 and 2,000 sq metres, had been popular with customers, in sites such as Oxford Street in London and retail parks. As well as the Oxford Street shop which opened within the former Topshop flagship site, Ikea opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York last year, followed by a small store in Chester. It also opened a “plan and order” site – dedicated to kitchen, bedroom, and living room planning – in Dundee, and one in Aberdeen last month.

events.title: US bank services returning to normal after major outage
events.summary: Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services, though Chase said its issue has now been resolved. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems was behind the glitch and it was not a cyber security incident. A spokesperson said "this was not a systemic issue" but noted the impact may have affected other banks "only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us". The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights . In addition, United Airlines also reported a "widespread system outage". The problems with the banks started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website. Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News, though Chase Bank told the BBC that customers still had access to their accounts and funds. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details. Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage Published 3 days ago Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech Published 4 days ago Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds". The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US. The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank. Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported. Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions. US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent. Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments. Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted. As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages. Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights". That issue resolved within a few hours. The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity. The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines. The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US. On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues. The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel. It will meet at least quarterly. The committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. events.title: Dubai's Al Maktoum Airport to undergo year of tests before first passengers arrive
events.summary: Moving operations from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Al Maktoum International (DWC) will be a complex transition, with the two airports initially running in parallel, operator Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. The new Al Maktoum International Airport will undergo at least a year of testing before its first passengers arrive, as the emirate prepares for one of the biggest operational moves in global aviation. Construction at DWC is continuing at full pace despite the Iran war, with the first phase due to open in 2032. More than 100,000 workers are on site at the $35 billion development, where piling and groundworks are under way, Mr Griffiths said in a media briefing on Tuesday. “The budget is something like $35 billion and I know major contracts are being discussed as I speak,” he said. “There are more than 100,000 workers on site. Piling is commencing. Groundworks are well under way. So, it's definitely a live project.” The testing programme will cover critical systems including baggage handling, check-in processes , Wi-Fi and other airport technology, with the aim of ensuring the airport is fully operational before passengers start using it. “The good thing is we have got the test period … of having DXB to test all this new technology before we migrate there, so there will be at least a year of testing before we even allow the first customer to cross the threshold,” Mr Griffiths said. “Then, of course, the transition is going to be enormous.” 'Particularly complex move' Mr Griffiths added that the move would be unprecedented in scale, involving several times the 20 million passengers affected when Hong Kong relocated its main airport in the 1990s. “We will be nearly five or six times that by the time we move from here. So that’s never been done on that scale,” he said. Dubai Airports has awarded Dh13 billion ($3.53 billion) worth of contracts this year for construction of the new DWC terminal, with another Dh55 billion to be awarded by the end of 2026, Mr Griffiths said in August. The move from DXB to Al Maktoum International will be particularly complex because of the scale of operations involved, he said on Monday. The transition will also require extensive recruitment and training. “The fact that we are about five years away from the opening of the new airport fills me with dread because there’s so much to do. We’ve got to recruit so many more people. We’ve got to train them. We’ve got to operate two airports, and then we’ve got to condense down to one airport. So, all of these challenges are pretty enormous,” Mr Griffiths said. “Our task here is to keep everything going to make sure that the transition between the two is covered.” The 70km shift from DXB to DWC in Dubai's south is not simply an airport infrastructure project but a wider urban development challenge, Mr Griffiths said. “We are taking the entire top left corner of Dubai, where we are sitting now, and we are transplanting it in the bottom right-hand corner, 70km away,” he said. “So that’s much, much more than just an airport project. The whole city has got to move.” Workers living in Dubai and the Northern Emirates will face significantly longer commutes to the new airport, making it necessary to develop communities closer. “All of those people living in the Northern Emirates, they won’t be able to commute every day all the way down to Al Maktoum International. So we’ve got to build cities for the airport sector workers as well,” Mr Griffiths said. Dubai Airports has already advanced its operational planning for the transition, with the concept of operations and master plans well developed. Critical contracts for DWC’s baggage-handling system and automated people movers are also under discussion, Mr Griffiths said. The broader objective is to ensure that the move does not constrain the emirate’s passenger growth or disrupt airport services. “Our real measure of success is: can we keep growth going in the city without constraining the supply of capacity, and can we seamlessly manage the transition?” he said. The first phase will give the new terminal an annual capacity of 150 million passengers. Ultimately, the airport is set to reach a capacity of 260 million passengers and 12 million tonnes of cargo a year when complete.

events.title: Trump administration weighs Marshall for FDA as Overton wobbles
events.summary: The Scoop Republicans are discussing Sen. Roger Marshall as a potential replacement nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration as Heidi Overton’s confirmation struggles in the Senate, according to four people familiar with the matter. The Kansas Republican, who just lost his reelection bid, is seen as a stronger potential nominee than Overton, who faces opposition from both anti-abortion activists and moderate Republicans in her bid to lead the agency. Republicans face a severe time crunch if Overton’s nomination is pulled or fails in committee; they have a month and a half left in the majority to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominees. “Marshall is viewed as an alternative if Heidi can’t make it through,” a Trump administration official told Semafor. “Senators have an easier time getting confirmed, traditionally. At this point, it’s hard to get anyone approved.” The Senate health committee is scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination on Wednesday. Marshall, a doctor who served two terms in the House before his Senate election in 2020, currently serves on the health committee. It’s unclear how quickly the White House might move on any alternative nominee, whether it’s Marshall or another contender. No final decision has been made on abandoning Overton, though there’s quiet acknowledgment internally that her path to confirmation is exceedingly difficult. “There is a growing view in the Senate that a senator would be the only person while we’ve got a majority so Roger Marshall’s name is quickly percolating as a person who would be confirmable,” said a senior Republican aide. The White House did not immediately comment. Marshall’s office declined comment. The FDA has operated under acting leadership since former Commissioner Marty Makary was pushed out in May after clashing with the White House over whether to authorize flavored vapes. He also faced pressure from anti-abortion Republicans who are pushing for restrictions on abortion pill mifepristone. Kyle Diamantas, a lawyer who worked as the agency’s top food official, was tapped as acting FDA commissioner and earned a reputation as a competent leader who helped stabilize the agency. But the Trump administration official said Diamantas — who did not want the top job on a permanent basis — is eyeing a departure from FDA regardless of what happens with Overton’s nomination. Notable If Marshall had defeated Kansas Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton this month, he may have been in line to take the health committee’s top GOP spot, as Semafor reported .

events.title: Shoppers slowed spending in October with high prices leading to caution
events.summary: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De... NEW YORK -- Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their money ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday. Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September, according to the Commerce Department. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%. Overall retail sales were pulled down by decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Auto vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September. “There are hints of weakening consumer spending as prices rise," wrote Carl B. Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. “Let’s call this report a mixed report card on the health of the consumer." Spending was mixed across different sectors. Business at furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, while clothing and accessories stores declined 0.7%. Sales at consumer electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. Sales at online retailers rose 1.2%. The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2% increase. The weaker sales data followed new evidence that inflation continued to weigh on Americans last month. Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data. Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped. Companies like Kohl’s and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing. Target said it’s offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl’s has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise. Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable. “More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they’re handling them well,” said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion. Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said. That signals that “consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays,” he added. events.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
events.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3. If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor. Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him. "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios. Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News. Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported. Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees : "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress. In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions. Most of the candidates for those senior roles are running unopposed and are still expected to be elected by voice vote because "people don't want long votes," said the senior House Democrat. Any recorded votes would still be secret ballots, unlike the Jan. 3 speaker vote in which members must stand on the floor and announce their choice.

events.title: Wind power's high cost-saving potential
events.summary: Adding wind power to solar and battery storage can cut the cost of meeting nearly all of global electricity demand by close to 20% , demonstrating how renewables can deliver reliable power when it is needed at low costs. Analysis by global energy think tank Ember found that the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand falls from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour when wind complements solar and batteries to generate power on short winter days and prolonged periods of cloud cover. The analysis assumes the remaining 10% is met by gas or diesel backup. In most countries, the trinity of wind, solar, and batteries reduces the need for energy storage systems, although it has little impact near the equator. It also significantly diminishes the risk of a solar and wind lull striking at the same time — a weather phenomenon often described by the German term , which refers to a dark and windless period. High costs of capital in some parts of the world, such as Africa, increase the cost of clean power, however. — Chloé Farand

What privacy? The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher's investigation. Forensic data analysis , published by Alexander Hanff, an attorney, computer scientist, and occasional contributor to The Register , with the support of SOMI (Stichting Onderzoek Marktinformatie), a Netherlands-based privacy group, details the dubious data flow. From October 1 to 3, 2026, Hanff took a clean Google Chrome browser profile and measured what happens when the browser loads the 100 most visited English-language websites for five minutes, without any consent banner interaction. At these 100 sites, visits were made to 265 pages – the home page, the privacy page, and the cookie notice when available – which resulted in 518,770 privacy events without any consent. All 100 sites produced what the report characterizes as Tier 1 events – interception, exfiltration, or high-entropy fingerprinting (a total of 14,675). Tier 2 consists of storage on the device, capturing device characteristics, and script loads without consent (284,463 events recorded). Tier 3 includes protocol mechanisms and passive reads used for tracking (219,632 events). The median website triggered 2,695 events, for a total of 28,695 events deemed high or critical. And 92.4 percent of the servers contacted during this process were on networks outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Most of these servers – 1,247 out of 1,400 – were in the US, and 1,034 belonged to third-parties. The EU General Data Protection Regulation governs the transfer of personal data outside the EEA. The EU allows data transfers to the US for organizations participating in the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. Beyond that, according to Hanff and SOMI, a valid legal mechanism like a contract must be in place or the transfer may fail to meet GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. In some cases, California Penal Code section 631 (interception) and section 502 (computer access) may also be relevant. On these 100 websites, there were 89,437 fingerprinting events, 1,492 cookies set without consent, 7,456 scripts loaded from other origins, 18 websites implementing CNAME cloaking, and 37 websites delivering code to use the browser's built-in AI interfaces. The privacy and cookie notices on these websites imposed a median reading time requirement of 28 minutes and none fully matched what their pages did. Among the sites' consent banners, 115 out of 165 used dark patterns, like steering visitors with emotional language about a "safer" or "better" experience, or "we care about your privacy." The report, released in conjunction with a presentation at the Field Talk conference , also calculates the estimated environmental impact to load all this third-party content on websites without consent: 1,271,444 kWh per year, or enough to power 353 homes in Europe at 3.6 MWh per home annually. SOMI is hosting a data finder to help people request access to the personal data companies have collected about them. Hanff in an email told The Register that he would be shocked if these findings fail to get the attention of lawmakers and regulators in the EU, UK, and US, given plans to file privacy complaints with relevant authorities. "Complaints will be filed against all of them and the EU supervisory authorities have a legal obligation to investigate them all – so we will have to wait and see," he said.

events.title: US data center emissions rival entire countries
events.summary: The largest data centers in the US collectively emit an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually — almost as much as Denmark, according to a study published in the journal Nature Sustainability. Harvard researchers found 403 data centers used almost 2% of US electricity , with most of the power being generated from fossil fuels. Sites in Iowa, Ohio, and Virginia accounted for about half the estimated emissions. The study provides the first peer-reviewed estimates of emissions generated by US data centers since the start of the AI boom, although it is not a comprehensive inventory. Without a publicly available list of facilities, researchers pieced together information using a commercial dataset, satellite imagery, and data on the power mix supplying each regional electricity grid. The findings are likely an underestimate as they exclude data centers that researchers could not sufficiently verify, as well as facilities that rely on on-site power generation. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Nvidia faces its own Lehman moment
events.summary: The position of Nvidia’s Colette Kress — a relatively unknown CFO, a rare female executive in an industry dominated by men, promoted in a storm and taking the mic for the high-stakes earnings call this afternoon — will ring familiar to old Wall Street hands. In March 2008, the day after the Bear Stearns rescue, Lehman Brothers put Erin Callan, its finance chief of barely three months, in front of analysts to clear some blood from the water and defend Lehman’s books. She was poised and persuasive, and the stock soared. Then short seller David Einhorn started picking apart her numbers. By June, Callan was out and Lehman was in a crisis of confidence from which it wouldn’t recover. Callan became a textbook case of the “glass cliff” — women promoted into the spotlight just as things go over the edge — and disappeared from Wall Street before a reputation-mending book tour. Kress, now interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned amid a probe into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and allegations of further affairs with subordinates, faces a different test today. Nobody doubts demand for Nvidia’s chips and its balance sheet is enviably strong. But she carries some of the same baggage, including a Wall Street Journal report that Huang called her a “deer in the headlights” in an August meeting. And she answers to a board that got its first-ever independent chair last week and will decide how long the interim title lasts. She got a vote of confidence from Citi’s Jane Fraser, who told me yesterday : “The company with Colette, at the moment, at the helm … is in very able, capable hands.” — Liz Hoffman

events.title: AI isn't out of energy yet
events.summary: Tim’s view The US data center buildout isn’t screeching to a halt quite yet, and the energy companies behind it still see plenty to look forward to. Between Democrats’ sweep of Congress and Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, the AI bubble has rarely looked so close to bursting. More restrictions are almost certainly forthcoming in newly Democrat-led states like Texas, and the wellspring of capital from Nvidia, both for hyperscalers’ construction ambitions and the comparatively modest needs of energy startups , could start to ebb. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World event this week, leading capital allocators, including Citigroup’s Jane Fraser and Mubadala’s Khaldoon Al Mubarak , pointed to warning lights in the digital economy. But neither seemed exceptionally worried. And as you can read below, Bloom Energy’s KR Sridhar sees “nothing but a huge opportunity” ahead. Last week at COP31, the CEO of power developer Acwa, which just made a $4 billion bet on US data centers, said the current trepidation is a “blip” that can’t reverse the undeniable and unchanging need for more electricity. Goldman Sachs said in a recent note that it hasn’t changed its expectation for $1.4 trillion in AI-related hardware spending by the end of next year; Mark Daly, head of data centers at BloombergNEF, told me he agrees that “the midterms didn’t present anything concrete that would cause us to significantly revise our views.” Even Fermi, the Texas AI energy startup that nearly imploded this year as it struggled to nail down an anchor customer, just landed a nearly $300 million deal with Amazon . Undoubtedly companies in this space will be prone to talking up their own books, and not every data center energy project will pan out. And there’s a big climate issue that hasn’t been adequately addressed: Only a handful of small countries have so far signed on to a COP31 pledge to “power and build AI infrastructure and hardware sustainably.” But no matter who’s in charge at Nvidia, US power demand is only going up. events.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
events.summary: Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors. On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China. This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank. China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests". This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips. One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO . Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands. The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said. Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University. But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient". Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand. These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent. But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips. The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment. Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure". Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls". The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week. Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models. Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

events.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
events.summary: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
events.summary: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. events.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
events.summary: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. events.title: Optimizely hack turns world's biggest websites into malware dispensers
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters BBC, Zoom, HSBC, and GitLab among those caught up in supply chain attack targeting visitors' crypto wallets, credit cards, and iPhones Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his very personal use 11 days ago Pokémon bakeoff reveals best JavaScript frameworks for AI 14 days ago Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps 19 days ago How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2 20 days ago UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest 22 days ago Some of the world's most popular websites spent Monday serving malware to visitors after crooks found a way into a piece of software used to A/B test web pages. Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, identified malicious JavaScript being served by websites belonging to at least 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce, HSB, and TalkTalk. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software. Optimizely allows businesses to tweak the content and layout of their websites without changing the underlying site code. Unfortunately, someone other than its paying customers figured out how to do just that. The attackers abused a feature that allows Optimizely customers to add their own JavaScript to web pages. The malicious code was distributed alongside the legitimate stuff from Optimizely's own content delivery network, giving customers little reason to suspect anything was amiss. Optimizely has since confirmed that the criminals exploited a vulnerability, dubbed "OPTIMJACK" by researchers, in the sign-up process for its experimentation software, adding that it had patched the hole, removed the offending code, revoked tokens, and notified affected customers. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said. “We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." Of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined by Helme and his team, 188 contained malicious code, including those used by Optimizely's own website and login portal. Given the researchers examined only a subset of the scripts, the number of affected businesses could be higher. The malware underwent several revisions over the course of Monday, with cryptocurrency theft among the crooks' money-making schemes. Copy a wallet address to your clipboard and the malware could quietly swap it out for one belonging to the attackers, diverting any funds sent to that address. A card skimmer added later in the day grabbed card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes from payment forms. However, according to a separate analysis by StepSecurity , card details entered into an iframe hosted by a third-party payment processor were beyond the malware's reach. There was something nasty in store for Apple users, too. The malware attempted to deploy the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits on iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS, though how many devices the criminals managed to compromise is anyone's guess. Helme traced roughly $7,000 in cryptocurrency to the attackers' wallets on Monday, though there’s no telling how much more the crooks stand to make from stolen payment card details. By 2152 UTC on Monday, TalkTalk was the only organization remaining on Report URI's list whose Optimizely code still contained the malware. All that money spent securing corporate websites, and the attackers found their way onto them via a bit of software the marketing department uses to tinker with web pages.

events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment … and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” and said he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering his return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Trump's former AI czar criticizes rush to judgment on ex-Nvidia CEO
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, argued on Monday the public was too quick to judge former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though he stopped short of saying whether the board should reinstate Huang as CEO. “You have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in a proper court of law,” Sacks, a longtime venture capitalist and co-founder of Craft Ventures, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. Sacks went on to say that the public “should wait until there’s a proper determination by a legal authority” on the allegations against Huang. The Trump administration and Congress have launched investigations related to the controversy. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week following revelations that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset as well as an Nvidia employee who had reported directly to him, sending shockwaves throughout Silicon Valley. Huang acted as a linchpin of the AI trade, deploying nearly $99 billion across the tech ecosystem to fuel the AI infrastructure buildout. Sacks cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, was spying on Nvidia, citing reports that US intelligence hasn’t arrived at a definitive conclusion. “This narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,” he claimed. Sacks is a staunch proponent of the AI buildout, and has argued that any guardrails on the technology’s development would hamstring the US in its competition with China. The venture capitalist played a decisive role on US policy while in the White House, pushing for softer AI regulation. Sacks drafted parts of Trump’s “AI Action Plan,” a comprehensive blueprint that involves cutting red tape and prioritizing private-sector growth over federal oversight. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram
