events.title: Soros joins family offices selling Nvidia last quarter
events.summary: George Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion (S$12.4 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Soros Fund Management cut its Nvidia stake by almost a fifth in the quarter to 30 Sept, selling about 206,000 shares worth up to US$47.4 million. Several family offices and firms also trimmed Nvidia, while others bought more. They still held more than US$1 billion in Nvidia shares at quarter end. Nvidia remains a key AI stock, but Jensen Huang’s sudden exit as CEO has hit sentiment. The company is searching for a successor and reports earnings on 17 Nov. LONDON – George Soros’ family office joined investment firms for the world’s ultra-rich in trimming Nvidia bets last quarter, locking in gains ahead of Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit from the vaunted chip designer. The billionaire’s namesake money manager cut its stake in Nvidia by almost a fifth in the period ended Sept 30, the biggest disclosed reduction for its Nvidia holding in 2026 after it had previously added to its position, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from quarterly regulatory filings. Michael Platt’s BlueCrest Capital Management, as well as an investment firm for Abu Dhabi ruler Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, also cut their Nvidia stakes during the same period. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s shares were up 22% in 2026 through the end of September, roughly double the gain of the US benchmark S&P 500 Index for the same period. The selling family offices – totalling at least a dozen – all kept at least some shares of Nvidia, with their combined holdings totalling more than US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) at the end of the quarter. For many of those firms, Nvidia remained one of their top US stock positions. Nvidia has ranked among the world’s hottest stocks in recent years as it rapidly became a poster child of the artificial intelligence boom, but Huang’s abrupt departure last week from the company that he has overseen for more than three decades has led to a reckoning. Huang, 63, was ousted as CEO on Nov 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Nvidia employees and a woman suspected by the US Justice Department of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s shares have fallen more than 25% since the New York Times first reported in late October that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot. Nvidia, which reports third-quarter earnings on Nov 17 , has begun its search for a successor, even as some of Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley – and President Donald Trump – are campaigning for his return to the top job. Nvidia’s dominance in the tech boom has made it an important part of many family offices’ investment portfolios, and some of those firms increased their positions in the stock in the third quarter. Among those buying Nvidia were firms managing fortunes on behalf of duty-free shopping tycoon Alan Parker, Brazil’s Moreira Salles finance dynasty and Missouri’s Van Tuyl family. Soros Fund Management, led by former UBS Group AG executive Dawn Fitzpatrick, sold about 206,000 shares in Nvidia last quarter worth as much as US$47.4 million, filings show. Its remaining Nvidia stake was worth nearly US$200 million as of Sept 30. Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Money managers overseeing more than US$100 million in US equities have to file a 13F form within 45 days of the end of each quarter to list their holdings in stocks that trade on US exchanges. It offers one of the few glimpses into how hedge funds and some large family offices invest. Other highlights from the latest 13F filings include: Jeffrey Skoll’s Capricorn Investment Group slashed its biggest holding, selling 9.8 million shares of SpaceX worth almost US$1.5 billion as of Sept 30. Alta Advisers, an investment firm for a branch of Sweden’s Rausing dynasty, increased its number of equity holdings by more than a third last quarter, with 114 new positions including stakes in ExxonMobil, Blue Owl Capital and AMC Entertainment. WIT LLC, which manages a portion of the Walton family fortune, is comprised solely of stakes in exchange-traded funds. It sold 2 million shares of the iShares ESG Aware MSCI EM ETF and bought 2.75 million shares of the Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets ETF. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
events.summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger. Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign , export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing. Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms. “For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University. Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan. One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity. “This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan. The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion. The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t. “I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.” Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense. Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said. Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales. Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low. “I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said. Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, had pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. An Aboriginal woman has been found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging. Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in state's northern midlands. Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania (STT). During hearings earlier this year, Ms Langford argued that STT had failed to comply with their legal obligations to identify and protect Aboriginal cultural heritage. She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered". ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Ms Langford said she had permission to be on the site from Palawa/Pakana elder Uncle Jim Everett, whom she described as the rightful owner of the cultural landscape. In a written decision handed down on Tuesday, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed that Ms Langford had cultural obligations. "Ms Langford was entitled to engage in cultural practices and prevent the logging contractors from commencing their work," Ms Geason stated. However, she said that once Ms Langford was asked to leave, that entitlement ended. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna was charged with trespassing at an anti-logging protest at Snow Hill. ( ABC News: Paul Yeomans ) Ms Geason said that while it was accepted Uncle Jim was a senior elder, he did not hold the authority to grant lawful permission for Ms Langford to remain at the coupe. "I also acknowledge the evidence of Ms Langford and her witnesses regarding the profound grief and responsibility experienced by Aboriginal people when old-growth forests are cleared. "However, the court is bound to apply the law as enacted by parliament." Ms Geason said, on the balance of probabilities, Ms Langford had not established that her cultural obligations amounted to a "reasonable or lawful excuse" to remain on the land. "As such, the charge of trespass is proved." Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna at the anti-logging protest in January last year. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) Ms Langford told the court she was "exceptionally disappointed". Outside court, Ms Langford addressed the media and her supporters. "And regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in country and country has spoken. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna says she is pleased with some parts of the chief magistrate's decision. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Despite the verdict, she said she was pleased with some parts of the written decision. "In my hands is the written reasons why this court denied my internationally recognised rights as an Aboriginal person," she said. "I am delighted to see that she has clearly recognised that as an Aboriginal woman, I have an obligation to protect country. "That those old trees hold our law, that that law exists, and that in the finding, the magistrate has recognised that that is true." Ms Langford said she would continue to practice her cultural obligations. "We will assert that our law is in country and we are the law holders," she said. In Tasmania, trespassing on land can incur a maximum penalty of six months jail, or a $5,325 fine.

events.summary: The Republic must defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, says former foreign minister George Yeo. SINGAPORE – Singapore must be prepared to withstand pressure from bigger powers and defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, former foreign minister George Yeo said. The Republic cannot become a “laundromat for contraband”, he added, stressing that while Singapore must remain flexible in navigating an increasingly fragmented world, there must be limits to how far it is willing to accommodate the demands of other countries. “Being small, we can come under pressure. But beyond a point, we say no. We have to be ourselves,” he said. He was speaking at a panel discussion titled Fault lines: Investing In A Fragmented World, at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026, where he joined fellow panellist Justin Muzinich, chief executive of Muzinich & Co, in looking at the implications of geopolitical tensions, shifting trade relationships and changing investment patterns. Yeo’s remarks come amid growing scrutiny of Singapore’s role as an international financial and wealth management hub , where its reputation for strong institutions, regulatory credibility and the rule of law is central to attracting global capital. He cited the controversy involving Singapore and Alice Huang – a Chinese former executive at Singapore-based firm Megaspeed and alleged spy who former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair with – saying the Government had responded firmly after The Wall Street Journal allegedly distorted the country’s role in the matter. Singapore cannot act on allegations without evidence, Yeo said. “If you tell us it’s contraband, we’ll investigate it, and please give us information. But if it’s just an allegation without proof, then we cannot continue withholding or impounding or detaining someone at your behest,” he added. For a small country deeply connected to the global economy, such situations can put Singapore in a difficult position, particularly when demands come from larger, more powerful nations. But Yeo said the Republic’s credibility depends on its willingness to stand by its principles rather than buckle under pressure. He recalled the 1994 Michael Fay case in which the American teenager was sentenced to caning for vandalism in Singapore. Then US President Bill Clinton appealed for clemency, and Singapore reduced the sentence from six strokes to four. The episode strained bilateral relations, with then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong unable to visit the White House for three years, Yeo said. Singapore paid a price for its position, but the country’s standing among other nations, including China and India, rose because it demonstrated it would not compromise its principles under external pressure. “So we are flexible, but beyond a point, no. And if there’s a price to be paid, so be it,” he said. Yeo said this firmness was not a departure from Singapore’s approach, but a longstanding reason other countries trust the Republic as a jurisdiction. His comments come as the global order becomes increasingly fragmented, with the rivalry between the United States and China reshaping trade, investment flows and the movement of technology and capital. Yeo described the world as undergoing a major transition, with geopolitical fault lines shifting and a new equilibrium gradually emerging. “We are entering an earthquake,” he said, adding that countries would have to remain watchful and careful as the transition unfolds. For Singapore, preserving its ability to manoeuvre will require a combination of flexibility and firmness, particularly as economic relationships become increasingly entangled with national security and political considerations. Yeo also cautioned investors against assuming that existing trends would continue uninterrupted. History, he said, has often been punctuated by sudden disruptions that could produce winners and losers. Investors should therefore consider potential failure scenarios, including a sharp disruption to the US dollar, an artificial intelligence bubble or geopolitical escalation in the Middle East. Yeo urged them to think beyond conventional market projections and consider what could bring entire economic or financial structures down. In an uncertain world, Singapore’s greatest asset may ultimately be the trust it commands. For Yeo, protecting that trust means knowing when to accommodate international pressures – and when to draw the line. Angela Tan is senior correspondent at The Straits Times’ business desk.

events.title: 'Bragyu' beef a milestone for famous outback station
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Remote Bullo River Station producing branded Wagyu Brahman beef Bullo River beef for sale in Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Bullo River Station in the NT has started producing branded beef, using its herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle. The first animals have been processed and are now for sale at some local butcher shops in the north. A butcher from Kununurra says it is the first time he has been able to sell locally produced beef. One of the most remote cattle stations in northern Australia has started producing its own branded beef, which is now being sold in local butcher shops either side of the WA/NT border. Bullo River Station in the Northern Territory is located about 800 kilometres south-west of Darwin and becomes impossible to access via road during the wet season months. Managers Joe and Catherine Atkins run a herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle and said it had been a dream come true to supply local beef to communities in the region. "About six years ago the owners of this station, the Burt family, put this idea together and we started breeding what we've branded the Bragyu," Mr Atkins said. "So this is a long time coming, but it's now on the shelves for local people and it's very exciting." Wagyu Brahman cross cattle at Bullo River Station, NT. ( Supplied: Bullo River ) Mr Atkins said the station sent a trial consignment of animals to the Rum Jungle abattoir near Batchelor for a service kill and would look to ramp up next year if all went to plan. "We want to initially support butchers in Katherine and Kununurra and also give visitors here at Bullo River the paddock to plate experience," he said. "It's a very different game to what I'm used to; I've long done live export, that was my world, but this is exciting. Butcher Murray Salter cutting beef from Bullo River Station. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Murray Salter took over the butcher shop in Kununurra 10 years ago and said being able to sell locally produced beef was a milestone for his business. "I've been waiting 10 years for a moment like this to source local beef for our customers," he said. "The local Brahman stock all get sent to the live export trade, but by crossing them with the Wagyu it's brought a quality meat to the Kimberley. "Our beef supply normally travels 3,000 to 4,000 kilometres to get here, but this is from just down the road, which is nice." Beef from Bullo River Station packaged up, ready for sale. ( Supplied: Tenderspot Kununurra ) Mr Salter said the beef was tender, juicy, could be cut "with a butter knife", and local customers had been excited to support it. The Bullo River beef is the latest in a growing trend of northern cattle stations selling products locally, including KAPCO beef in the Kimberley, Eva Valley Meats in the NT, and the Niceforo family processing its cattle near Katherine for a new Darwin steakhouse. Joe Atkins said in terms of dollars, selling branded beef was not too different to selling direct to the live export trade, but there were other benefits. Bullo River Station is located 800km south-west of Darwin and 200km east of Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) "There's satisfaction for us is supporting local people and not doing live export," he said. "I've lived up here 40 years and have never been able to buy local beef from our local butcher store, so yeah, I think this is the future. "Actually 45 years ago there was a small abattoir here on Bullo River Station, so it's funny how the wheels have turned around and that is definitely our grand plan to have a micro-abattoir on the property.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Large amounts of fencing has been dumped by the roadside in Noranda. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Main Roads says it removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from Perth's road network over the past two financial years. Perth resident Robert Parker says he reported what appeared to be asbestos and fencing dumped on Reid Highway, and blames costly, restrictive tip rules. Main Roads says the dumped material on Reid Highway will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week. Tonnes of rubbish and potentially toxic old building material are being dumped on Perth roadsides and nature strips by what is believed to be contractors and others avoiding council tip fees. WA's Main Roads department says it has removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the Perth metropolitan road network over the past two years. Dianella resident Robert Parker told 102.5 ABC Perth he recently saw what appeared to be 10 tonnes of material by the side of Reid Highway when he was out walking. "There's what appeared to be a bit of asbestos or fencing being dumped in the scrub down there," he said. "Later on, I was driving and [it appeared] a commercial contractor has chosen to use the verge on Reid Highway as his yard and dumped asbestos material and other products that should go to landfill or the appropriate recycling facility." Mr Parker said he reported the dumping to Main Roads, but also believed councils were making it too expensive for people to legally dispose of their hard rubbish. "You go to the tips, and they say, 'Oh no, we don't accept super six fencing here anymore, we don't take hardy fence', or it's only so many sheets per time. Construction waste dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Listeners to 102.5 ABC Radio Perth said there were significant barriers to disposing of rubbish legally. Matt : 'It's very expensive to take waste to the recycling centre. Last week they would not accept some bathroom tiles. They said it was construction waste, and won't be accepted. No wonder people do illegal dumping.' Anon : "It's a no-brainer: getting rid of waste in the community is far too expensive. It should be free and funded by the state government through our taxes, a clean city with proper disposal is good for everyone and everyone should pay through the taxes. Illegal dumping goes away then, and we return to a beautiful litter-free city." Anon : "I took a broken office chair to the local tip. The guy on the gate said it would cost me $45 to dump it. I guess that's why people dump stuff illegally.' Sivwarr : 'I drive up to Gidgegannup quite regularly on Toodyay road the illegal dumping starts at the bottom of the hills and just doesn't stop." Rick : "The reason for illegal dumping is laziness, selfishness and a sense of self-entitlement." Rubbish dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway between Camboon Road and Alexander Drive. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) In a statement, a Main Roads spokesperson said the department was aware of the fencing material on the southern side of Reid Highway. "The material has been programmed for removal and will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week," the spokesperson said. "Across the 2024/25 and 2025/26 financial years, Main Roads removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the metropolitan road network alone." They said the department continued to monitor known dumping hotspots and used "targeted measures" to deter offending.

events.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
events.summary: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

events.title: ‘Due for a reset’: Mubadala CEO says global AI economy faces compute shortage
events.summary: The global AI buildout and broader economy is due for “a reset of sorts,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said Monday. Asked whether “winter is coming” — a nod to fears that the AI boom could face a correction — Al Mubarak said it was, but that “winter doesn’t mean minus 30 degrees. It could be a nice pleasant winter,” he said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The AI buildout is part of “a cycle,” Al Mubarak said, adding that the global economy has had “a very good run.” The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund is a major investor in AI infrastructure and software, with big bets on data center developers and both OpenAI and Anthropic, through MGX, a separate funding vehicle it co-founded. Mubadala has become one of the most aggressive Gulf sovereign wealth funds, embarking on a dealmaking spree , tying up with some of the biggest names in global finance, and taking a more active role leading on investments rather than being a passive capital provider. About 44% of Mubadala’s assets are in North America, and it has aligned itself with the US’ efforts to dominate the AI race with China. “There’s no navigating” between the US and China, Al Mubarak said Monday. “You either go US or China, and we’re betting on the US technology stack.” Al Mubarak said he’s “hoping that any US government, Republican or Democrat, is going to be partnership-oriented.” He said he isn’t worried about energy, and that access to capital is “OK,” but that getting enough compute is the biggest challenge. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite backing from big names
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite big names backing his return Jensen Huang stepped down from the Nvidia board last week. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Nvidia is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang, despite Elon Musk and Donald Trump supporting his return. Mr Huang was forced to step down amid revelations about affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters. Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return. Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO . Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen". The message "Taiwan heart Jensen" was projected on the Taipei 101 building in Taipei in support of Jensen Huang. ( Reuters: Ann Wang ) It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online. "We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said. The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known. However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back." The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor. Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings. Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said. Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity". Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom. Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan. He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia. "His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said. "But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

events.title: Greens offer government a path to pass trusts and capital gains tax changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens narrow demand on trusts and capital gains tax changes David Shoebridge has raised concerns about an exemption to Labor's trust tax for private schools and other tax-exempt entities. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The Greens want the government to commit to reforming charity rules in exchange for passage of its tax bills. A "name and shame" proposal for trusts and beneficiaries is not a red line and the Greens have no major issues with the government's CGT carve-out. The government is trying to pass two tax bills through the Senate by the end of next week. The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector. Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime. The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate. The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC. The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions. But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday. Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal. That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable. Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated". The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods". Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update. Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler. In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns". "Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote. "Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less." In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex. "This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote. He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax. In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model. "I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said. Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment... "The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now.

events.title: 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer
events.summary: Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error. We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting. Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us.” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy.” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia. Others will work from India and the Philippines. While Bunnings follows the template of a big box retailer, each of its stores allows charities and community groups to run fundraising barbeques in its forecourt every weekend. Those barbeques are a significant source of income for many non-profits and have earned the chain a broad social license. The hardware barn is so well-known that children’s TV show Bluey – the most viewed program of 2024 and 2025 in the US – gently parodied it as "Hammerbarn" it in an episode. The Register mentions this because we understand the reference to TCS staff helping to deliver the Bunnings experience has gone down badly, as the chain’s employees wonder how offshore workers who have not experienced its stores and atmosphere can deliver a service that preserves its culture. Bunnings says its new IT operating model will commence in July 2027 and that “Impacted team members will be supported in their roles through Christmas, with any changes taking effect in the new year.” The company’s IT team will still employ around 500 people. These job losses add to a rotten year for Australia’s tech scene, which this year saw local heroes Canva and Atlassian farewell hundreds of staff. Iconic Australian airline Qantas last week outsourced hundreds of jobs to India through Accenture. ®

events.title: Dubai airport on target for 70 million passengers this year amid recovery from war
events.summary: Dubai International Airport handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, even as the Iran war disrupted travel. The airport sustained vital connections for tourism, trade and business during the period, with continued investment in artificial intelligence, connected systems and smarter processes aimed at boosting future growth, state-owned operator Dubai Airports said on Tuesday. Passenger traffic in the nine months to the end of September fell 28.1 per cent year on year, while third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, Dubai Airports said. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. The airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, as airlines resume services and its global network strengthens, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year , the highest annual international passenger traffic recorded by any airport. DXB has also delayed its target of 100 million passengers to 2027. “We are focused on continuing to accommodate future growth … innovation is central to that approach,” he said. Return of global airlines The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted air travel this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. This month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group also said last week that it would resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. Other airlines are scheduled to resume operations in the coming weeks, Dubai Airports said. DXB, the world’s busiest international hub for passengers in 2025, is served by 57 airlines connecting Dubai to 235 destinations across 101 countries. Mr Griffiths said in September that DXB was determined to hold on to the top spot despite war-related disruption. India was DXB’s largest country market in the third quarter of this year, accounting for 2.6 million passengers, followed by Saudi Arabia with 1.4 million and the UK with 1.3 million, Dubai Airports aid on Tuesday. London was the leading city destination, with 784,000 passengers, followed by Mumbai with 528,000 and New Delhi with 525,000. No spillover impact from war Mr Griffiths said he is not expecting a spillover impact from the ongoing attacks in the neighbouring countries of Saudi Arabia and Bahrain. “People tend to lump the [Middle East] region as one big trouble spot,” he said. “Yeah, but it's not. You can't say that the whole of the Middle Eastern area is one homogenous area because it isn't. And obviously, the issues between the Saudis and the Yemenis are one thing. The issues between Iran and the rest of the region is another thing.” He said there is a “sense of optimism” now. “I think the collective view now is that hopefully a diplomatic solution to the position we find ourselves in here is perhaps more likely than a military solution. I think that is the optimism,” he said. Mr Griffiths also said he is not seeing any deterrence in the number of international travellers that want to come back to Dubai. “In fact, the appetite is incredibly healthy and I think we feel quite positive about the prospects,” he said. “We may even see close to our magic 100 million by the end of next year.” In terms of capacity, the airport chief said it is about “83 per cent” back. “There's absolutely no barriers for us to get back to 100 per cent capacity and I think if you look at the recovery rates of the airlines, particularly Emirates, they are in the 90s [per cent], so they're very, very close to where they were last year,” he said. Technology leads the way Dubai Airports is investing in AI, predictive analytics and biometric technology to improve passenger flows and increase capacity within existing facilities, it said. The initiatives bring together data and visual feeds from airport systems to give operations teams a real-time view of passenger movements, aircraft activity and airport facilities. AI tools help identify potential bottlenecks and allow staff to address pressure points before they affect operations. “Every process we simplify and every bottleneck we remove helps us use our existing facilities more efficiently,” Mr Griffiths said. “By combining technology with better ways of working, we can unlock additional capacity without expanding the airport’s footprint, while improving the experience for our guests.” Operational performance Aircraft movements fell 27.6 per cent to 243,000 in the first nine months, while cargo volumes declined 23.2 per cent to 1.215 million tonnes. The average passenger load factor stood at 74 per cent, three percentage points lower than a year earlier, Dubai Airports said. The airport processed 48 million bags during the nine-month period, with 91 per cent delivered within 45 minutes of arrival. In the third quarter, 99.9 per cent of passengers waited less than 10 minutes at departure passport control, while the same proportion cleared arrival passport control within 15 minutes, Dubai Airports said.

events.title: Bunnings cuts 230 jobs in partial offshoring of tech services
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bunnings to make 230 jobs redundant amid partial offshoring of tech services Bunnings is planning to cut more than 200 permanent jobs. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Bunnings has announced plans to cut 230 tech jobs and end 120 contractor agreements. The retail giant has signed an agreement with an Indian-based tech firm to offshore some of its tech services. The company says job cuts will begin in the new year. Hardware retailer Bunnings will cut roughly 230 jobs and end 120 contractor agreements as it shifts part of its technology department offshore. The Australian retail giant announced today it had penned a new agreement with Indian-based tech firm Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as part of a restructure of its technology services. Roughly 230 permanent roles will be made redundant and an additional 120 contractor roles will end as a result. Australia cashes in on India's IT jobs machine India has positioned itself as a global hub of skilled, cheap labour, and Australian companies are moving more jobs to its shores. In a statement, Bunnings managing director Mike Schneider said the changes aimed to respond to evolving consumer needs. "This is a necessary but important change. We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us," Mr Schneider said. The transition is due to begin in December and continue through to June next year, the company said. Affected staff will be supported in their roles over Christmas, with job losses to begin in the new year, while the retailer will retain a core in-house technology team of approximately 500 people based in Australia. Remaining services will be delivered by TCS teams based in Australia, India and the Philippines. Mike Schneider says impacted staff are being offered support. ( Supplied: Bunnings ) Mr Schneider said Bunnings would support impacted team members through various means, including redundancy packages. "We know that this is difficult for our Technology team members, particularly those impacted by the change," he said. "We're managing these changes with care and respect, including through redundancy packages, career transition, redeployment wherever possible and wellbeing support." Bunnings is the latest in a growing list of Australian companies , including Qantas, NAB, Officeworks, Woolworths and Coles, to announce plans to outsource jobs overseas. 'Difficult news to share', executive says Staff were given the news earlier today by Bunnings chief information officer Genevie Elliott, who said it was "difficult news to share". In a virtual meeting with employees, Ms Elliott said many of those impacted by today's announcement had helped build up the company's technology services, which remained in use across its network of stores. Bunnings is the latest major Australian company to offshore part of its operation. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I want you to know these changes we're announcing are not a reflection of anyone's performance or their contribution or value," she told staff. "So I think it's really important you all understand why we've made this decision. Over the last two years, we've deliberately strengthened our tech function. "We've evolved our structure, our ways of working, how we prioritise and deliver work, and that structure has served us well. "I don't want anyone thinking those changes didn't work. They did. But this decision that I'm sharing today builds on that work." Ms Elliott said bringing TCS on board would allow the company to drive down business costs and tap into "specialist expertise and global retail experience". "We need a model that allows us to remain competitive without continually increasing our costs. This partnership will help us do that," she said. She said the company had to evolve alongside a rapidly transforming online retail environment impacting how consumers shop. "And we all know that tech is rapidly evolving, and the pace of change is only going to increase. That means we need to respond to keep up.

events.title: Robert Pattinson as James Bond throws out the 007 playbook
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts As James Bond, Robert Pattinson prepares to lead his biggest franchise yet Robert Pattinson has capped off a blockbuster year by snagging the coveted role of 007. ( AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision ) Who knew Twilight would have predicted the next 007? Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond , succeeding fellow Englishman Daniel Craig in one of Hollywood's most recognisable roles . But it's a scene from Pattinson's breakout film that has resurfaced for its eerily prophetic nature. In the 2008 vampire hit, the prom theme is Monte Carlo, with the students of Forks High School told to think "gambling, tuxedos and Bond … James Bond". The camera than cuts to Pattinson's Edward Cullen, who steps out of a sleek silver Volvo sporting Ray-Bans and a smirk. Fast forward nearly 20 years and that parallel is now a reality. Pattinson brings maximum star power to the James Bond role, reportedly beating out fellow Brits Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor. "I think Robert Pattinson is one of the most dynamic and most interesting actors working in Hollywood," film critic Luke Goodsell says, noting his roles in this year's Primetime , The Drama and The Odyssey . Several of Robert Pattinson's projects have hit theatres this year, including Primetime. ( Supplied: A24 ) Pattinson's appointment also marks the first time James Bond has been cast since Amazon reportedly paid more than $1 billion for the 007 intellectual property in February last year. The announcement of a new actor to play James Bond gives the franchise an opportunity to reinvent itself for a new audience. "It's been remarked on that it's the first time the Bond franchise has cast a big A-Lister," Goodsell says. "Obviously, Roger Moore was famous for The Saint and Pierce Brosnan was famous to some degree for Remington Steele, but this is the first time they've really gone for an A-list actor. Which is unusual, Goodsell says, because "the former producer Barbara Broccoli was always adamant that the actor should not be bigger than 007". "But I think repeating the same old playbook where they cast a relative unknown would be the least interesting choice at this point in the franchise," Goodsell says. "For them to dive straight in, headlong into a major movie star, and a really interesting and slippery actor who is also a movie star, is a really fascinating choice." Pattinson is no stranger to franchises. One of his first major roles was in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005, where he played the dashing but doomed Cedric Diggory, his death marking the moment the series goes from whimsical to something much darker. But Pattinson was launched to stratospheric levels of fame in 2008 when he landed the role of Edward Cullen in Twilight, the film's success cementing his heart-throb status in Hollywood and making him a household name, in the homes of teenage girls, at least. Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Edward Cullen in Twilight. ( Reuters: Mario Anzuoni ) Despite his fame, Pattinson rallied against his handsome, alluring on-screen persona, instead using his countless interviews on the Twilight press junket to begin a years-long affinity for creating bizarre, fabricated stories. In a 2024 interview with The New York Times , the actor revisited a 2011 interview in which he spoke extensively about watching a clown die in a little-car explosion as a kid. "There was absolutely no hesitation at all [in my voice]," Pattinson said with a combination of "pride and alarm". His reason? Boredom, explaining "the only thing people would ever ask me about was being famous" and "you go into, like, a fugue state". Goodsell says Pattinson's career has been "compelling to watch". Post Twilight, Goodsell says Pattinson and his co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'". With five Twilight movies complete, Pattinson had the freedom to get weird. Robert Pattinson (right) starred alongside Willem Dafoe (left) in The Lighthouse. ( Supplied: Universal ) He dived into independent films, teaming up with David Cronenberg for Cosmopolis, starring in the Safdie brothers' Good Time, and Robert Eggers' psychological horror The Lighthouse. In 2020, he would star in one his most Bond-esque roles to date: Christopher Nolan's Tenet. He even explored voice acting for the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron. "He really kind of, let's just say it, lets his freak flag fly. He loves a weird voice," Goodsell says.

events.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
events.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

events.title: MP declares shares in data centre developer before calling for moratorium
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts MP Peter George declares shares in data centre developer before calling for Tasmanian moratorium Peter George has been critical of the Tasmanian government's approach to data centres in the state. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmania's parliament is set to debate a bill for a moratorium on new data centre developments until binding rules are put in place. The MP who put forward the moratorium bill — Franklin independent Peter George — has disclosed shares in an Australian property company which has almost 80 per cent of its development pipeline in data centres. Mr George says his interest in Goodman Group centres on its commercial buildings, which have "a wide range of uses". A Tasmanian independent MP who has tabled a bill for a moratorium on new data centres has declared shares in a property giant whose global development pipeline is almost 80 per cent data centres. Franklin MP Peter George listed Sydney-headquartered Goodman Group among the interests in his "retirement plan", previously described as his self-managed super fund. The company was not included in his disclosure 12 months earlier, when the Climate 200-backed MP listed shares in Origin Energy and poker machine venue operator Endeavour Group , both of which he divested as being "inappropriate" to his values. In its full-year results, released in August, Goodman Group outlined that data centre development accounted for more than $15 billion out of its total $19.7 billion global work in progress. The proportion has increased substantially in the past 18 months for the industrial and logistics property group, rising from 57 per cent to 68 per cent by September last year, and now at 78 per cent, building large facilities aimed at cloud and AI customers. Liberals' vote hits 25-year low as One Nation continues Tasmanian surge Tasmanian brand Coal River Farm enters voluntary administration Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Multiple shots fired at Tasmanian home with person inside US tech billionaire flags interest in Hurricanes, Hobart stadium Peter George with supporters during his election campaign. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) Mr George has been critical of the Tasmanian government's lack of specific planning controls and broader framework for data centre development in Tasmania, describing "deep uncertainty" about their costs and benefits, with "growing resistance from communities globally". He tabled a bill for a moratorium on data centres on Tuesday until issues around location, energy and water use had been addressed, saying there is concern in Tasmania "about the impact of giant data centres on communities and natural resources". His bill would ensure data centres could only be built in specially designated zones, and that public consultation and appeal rights are retained. Mr George confirmed he bought the shares in the past 12 months and said his interest in Goodman Group was due to its commercial holdings. He said he would review his shares as Goodman "changes its portfolio listings" to ensure he is comfortable with the company's direction. "It just shows that I am technologically neutral," he said. "I am quite happy to engage with a company which, in part, develops data centres but also other commercial undertakings, other commercial buildings at the same time. Goodman Group recently withdrew plans for its proposed $1.2 billion Project Mars facility in Sydney's north shore after community opposition and regulatory changes . It does not have any publicly announced proposals for Tasmania. Mr George said data centres needed to be placed "in the right places and under the right conditions". Approach is 'one of caution', MP says The Tasmanian government last week released an "expectations" document for data centre developments. It included partnering with new renewable energy projects, but not be expected to procure or construct new firming capacity if this was already available from Hydro Tasmania. They would need to "use water efficiently" and minimise water demand through the design phase. Progressive politician has shares in mining, pokies An independent MP who received more than $72,000 in donations from Climate 200 says he will divest his shares in a fossil fuel company, miner and pokies venue operator, as they conflict with his "approach to life". A community benefit fund would also be established, a common method for any new development type involving large companies. The expectations were criticised by Labor and the Greens, who both called for binding rules prior to developments proceeding. They both supported a pause on new data centres until these are in place.

events.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
events.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 5 days ago The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? events.title: Singapore discussing effect of new chip rules with US, minister says
events.summary: Singapore is pressing Trump administration officials for details on new rules designed to crack down on China’s access to advanced US-made chips, and which pose a potential threat to the country’s booming AI sector. Josephine Teo, Singapore’s minister for digital development and information, said Monday her government is “engaging with our US counterparts as to the scope of implementation.” “I think more importantly, how we can facilitate trusted access to this very important AI infrastructure,” Teo said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, noting she has spoken with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. The new US Commerce Department rules include closing a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced US semiconductors via third-country data centers, which the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, at the center of the Nvidia scandal that took down CEO Jensen Huang, is accused of exploiting. Singapore has also been added to a list of countries that faces export restrictions on advanced chips, a move US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had postponed repeatedly until his agency came under scrutiny in recent days. “Singapore takes very seriously the upholding of the rule of law,” Teo said, noting that there are about 6,000 US companies in Singapore: “We safeguard our integrity in the business environment and we do not condone anyone… violating the laws of other countries.” “If they also violate our laws, they can be very certain that we will actively investigate and also hold them to account,” Teo said. Teo declined to comment on her government’s claim that the US had been unhelpful in the city state’s investigation of Megaspeed — whose former executive, Alice Huang, is accused of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset — but noted that Singapore’s own investigation into the company predated its knowledge of an investigation by the US Bureau of Industry and Security. “Suffice to say, investigations into Megaspeed are still continuing,” Teo said. Teo said the environment in Singapore for AI companies would continue to remain favorable, and pointed out that firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had deepened their presence in Singapore in recent months. “There is positive momentum. We’d like to keep it going.” “I think we will try our best to understand the impact and help ensure that we continue to have trusted access to the critical infrastructure needed for legitimate businesses,” Teo said. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Government backflips on backpacker policy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government backflips on backpacker regional work policy Tony Burke has backed down on proposed changes to backpacker visas. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) The government has backed down on planned changes to working holiday visas. The cap on third-year visas will rise from 5,000 to 25,000, while second-year applicants will have tougher regional work requirements. British backpackers remain exempt from regional work rules. The government has backed down on its planned overhaul of the working holiday-maker program, agreeing to increase the number of backpackers eligible for a third-year visa and tightening regional work requirements. Under changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, working holiday-makers would need to complete 120 days of regional work, up from 88 days, to qualify for a second-year visa. In a major speech in September, Mr Burke had announced third-year visas would be capped at 5,000 places, a reduction on the current level of about 31,000. That cap will now be set at 25,000 places, while the introduction of a ballot system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee has also been delayed to next year after it was originally scheduled to start in November. The shift follows months of pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors over the government's original proposal, with businesses warning it would significantly reduce the supply of seasonal workers and leave them struggling to fill jobs over summer. The new arrangements will apply from March 1, while backpackers who complete their regional work requirements before that date will remain eligible under the existing rules, creating a transition period for those already in the country. A visa is the reason backpackers take on the tough jobs in regional Australia. The cap on second-year places would be set at 45,000. Mr Burke rejected suggestions the government was abandoning its original reforms, arguing the final package had been shaped by consultations with industry and would ultimately deliver more workers to regional Australia. "From the day after the speech … we started consultation with industry to work through what is the best landing place to deliver the total numbers that we're talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry," he said. "This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them." He said the government had been able to refine its approach because of a go-slow in visa processing which had created "head room" to adjust the broader working holiday-maker reforms while still pursuing an overall lower migration number. The number of backpackers getting visas to Australia has fallen dramatically since July, when the go-slow was introduced as a temporary fix designed to put the brakes on international arrivals. Since then, 44,469 visas have been approved, which means a total of 177,876 backpackers would be granted entry to Australia this financial year, if the government maintains its current rate of processing. Last financial year, a record 323,077 backpacker visas were granted in Australia. Mr Burke said Australia would continue to welcome working holiday-makers. "These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term," he said. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the changes were 'complete nonsense'. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Opposition rubbishes changes as 'complete nonsense' Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the proposal as "complete nonsense" and vowed to repeal the changes if the Coalition was elected. "They've created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot. They've said they're going to delay it … they should just axe it," he said. The sentiment was echoed by Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said the backdown was "inevitable" but warned the government had already damaged confidence in the sector. The National Farmers' Federation welcomed the changes but said key questions remained unanswered. "We need more details on the logistical realities of this reform before we can fully throw our support behind it," president Hamish McIntyre said. In WA, Premier Roger Cook acknowledged the federal government's need to bring down net overseas migration, but said he would make sure it "doesn't impact on Western Australia's economy". He said he hoped further adjustment to the system would improve the number of working holiday-makers heading west. "What I want to see is less people going to the east coast and more people coming to the west coast," Mr Cook said.

events.title: The tech industry has a public image problem, Arianna Huffington says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” corporate leaders who “just lack wisdom,” Arianna Huffington said Monday. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. “We see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,” said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. “We need to invest in making humans better.” Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is “ridiculous.” Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isn’t considering it . Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, “doesn’t even come close to computing. You can’t bring Jensen back.” Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public. “The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials “to communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.” Huffington said that people’s anxieties and fears stem from how life — not just the economy — is changing. “There was no effort to really tell a story that would touch people’s hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.” Rattner, who led the Obama administration’s 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldn’t take stakes in AI companies. “We did not to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,” he said. “I think it’s a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.” — J.D.
