events.title: Medical students should ‘learn the hard way,’ AI startup CEO says
events.summary: The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI. “The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to “train classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,” he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie. Nadler’s company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians. The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI. He noted that all of his company’s engineers use “dozens and dozens of AI buddies.” Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry “AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.” Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers “did more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,” he told Sergie that “some people underestimate how big pharma is.” “We’re early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier — and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,” Liu said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: OpenAI CFO says latest funding round was unplanned, prompted by news report
events.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is “good for the ecosystem” and “good for us,” Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that the company was unconcerned with being second. Retail investors are ready for access to frontier models, not just hyperscalers which come with “pros and cons,” she said. After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said that the company was closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested that the latest round was unplanned and “opportunistic,” and was prompted after a “very well-respected, well-known publication… announced we were fundraising, which we weren’t.” “That caused a whole bunch of inbounds from investors, and so we said, okay, if we can be super fast and in kind of a six-week period, go in and out of the market, be done by the midterms, let’s do it because why not?” Friar said. Friar also said that OpenAI’s advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue in under 200 days — a record for the company. Addressing the public resentment in the US over data centers, Friar said that for companies to regain trust, “you have to show up in those communities” and “be accountable.” She noted that in Georgia, where the company is hoping to build a 3.2 gigawatt data center, OpenAI has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. But she acknowledged that OpenAI is still seeing the backlash to the AI buildout that was evident in the US midterm elections. “People are getting way too bombarded by kind of the rage element to not feel that there’s something they should be reacting to,” Friar said. “But when you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Trump cyber director: FAA, other outages not a cyberattack
events.summary: White House cyber director Sean Cairncross said Monday that a cyberattack was not behind the Trump administration’s nationwide ground stop of air traffic or other outages reported on Monday, attributing the problems to upgrades of old technology. “No, this is not any sort of coordinated, nefarious cyberattack from a malicious actor,” Cairncross told Semafor. “What we are seeing, and frankly I’d expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems.” He said the US government is tracking all recent software outages in the last few days. Cairncross told Semafor in an earlier interview that the Trump administration has no plans to release, or require compliance with, its voluntary framework for review of new advanced AI models — adding that frontier labs have cooperated. “The labs have been extremely good about being in communication with us and giving their new models for evaluation to be assessed,” Cairncross said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Putting a strict regulatory regime in place “isn’t going to work at the speed that we need,” he added. Cairncross said that the administration did not release the full text of the framework, which was set in motion by a June executive order, to enable a “frank conversation” with AI companies. He did say he believed the White House will soon make “it much more clear how this is working in practice.” The White House has taken a lighter-touch regulatory approach to the AI industry compared with Europe or the Biden administration; it has also taken steps to block states from stepping in. On the question of cybersecurity, Cairncross was bullish on AI’s defense capabilities, which were “unimaginable even a short time ago,” he said. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, appearing on stage with Cairncross, pointed out that Russia’s hacking capabilities have improved along with AI in the last year. Michal said the country’s ultra-wired government has been increasingly under attack, blaming private actors, as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran. When asked whether cyber attacks could be considered acts of war, Michal said he believes some could rise to the NATO definition of “attack” covered by the alliance’s Article 5. “It’s mainly a question about the consequences,” he said. — Laura McGann

events.title: Bloom Energy sees 'nothing but a huge opportunity' amid AI headwinds
events.summary: The CEO of fuel cell maker Bloom Energy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he’s not worried about rising natural gas prices or political pushback to data centers, as the economy-wide scramble for electrons marks an “architectural shift” for the grid that will favor onsite power production. Bloom, whose gas-fueled mini power plants are used by data centers, hospitals, retailers, and other big power consumers, has faced some headwinds recently: Its share price is down 20% in the past month thanks in part to economy-wide jitters about the pace of the AI buildout, and its flagship data center project in New Mexico has been held up by permitting issues . Still, CEO KR Sridhar said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, “I see nothing but a huge opportunity.” Power use continues to surge across the economy, and if the price of natural gas — Bloom’s crucial input — rises because of increased demand or trade disruptions like the war in Iran, “our value proposition gets even better,” Sridhar told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport, as the technology can operate more efficiently than conventional gas turbines. Bloom is on a steep growth trajectory: Its net profit hit $250 million in the third quarter, up from a $23 million loss in the same period last year. The company is expanding its manufacturing base, and targeting projects in the Middle East and elsewhere, Sridhar said. Though he is eyeing projects abroad, the company will continue to invest in the US. “We should not cede this opportunity to any other country, but from our perspective, we will be happy to sell our power to neighboring countries,” he said. “Nothing is NIMBY-proof,” he said, of backlash to data centers in the US. Still, “AI happens to be a catalyst pushing everything to the right very steeply.” — Tim McDonnell

events.title: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
events.summary: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations. The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities. US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers. No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import. Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers. Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators. “Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.” He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.” “Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.” Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China. It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub. Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers. Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.” Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ® UDPATED AT 05:45 UTC, November 17 to add news that late on Monday the US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Megaspeed. In the announcement, the two departments detail investigative activities they conducted across 2024 and 2025, including a June meeting with Alice Huang in Singapore, and state those details "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." Singaporean authorities have also said that meeting took place, but say they asked asked US counterparts for help with their own investigations and received frustratingly little support. Singapore also investigated Supermicro's possible role at Megapseed, and complained that the server-maker didn't co-operate either. Supermicro today told The Register it " does not conduct business with these entities" and operates a "robust compliance program." "We are committed to complying with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws and regulations, and we require our distributors and resellers to do the same," according to a Supermicro statement sent to The Register .

events.title: Democrats dig in for grueling leadership fight
events.summary: The News Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mimed a coin flip on Monday night when asked if he’ll support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer over his insurgent opponent, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. It was a joke — but one that also showed how Democrats are wrestling with the decision. “Leave it to the Democrats. We flip nine seats and the person who actually helps put it together and do all that, all of a sudden there’s a revolt,” Hickenlooper said. He quickly made clear he didn’t mean that as a Schumer endorsement: “I haven’t picked a position. I do think it’s useful to go and look at: How could the caucus be better?” If the first few days of the leadership race are any indication, it’s going to be a very long two weeks for Senate Democrats. Several declined to comment on Monday night after days of celebrating their big election wins, with one senator saying Schumer’s challenge is all reporters have been asking about. But that’s because it’s such an unusual moment for the party: The vast majority of sitting Senate Democrats have never experienced a contested leadership race for the top job. And Van Hollen’s rebel campaign isn’t following crushing losses, but instead a historic victory. “No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anyone else in the caucus and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. “The voters are also demanding change.” Kaine, who will chair the Budget Committee next year, also declined to publicly come out for or against Schumer. Van Hollen’s pitch for change Van Hollen is not exactly an obvious change agent: He previously chaired the party’s campaign arms in both the House and Senate and has been in elected office since 1991. But he is seeking to draw bright contrasts with Schumer, pushing for a prohibition in the next spending bill on offensive weapons for the Iran war and highlighting Schumer’s opposition to the Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. And while Schumer has several times the public support of Van Hollen, most of the incoming 56 Democratic Caucus members next year have declined to publicly endorse either one. Van Hollen said he knows “for a fact” some public reporting about senators’ support for Schumer is not true: “Some are voting for me and others are undecided on that list.” “People are still listening. They’re very interested in having a debate,” Van Hollen said on Monday evening. One of his supporters, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he thinks the Maryland Democrat has a real chance to defeat Schumer. Most Democrats still see Schumer as the heavy favorite given the election results, however. Still, a number of other longtime Democratic senators who know Schumer well are keeping their powder dry. Asked about the race, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said only that he’s “laser-focused” on his agenda next year leading the Finance Committee and pushing Medicare for All, a billionaire’s income tax, and repealing tariffs. “Everybody deserves to be heard and then our caucus will make a decision,” said Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who will chair the Appropriations Committee. “I have not declared anything,” The next leader will decide when Murray or Wyden’s legislation will come to the Senate floor over the next two years — giving them incentive to stay neutral. And many Democrats are still digesting how to handle a secret ballot election that comes after the party’s most commanding win since Barack Obama became president. “Every candidate should make their pitch. And I’ll hear out any candidate for leader,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who obliterated his opponent in his reelection bid. “I’m grateful to everyone for their efforts, including Leader Schumer.” Schumer has served as Democratic leader for a decade, during which time the party’s activist base has soured on him; he’s also the architect of multiple Democratic majorities and made the most of a 50-seat Democratic majority during the first two years of Joe Biden’s presidency. But no leader hangs on forever: both former Democratic Leader Harry Reid and former Republican Leader Mitch McConnell lost a handful of votes in their last leadership races, before stepping down from the job. Schumer’s given no indication he would do that, but he’s up for reelection in 2028 and has a big decision ahead of him. And Van Hollen knows it. “That’s a decision for him,” he said of Schumer’s 2028 plans. Room for Disagreement Some Democrats said it’s healthy to have this debate after more than three decades without a real contested battle for the leadership race. “We’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats,” Kaine said. “We like democracy.” “It just comes with the territory,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. Burgess’s view Van Hollen’s leadership challenge to Schumer has made things very awkward for Senate Democrats. The contest will supercharge the debate about the party’s agenda in 2027 as well as how they handle the lame duck. And regardless of the outcome, it’ll have long term consequences for the usually tight-knit caucus. Notable Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer but not by an overwhelming margin , according to polling from Data for Progress.

events.title: 'Unfair and unjust': Anger from David Jones suppliers as debt revealed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million, administrators confirm David Jones creditors have been updated. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) The first David Jones creditors meeting has revealed the company has almost half a billion dollars in debt. Suppliers left unsure if they would ever have their debts paid. The second creditors meeting is expected to be held in March 2027. David Jones is deeply in debt, with its liabilities revealed so far reaching almost half a billion dollars. The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. 6,242 employees: Estimated claims of $11 million including annual leave, long service leave and potential redundancy payments Secured creditors Hilco: Estimated claim of $155 million and ACP estimated claims of $80 million 940 unsecured creditors: Estimated claims of $180 million 802,319 gift cards: Estimated claims of $33 million The debts were revealed at the almost two-hour first creditors meeting for the embattled department store, which was placed into voluntary administration earlier this month. It has already been announced that the receiver will close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores by the end of 2027 . Administrators are now trying to find a buyer for David Jones to keep the legacy brand alive. McGrathNicol's role as voluntary administrator is to tally the company's debts and possibly find a buyer to recoup cash for entities owed money, such as suppliers and landlords. The retailer's key secured lender, Hilco, will be first in line to claw back money. It has appointed a receiver, FTI Consulting, to David Jones and now controls its day-to-day operations. The 188-year-old department store's collapse came after negotiations broke down with Scentre Group, the owner of key shopping centre chain Westfield, which confirmed David Jones was behind on its rent since September. David Jones has more than 1,000 suppliers. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) A long list of woes is blamed for David Jones's collapse, including difficult trading as the cost of living bites, competition from online retail, and an "unsustainable" business model, McGrathNicol said. The meeting, attended by just under 500 people, heard from suppliers of everything from clothing to truffles, with anxious brand owners asking questions about when, if ever, they would see debts paid. "It has become pretty apparent to others in the market that some suppliers, specifically the larger ones, were given preferential treatment," one supplier told the meeting. Store suppliers have told ABC News they have been struggling to get invoices paid for months. Some are owed more than $100,000. David Jones has more than 1,000 suppliers, 6,000 employees and a similar number of concession staff, all impacted by the collapse. The main retail union, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employee's Association (SDA) confirmed after the meeting that 1,689 direct jobs were on the line and only 170 positions have been offered redeployment. NSW branch secretary Bernie Smith said the union expected further job losses from staff employed by concessions, but did not have exact numbers. Unsecured creditors, which include suppliers, are lower on the list to be repaid, behind employees and secured creditors Hilco, Anchorage Capital Partners (ACP) and Commonwealth Bank. David Jones is due to close half of its stores. ( ABC News ) One supplier asked if for a possible range of how much they might receive to the dollar, which McGrathNicol administrator Matthew Hutton said it was too soon to know the value or an exact timeline. He said there were "too many variables", including not having engaged with enough bidders to know the value, pre-Christmas trade and the upcoming store closures, adding they might not know the potential return to creditors until mid to late January. Brands that have been selling stock in David Jones stores within their own sub-leases under concession arrangements, also asked about whether they would see sales revenue repaid. "If David Jones was to go into liquidation can partners take their stock back prior to the company being liquidated?" asked one brand owner, with McGrathNicol confirming this was the case. Administrators also confirmed some brands had pulled out of David Jones since the administration, but this was "limited" and the receivers now controlling the stores were experiencing record sales. Several suppliers expressed frustration with a lack of correspondence from FTI regarding stock levels and sales since November 5. Julie Mathers left the meeting frustrated.

events.title: AI leaders helping drive ‘unnaturally negative’ narrative, Palo Alto Networks CEO says
events.summary: The leaders of the world’s most advanced AI companies are helping drive an “unnaturally negative” narrative around the technology, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. In an interview with MIT Technology Review’s Mat Honan, Arora argued that the focus on AI’s risks is overshadowing its potential benefits of the fast-moving technology. “I find it strange that sometimes the leaders of frontier [large language models] want to come up here and talk about the dark side of AI. Every technology has a dark side,” Arora said at the event, adding that the negative narrative has “been driven by some of the people who should be espousing the benefits.” Arora described AI as a “transformational technology” with “the potential of uplifting a huge amount of humanity” and “democratiz[ing] intelligence.” “A villager sitting in India or anywhere in the world will have the ability to not just read 10 websites, but have them summarized and have the best intelligence available to them,” he said. Arora also challenged concerns that growing domestic resistance to data center construction could slow innovation, arguing that constraints on computing capacity would instead accelerate efforts to make the technology more efficient. “Scarcity breeds innovation,” Arora said. “If you say there’s only so many data centers that can be built, think about the amount of companies that are going to come back and say, wait, I’ve got this compression technology which makes tokens more efficient.” But Arora also acknowledged that AI’s growing capabilities are inevitably intensifying cybersecurity risks by making it easier to uncover vulnerabilities in software. “All the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans, is now going to be found out,” he said, warning that as more vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited, the higher the risk of systems being forced offline as companies scramble to patch longstanding weaknesses. “I don’t think there’s a panacea. I don’t think there’s a quick solve. I just think we’re gonna power through all of these and grind ourselves through them,” he said. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
events.summary: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October. A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals. The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in. But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation. "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal. "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year." "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it. Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress. But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda. "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios. "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added. "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

events.title: AI agents still act like ‘Day 1 employees,’ Glean CEO says
events.summary: AI agents are nowhere near having the “context” to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday. “When you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,” Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “That’s the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.” Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said “nobody’s anywhere close” to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring “tacit knowledge” and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that “Day 1 employee” problem. Despite AI’s limitations, Jain also said companies are under “enormous pressure” to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines. “Sometimes businesses didn’t get time to actually set the right foundation” before rolling out AI tools, Jain said. Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining “10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: United Airlines, major US banks report system outages
events.summary: Customers of major US banks reported difficulty accessing their accounts Monday, as United Airlines also reported a widespread system outage, elevating concerns about the durability of US digital infrastructure days after a tech failure grounded commercial flights nationwide. United said later on Monday that it was able to quickly resolve the outage, which the airline clarified was not “a cybersecurity-related issue.” A JPMorgan Chase spokesperson told the Associated Press that its own problem resulted from a “ temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system” and was “not cyber-related.” The reports come as widespread integration of AI into digital architecture exposes new cyber vulnerabilities, and as experts and government agencies warn of adversarial governments and non-state actors seeking to exploit those vulnerabilities. Asked about the disruptions Monday, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Anthropic’s Mythos announcement was “the inflection point at which it’s become apparent that all the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans is now going to be found out.” “You’re going to see more of this, unfortunately, for the next few years,” Arora added. “I don’t think there’s a panacea… I think we’re just going to grind ourselves through it.” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
events.summary: The Pullman family, on the left, and the Wilcox family, bought a home together soon after meeting When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith. They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together. Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in. "We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector. With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best. That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family. They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children. In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m. The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs. Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars". Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosai says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices. Gosai is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger. It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says. It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche". "I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don't know." The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out. While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer. "If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth. Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says. Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people. While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income. She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home." They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements. "It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says. Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out. For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share. Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says. Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

events.title: Reducing High-Bandwidth Flash Latency In GPU Systems (Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Georgia Tech, NVIDIA Research , and Stanford University published “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” “Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20 μ s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).” Find the technical paper here . November 2026. Saxena, Anish, Hritvik Taneja, Christos Kozyrakis, and Aamer Jaleel. “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2611.14776 (2026). events.title: California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models. The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision. "While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," said Attorney General Bonta. At a press conference , Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public." The legal salvo comes after Bonta in September sent OpenAI a letter seeking information about these agentic attacks. According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena. In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims. Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public. Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions , suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds. The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry. At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation. "Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety issues, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind." AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains in certain areas like coding, albeit at an unknown cost to future job markets. But as AI boosters insist, miracle drugs and endless vacations aren't far off … perhaps along with existential crises. Katharine Trendacosta, director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told The Register in an email that the EFF is glad to see state officials taking action against AI companies taking unreasonable risks with public safety. "Several recent cybersecurity incidents at AI labs could have been prevented or substantially mitigated by adhering to longstanding cybersecurity best practices, such as proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging," said Trendacosta. "AI agents can be useful tools when deployed appropriately, with adequate safeguards designed to mitigate the risks. Companies should carefully consider the risks of every use case, including the consequences, reversibility, and sensitivity of any action an agent is used for." ®

events.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
events.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes. Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop . What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer. "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com . Thanks for bearing with us!" The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem. United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights." "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said. About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website. United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

events.summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her. Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González , which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years. Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General. In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana. Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed. Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000. Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her. Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down. events.title: ‘America needs to have more Jensens’: Perplexity CEO lauds Huang as industry titan
events.summary: Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas on Monday said the US needs more entrepreneurial tech CEOs like former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an interview at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “He’s one of the greatest founders in American history,” Srinivas told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “America needs to have more Jensens.” Tech CEOs and entrepreneurs have long lauded the former CEO of the world’s biggest chipmaker as the epitome of the American dream; Huang started the company in a Denny’s restaurant. But revelations of the former CEO’s extramarital affairs have sullied his reputation. Huang resigned as CEO last week. Srinivas said that Huang’s advice to him as a young founder was to act like he was going to run out of business in six to 12 months. “He would run the company like as if he would run out of business in the next 30 days,” he recalled. “So that attitude that relentlessness, grit, determination, always wanting to push the frontier is the spirit that every American founder should take.” Despite praising Huang, Srinivas dodged a question on whether Nvidia’s board should reinstate him as the company’s head amid reports Huang was eyeing a comeback. Srinivas also announced onstage that Perplexity just crossed a $1 billion annual run rate on Monday, while maintaining a burn rate that he said is five times lower than that of hyperscalers. He attributed this to the startup’s capital-efficient model. Unlike frontier labs, Perplexity is primarily a model aggregator, routing users to other AI models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude instead of operating a flagship foundational model. The company is built on the idea that users don’t care which model they’re using. “They really care if the work actually got done,” Srinivas said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards. In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems. Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab". Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks. But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state. Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack? Published 25 July OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies Published 29 July Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment. The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks. Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe. "The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday. OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office. "We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said. The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents. Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about". "OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said. events.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
events.summary: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . See notice regarding software product information. events.title: AI makes everyone more vulnerable, AT&T CEO says
events.summary: Everybody is more vulnerable because of AI, at least for now, AT&T CEO John Stankey said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Stankey believes that can be turned around to make things safer, but it will take some time to figure out “how to turn that technology into advantage rather than liability.” Stankey said he is by no means a “doomer” when it comes to AI, but it’s hard for anyone to know what the true full effect of these AI models will be. He added that “anxiety levels are pretty high right now” because of the added cybersecurity risks brought on by artificial intelligence. While there’s been a lot of concern around data centers and the public reaction to them, Stankey urged consideration of the downstream effects. If “a metropolitan area doesn’t have power for a period of time, or we start seeing cell phones drop from the network,” Stankey said. “We’ve got to make sure we’re doing the right things to prevent that from happening.” We can’t have “technology for technology’s sake,” he said. “If the public loses trust, if an economy is interrupted, and it can’t transact business in the way it should transact business and grow, then we’ve got technology that is built on a bad foundation.” He added that additional government regulation may not be the answer, but urged his peers to think about the fundamental needs and pacing as the environment continues to evolve. Data sovereignty was also a major concern for Stankey, adding that the notion that “my data isn’t my data” is very important. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Replit CEO calls Huang’s ouster ‘attack’ on open models
events.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia’s CEO “an attack on open models” at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. “Jensen is the premier champion of open models,” Masad told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami. “If it wasn’t for Jensen, there wouldn’t be a lot of funding going into US open model companies like Reflection and others.” Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Masad, who founded Replit, an AI app and website-building company, has championed the push to reinstate Huang. When a friend told him about a petition on Replit calling for the fallen CEO’s return, “I literally jumped in and did tech support for them,” Masad said. Huang has been “a great voice on pushing back on the narrative that we need to lock down AI, that the only safe AI is a closed AI,” Masad said. He added that not having Huang at Nvidia would be a “huge loss” and “potentially bring about a world where there’s only the frontier model labs that exist.” Software engineering careers ‘an accident of history’ When asked about the future of tech jobs, Masad said on Monday, “The modern career of software engineer is a bit of an accident of history.” Now, many of his customers have zero software engineers on staff. “I used to get attacked a lot for saying that, but now everyone agrees with me,” Masad said. Ben Lamm, the CEO of the biotech and genetic engineering de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences, agreed, saying, “We’re doing what we used to do with 80 engineers with, like, five.” And Edwin Chen, the founder and CEO of AI-training platform Surge AI, said that his headcount will likely remain stable. “If you look at the latest models, they’re not just writing code anymore. They’re often coming with ideas on their own,” Chen said. “They’re helping our engineers understand certain kinds of security risks or architectural trade-offs.” All this, Chen said, means he doesn’t see a need to hire product managers or expand headcount dramatically. Masad said he still foresees hiring entry-level employees, in part because in the agentic era, people’s jobs are changing every three to six months. “You need people who are willing to continue relearning their job,” he said. “And I think, you know, just because of brain plasticity, younger people are actually pretty good at that.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
events.summary: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register . According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

events.title: China's rare earth curbs put new emphasis on Latin American investment
events.summary: Latin America is seeking to become a viable destination for investment in critical minerals , as western governments seek alternative supplies to reduce dependency on Chinese imports. China is the dominant player in the global critical minerals supply chain. It holds a market share of 70 per cent or greater for 19 of 20 minerals listed as strategically important by the International Energy Agency, and accounts for about 90 per cent of global rare-earth processing. China imposed sweeping export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements in April 2025, before increasing that list in October. The IEA estimates those controls would cost $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China if fully introduced. Beijing last week announced it was extending a pause on the curbs until January. "I think we're learning the hard way that we need to be more competitive in these environments," said Andrew Wilson, executive director at the Centre for International Private Enterprise. Mr Wilson spoke to The National on the sidelines of a critical minerals summit in Washington. Latin America and the Caribbean hold 38.3 per cent of global lithium reserves and 32.5 per cent of copper reserves, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Experts argue this places Latin America as a key centre in supply diversification, with lithium demand expected to triple by 2040. The region also holds major shares of silver and graphite, well as other metals and speciality minerals used for advanced technologies, aerospace and defence. Foreign direct investment in the region is volatile, despite averaging 11 per cent in recent decades, according to the OECD. "The question is, how do we regain those markets, regain the security guarantees, the economic guarantees, without sacrificing standards, compliance, rule of law and otherwise?" Mr Wilson asked. "It's important for us to be pushing countries where we want to invest to up their game through our own leadership, our own corporate requirements, than it is to lose those opportunities to investors who cornered the market. But the region faces challenges including high financing costs, infrastructure gaps, skill constraints and trust with local stakeholders, according to the IEA's 2026 global critical minerals outlook. It only refines about 20 per cent of its mined output of key energy minerals, except for lithium. The IEA estimates if lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths were refined locally and two-thirds of copper production were processed in the region, the economic value generated would increase by nearly 50 per cent from current levels and reach bout $220 billion by 2035, the IEA said. Gulf states are also been deepening their investment ties into the Americas. Abu Dhabi's ADQ and US-based investment firm Orion Resource Partners in January announced a joint venture to invest in companies in Latin America, Africa and Asia. US President Donald Trump 's administration also entered into bilateral preliminary agreements with Argentina and Peru in February. The UAE and Brazil signed a $2.5 billion preliminary agreement last year to explore and develop strategic minerals essential for the global energy transition. Brazil released a list of 27 critical and strategic minerals last week in an effort to boost investment and increase domestic processing. Copper, lithium, uranium and rare earths were among metals listed as a top priority for government support. The UAE and Argentina also began talks on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to increase investment access across mining and minerals, AI and other sectors. Saudi Arabia also signed non-binding agreements with Brazil and Chile during the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh this year, as the kingdom looks to expand its international partnerships and investment co-operation in the mining and minerals sector.

events.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
events.summary: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect." events.title: Advocates dub midterms the ‘care election’
events.summary: This month’s midterms were the “care election,” according to a sweeping new report by Care Can’t Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor . The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout — citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach — as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care. “There’s this undeniable sense of momentum,” leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is “looking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.” Seven in 10 voters said it’s important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action. Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government “immediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,” including by tackling child care. Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 95% of Democrats and 69% of men. “Democrats won on these issues, and now they need to take action within the first 100 days of this new Congress,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, told Semafor. She called for lawmakers to “put them on the president’s desk, and then force him to decide whether he wants to veto.” GOP cuts to Medicaid funding helped mobilize “many first-time care-worker activists,” SEIU Executive Vice President Leslie Frane said. Advocates are hopeful the Trump administration agrees to repeal some of those cuts — but they’re not holding their breath on other issues. “When the time comes to be smart about making choices and tradeoffs, we will. But I think we’re really far from that time,” Poo said. “So this is a moment where we have the momentum to do big things, and there’s no reason why we should not.” Democrats had tried to enact paid leave and universal pre-K amid the pandemic , but fell short given their narrow Senate majority. Advocates are now optimistic that the latest wave of policymakers will see more success. “We have a whole crop of new leaders coming in with a clear mandate on these policies — and that was intentional,” Poo said. “That was a big lesson from Build Back Better, is that we need a whole different level of consensus.”
