events.title: Center-left previews 2028 in Denver
events.summary: The News DENVER — The race for the next Democratic presidential nomination has begun, with a festival of agreement. There was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, telling the What’s Next conference that voters demanded action, not “shallow litmus tests or where we fall on some political spectrum. ” There was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, explaining that voters did not want “marginal change” and Democrats weren’t in a battle of “progressive versus moderate .” And there was Pete Buttigieg, who’d noticed the Democrats borrowing his formula. They wanted to pass cost-cutting, pro-family bills with their new majority, then convince voters that they would never go back to pre-Trump neoliberalism. “It sounds good. It’s easy to say,” said Buttigieg. “Everybody thinks they already agree with this.” The post-midterms conference, organized by Majority Democrats, was a payoff of a two-year investment by moderate donors. Two years before strategists and elected officials landed in Denver and grabbed their lanyards, the venture capitalist Seth London circulated a memo about how new candidate and media investments could steer the party away from “race and group-based identity politics,” and toward “prosperity for more Americans.” This year’s Democratic landslide carried along every kind of candidate —the ones plugged into the Majority Democrats network, and the ones who worried it was a big-money ploy to defeat the populist left. But the conference elevated the candidates who wanted to build a supermajority, battling big tech and environmental attorneys. Some donors were in; the donors who wanted them to move left were out. “Tell us which ideas you’ll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or didn’t work,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, the pedigreed Massachusetts Democrat who chairs the Majority Democrats PAC. “Tell us which privileges you’ll confront, even if your donors or allies object.” Celebrating the center The donors did know how to throw a party. What’s Next resembled the sort of well-funded, media-friendly conferences that many Democrats have envied on the right, like the multi-day “AmericaFest” put on by Turning Point Action. This was a party for the Democratic mainstream, the staffers most likely to work for center-left presidential candidates than for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY. For two days, blocks of Denver’s River North Art District were cordoned off for Democrats, the people who elected them, and the reporters asking if they were running for president. (Their answers were variations on “not yet.“) There was conflict, but it was largely limited to the argument over who should lead Democrats’ new congressional majorities. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who announced his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Thursday, paused for 10 seconds of applause when he took the stage and explained why he was running. “Candidates from different backgrounds and different parts of our party – they ran on a strikingly similar platform,” said Van Hollen. “They didn’t run on the tired Washington labels of progressive versus moderate. They ran on an economic populist message, on a commitment to fight for working people and take on a rigged economic and political system.” Many of those winners showed up in Denver, like Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. They shared road stories of how they listened to Republican concerns, and would work with the willing ones to lower prices. But it was implied that Democrats should focus on building homes, lowering bills, and expanding health care before they did anything else. Not every attendee agreed. “The organizers here want a big tent, one big enough to even invite anti-establishment voices like me,” said Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Ca., who Democrats see as a competitor for a Sen. Bernie Sanders lane in the primary. “A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.“Apart from Khanna, the likely presidential candidates didn’t quite do that. Mallory McMorrow, who Majority Democrats supported in her unsuccessful U.S. Senate bid in Michigan, told Semafor that her party had just shown that it could have a loud primary argument and then unite on the basics. “It’s anti-corruption, getting money out of politics, protecting democracy, ending wars,” said McMorrow. “The disagreements are around the edges.” David’s view There will be many Democratic “cattle calls,” but I am focusing on how What’s Next was built because it’s the fruit of a two-year effort to ensure that the 2028 primary plays out differently than the 2020 primary. There is widespread agreement among Democratic strategists that their last open primary was defined by left-wing organizations that wanted candidates to commit to their ideas, eyeball to eyeball, on camera. That meant forums organized by groups like Planned Parenthood and MoveOn, and more progressive labor unions like SEIU. That meant the ACLU asking candidates if they would commit to cutting the federal prison population in half, and Movimiento Cosecha bird-dogging Joe Biden at his own events until he committed to stopping most deportations.If the left sees Majority Democrats as an effort to swipe their strongest messaging and junk the rest, they’re right. The economic populism in Denver was more sincere than they might think, but it is against degrowth and for permitting reform; skeptical of single-payer health care, but for incremental steps to “universal” health care; basically, right in the sweet spot of the Democrats’ congressional caucuses. Right now the Schumer-Van Hollen contest is where the fights over ideology and priorities are happening. The 2028 candidates would prefer to agree, for now. Room for Disagreement The left was not letting the rest of the party adopt its ideas without a fight. In the run-up to What’s Next, reporters from three left-leaning outlets that had been critical of Majority Democrats – The Lever, The Intercept, and The American Prospect – announced that they’d been denied access. All were eventually allowed in, becoming a First Amendment nuisance for donors who didn’t want to interrupt happy hours with hard questions. And on Friday, four protesters accessed the Mission Ballroom to interrupt the most powerful Democrat at the conference, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. As liberal pundit Jessica Tarlov asked the likely House Speaker about his agenda, they jumped up, one after another, accusing him of complicity in genocide. A protester with Climate Defiance, pushing back at the bouncers who dragged him out, turned to the stadium seating reserved for reporters and shouted “f— you all!“Nicole Shea Niebler, a 31-year-old organizer with the Sunrise Movement in Denver, said that she interrupted Jeffries because “the conference made it pretty clear that strong progressives are not invited to participate at the scale that centrists were.” That limited the bounds of debate in a room where media taste-makers were starting

events.title: Under pressure, Lutnick joins Trump in China
events.summary: Howard Lutnick is expected to travel on Air Force One with the president to China this week as the commerce secretary fights to regain his footing after clashing with Trump officials over Nvidia and China chip controls, according to people familiar with the matter. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Lutnick has become the target of Washington finger-pointing for slow-walking Commerce Department restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, as well as his close relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia customer suspected of being a Chinese spy, and media reports of two affairs with subordinates. The woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, which the US is investigating for improper chip smuggling into China. Republicans are accusing Lutnick of defying Trump — and warning his job could be on the line — after reports emerged that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had pushed the commerce secretary to place the Nvidia customer, Megaspeed, on a blacklist of companies that pose national security concerns. Treasury “has been pushing for this for months” but Commerce “has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC last week. Bessent, who has directly criticized Lutnick’s handling of the matter, is also expected on the trip. A senior US official told reporters ahead of the China trip that the Nvidia scandal “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the official said. ‘Nine lives’ They have accused Lutnick of allowing the chipmaker to indirectly sell more advanced chips to China than previously known or allowed under US export control laws, through loopholes he has so far declined to close. He’s also been criticized for giving Nvidia unfettered access to rule-making that would impact the entire industry. The White House has said it “maintains complete confidence in the secretary.” Lutnick had been expected to attend Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World convening this week alongside OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Amazon’s Andy Jassy, and hundreds of other CEOs, but will instead be with the president. And while plans could still change, Lutnick’s inclusion in the trip signals that Trump wants to keep Lutnick around long enough to at least accompany the president to China for his visit with Xi. “This guy has nine lives,” a person close to the White House previously told Semafor. “How many does he have left?”

events.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO. Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth. The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market. Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans. Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance." "This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said. For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks. The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others. In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports. As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports. What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

events.title: Trump's border crackdown faces a new blue wall of governors and House members
events.summary: Voters have handed Democrats every House district touching Mexico and all four border-state governorships. Why it matters: Starting next year, the sweep gives Democrats new leverage over state resources, border spending and legal challenges during President Trump's final two years. By the numbers: Democrats last held all four governorships — California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas — in January 1979, according to National Governors Association records . 10 for 10: Democrats swept all 10 House districts touching Mexico for the first time since 2008, according to an Associated Press analysis . Three flips: JoAnna Mendoza ousted Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona. Bobby Pulido and Katy Padilla Stout flipped Republican-held seats in Texas. Four attorneys general: Democrats also won the top legal offices in all four border states, including Texas , where the party hadn't won an attorney general race since 1994. State of play: Trump built his immigration crackdown around the southern border. He declared a national emergency on his first day back, expanded the military's role and border barriers, and launched a sweeping deportation campaign. Southwest border apprehensions dropped roughly 91% in the 12 months through August compared with Biden's final 12 months, according to FactCheck.org's October analysis . The crackdown has also reached further into American communities, with ICE arrests surging during the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott could bring the most immediate border changes. Abbott spent about $11 billion on Operation Lone Star, deploying state police and National Guard troops and building Rio Grande barriers, according to the Texas Tribune . Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect, has questioned that spending. She can rethink state deployments and enforcement priorities, though existing laws and federal authority limit her options. Democrats also flipped the Texas House and elected a Democratic attorney general, giving Hinojosa allies in funding and legal battles. Republicans retained the state Senate. The intrigue: Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed more than 20 lawsuits against Democratic immigration policies and defended Gov. Greg Abbott's border crackdown. His Democratic successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed to challenge unconstitutional federal border tactics — potentially turning the office from a powerful Trump ally into an adversary. What we're watching: Several Democrats newly elected to represent border districts in Washington campaigned on both strong border security and pathways to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants. Bobby Pulido, who flipped a Texas GOP-held seat, said in his launch video : "Yes, we have to get the criminals out and secure the border. But we can do that without destroying families and our South Texas economy." He also told the Texas Tribune that one of his congressional priorities will be codifying a pathway to citizenship. JoAnna Mendoza, who flipped an Arizona seat, also backs a strong border and legal pathways to citizenship. That aligns with many border voters' views: An October N+ Univision/YouGov survey found 56% of Texas Hispanic voters thought immigration enforcement had gone too far. Yet 62% wanted border security and a pathway to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants pursued together — suggesting Democrats can make gains without abandoning enforcement. Zoom out: Trump's tariffs and immigration crackdown have rattled businesses that depend on trade and shoppers from Mexico, giving Democratic governors another reason to challenge Washington. Laredo businesses report fewer customers, while merchants near San Diego's border crossings say tougher immigration enforcement has hurt foot traffic and hiring. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs pressed Washington over tariffs and trade uncertainty. Manufacturers near Santa Teresa, New Mexico, have put projects on hold amid tariff threats and uncertainty over trade rules.

events.title: Trump heads to Asia with hopes of shifting the momentum after midterm setbacks hurt him at home
events.summary: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, hoping to make some big attention-grabbing moves on the world stage after his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections , diminishing his standing at home. The Republican president is using the international trip to try to shift momentum, and he is poised to make a splash with a historic three-way meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. Trump has long boasted about leveraging his relationships with the leaders of two of America’s biggest global adversaries, though he has failed so far to achieve major breakthroughs with them. He first heads to the Philippines to meet on Tuesday with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. Trump will then go to China on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. There, he will have his third face-to-face meeting this year with Xi and see Putin, too. A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028. “I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell , a former deputy secretary of state in Democratic President Joe Biden's administration and chairman of The Asia Group, a consultancy. It's a pattern followed by some of Trump's predecessors. Democratic President Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate in 2014 to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. Republican President George W. Bush went to APEC in Vietnam after the GOP lost control of Congress in 2006, though the Iraq War hung over his travels. The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila as well as a host of commercial deals and will be the “guest of honor” at a leaders' dinner. In Shenzhen, he will focus on trade issues before the meeting with Xi and Putin. Trump is leaving as airlines struggled to get passengers onto flights after a nationwide ground stop on Friday led to thousands of flight cancellations. Trump and his officials have blamed their predecessors, a contractor and Congress for the problems. Trump is about to be bogged down at home in ways that may curb what he can do overseas. His tariffs and war with Iran proved to be poisonous with voters. Going forward, Trump's ability to threaten import taxes or military assaults — two of his major foreign policy tools — will be limited by Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill in the new year. Just last week, in a newfound vulnerability, his push to boost artificial intelligence was complicated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Huang had traveled with Trump on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on AI and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. But Trump does not plan to confront Xi on the issue, said administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president’s plans on a call with reporters. The officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip. Even though the administration is discussing ways to close loopholes and further prevent Chinese businesses from using advanced chips made by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, the officials said they do not expect the restrictions to cause retaliation by Beijing. Trump will be accompanied by Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is the world's wealthiest man and a frequent adviser to the president. Musk spent at least $445 million to try to help Republicans keep control of Congress, and Democrats are keen to investigate his ties to the administration. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Trump may find it easier to be in the company of foreign leaders than his own crumbling coalition at home. But his words and actions at the summits are now more likely to draw scrutiny in committee hearings when he returns to Washington. “We’re going to have a very close eye on it," said Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

events.title: UAE engineering firm Kent heads for record order book despite Iran war
events.summary: Kent, the Dubai-based energy engineering company owned by Saudi Arabia's Nesma & Partners , expects to end the year with a record order backlog as Gulf producers press ahead with major projects despite months of disruption caused by the Iran war. The company is on track to meet its revenue target of about $1.5 billion this year and deliver on earnings, chief executive John Gilley told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. The war involving the US, Israel and Iran, which began in late February, has disrupted energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged critical infrastructure across the Gulf. But it has also generated a wave of work for engineering contractors with a deep presence in the region, from repairing damaged plants to building export routes that avoid the strait. Rystad Energy estimates the cost of restoring energy infrastructure damaged in the conflict could reach $58 billion. Kent is helping energy producers in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE assess damage to plants after the attacks. While some repairs are relatively minor, others require extensive planning before operations can resume. "We're very proud of the fact that we'll probably hit budget this year at a time when supply chains have been massively disrupted," Mr Gilley said. Kent's order backlog was nearly $3 billion by the end of 2025, much of it concentrated in Gulf countries, and was expected to reach a record by December. Its contracts with Adnoc Gas are progressing, including a $1.1 billion deal to expand the Asab and Buhasa gas processing plants under Adnoc Gas's $5 billion Rich Gas Development project . Supply chain bottlenecks have slowed progress, but Kent still aims to deliver on schedule, Mr Gilley said. New urgency for bypass pipelines Gulf producers are accelerating projects that allow them to export crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco has started work to expand its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, while Adnoc is fast-tracking a new West-East pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Mr Gilley said he did not see a major change in strategy from oil companies, but the war has transformed how such projects are viewed. "In the past, when these types of projects, which really don't add any production, are talked about, they're always on a slow burn," he said. "Now the risk rating and the benefit for the project have increased exponentially, so they're much more likely to go ahead." Kent does not expect to significantly increase capital spending next year, relying instead on its 5,000 to 6,000 engineers worldwide, including teams across five offices in India. Iraq emerges as major market Iraq is becoming a "very, very large" market for Kent as international oil companies expand their involvement in the country's energy sector. The company has a major framework agreement with Basrah Gas Company, works with BP at the Rumaila oilfield and with China's Sinopec, and has secured a new contract with BP at Kirkuk. Mr Gilley expects ExxonMobil , and potentially Chevron, to return to Iraq, creating opportunities for contractors at major fields, including Majnoon. LNG a key growth area Mr Gilley expects liquefied natural gas to remain a major growth area over the next decade, and Kent is pursuing opportunities linked to Mozambique's LNG developments. However, volatile prices complicate the long-term supply agreements needed to finance projects costing billions of dollars, he said, and contractors rarely share in the upside when commodity prices rise. "When the prices of gas and oil reduce, our customers ask us to reduce our rates," he said. "But they never get us to increase our rates when they make such profits." Kent is also expanding into data centre engineering, advising operators on grid optimisation and renewable electricity supplies. Mr Gilley said the business was "absolutely flying". "The world is addicted to two things: energy and data," he added. "The problem with increased demand for data is the increased demand for power. As an offering, we can do both." Kent has reduced its carbon intensity by 43 per cent, exceeding a 30 per cent reduction target set for 2027, and aims to achieve net zero by 2040. That does not mean retreating from hydrocarbons, particularly in the Gulf, where production costs and emissions intensity are relatively low. "We'll continue to proudly produce fossil fuels," Mr Gilley said.

events.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
events.summary: Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant. Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates. By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute. Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet. That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said. Zoom in : For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat. For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value. An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity . A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction. Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings. Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself. About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom. If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message. "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added. Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline. "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios. Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter. Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions , which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days. Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops. It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil. Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance. The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

events.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
events.summary: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions . What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts. "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks." By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers. In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year. SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation . Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively. Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview. "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet." The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

events.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
events.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

events.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. events.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.  When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family. “Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.” Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground. “I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.” According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.” In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences. The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder. But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell. His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.  In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison. A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.  Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court. “During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”  As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said. Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital. “If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email. Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion. “Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.” Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.  “I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.  She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.
